As the Italian acknowledged when joining, he is in a "dream situation", inheriting a well-balanced squad with incredible talent and depth, built by Guardiola. "It provides the consistency I need to do my job effectively," he said.

The demands will therefore be the same as what were placed on Guardiola, without necessarily having the unique job security the Spaniard was afforded. Guardiola always managed on his own terms. Maresca has a strong bond with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, but won't necessarily get the same privilege.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports football journalist Laura Hunter says Enzo Maresca won't be afforded time to excel as Manchester City boss

How much time will players need to adapt?

In terms of style, it's not quite rinse and repeat but there are plenty of similarities between Maresca and Guardiola's preferred way of playing.

Both are rooted in possessing the ball, favouring control, and pressing aggressively. Maresca is arguably more expansive, though, wanting to stretch the pitch with wingers that play high and wide.

Image: Chelsea's stats in their only full season under Enzo Maresca

City's wingers have been coached more recently to play a style where they tuck inside and rotate to create central overloads. Most of the play revolves around Rodri, but it's fluid.

Watching City under Guardiola often meant seeing defenders step into midfield, midfielders become forwards, or even drop into full-back. Maresca's more rigid 4-2-3-1 structure will likely make for more traditional roles.

It also requires a high-functioning No 10 to link play. At Chelsea, that was Cole Palmer. Maresca has got Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki to choose between, should he wish to adopt the same setup here.

How is the squad shaping up?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom explains why Manchester City decided to sign Elliot Anderson for £116m, making him the most expensive British player in history

There has been a concerted effort over the past two or three transfer windows under Hugo Viana to lower the average age of the squad. It's dropped from 29 to just over 25, albeit a leadership void has appeared following the departures of Bernardo Silva and John Stones this summer - and Kevin de Bruyne before them.

Rodri and Ruben Dias are important, while last season saw City lean further into a leadership role for Erling Haaland. Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol are also experienced, stable figures, plus Mateo Kovacic. The spine of the team remains incredibly strong.

Business to date has been costly but smart. Elliot Anderson, signed for mega money from Nottingham Forest, has been bought to add robustness and future-proof midfield and young Jeremy Monga has been poached from Leicester.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With Rodri linked with a move away from Manchester City, Sky Sports News reporter Ben Ransom discusses whether Ayyoub Bouaddi could be brought in to replace the midfielder

The wish list also includes a right-back and a winger, while keeping tabs on Lille teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi, who excelled at the World Cup for Morocco. Arsenal are also admirers of him.

Depending on potential suitors meeting the club's valuation, outgoings might comprise a selection of: Savinho, Omar Marmoush, Nico Gonzalez, Jack Grealish, Tijjani Reijnders and Rico Lewis. Transfer activity is expected to accelerate now the World Cup has concluded.

What are Maresca's main challenges?

This is the first time since the Abu Dhabi takeover that the plan is uncertain. 10 years ago, all preparation went into building a club to lure Guardiola to the Premier League. That vision has been and gone, so where now?

City have forged a culture geared towards winning silverware, anything less is unlikely to be tolerated for a sustained period. Fans arrive at the Etihad expecting to be entertained, but above all, demanding to win. Balancing both is where Maresca's Chelsea failed.

The 46-year-old does have the benefit of not being the only managerial newbie at one of the top clubs, though, making for a changeable Premier League landscape as the natural order figures itself out. At City, that is being viewed as an opportunity to take advantage of.

Andoni Iraola at Liverpool, Xabi Alonso at Chelsea and, perhaps to a lesser extent, Michael Carrick at Man Utd, all hold question marks. This era of unknowns is fertile ground for anyone with ambition to make a mark. Very much sink or swim.

What about the 115 charges?

115 Premier League charges still cloud the club. Maresca will have to field difficult questions from the media over it.

Guardiola was the master of public-facing confrontation, having had to handle media glare at some of Europe's biggest clubs all his career. He knew the City press pack well and how to shut down any exchanges he wished not to speak on.

Maresca came under fire at Chelsea at times but mainly over football matters. How he handles this situation will likely impact his first 12 months - assuming a verdict is reached within that timeframe.

Maresca is due to give his first Man City press conference on Friday, July 24. You can follow everything that is said in our dedicated live blog here.

Sports.title: 'Fery can improve but that's exciting' - Henman optimistic as Brit eyes US Open run
Sports.content:
British No 1 Arthur Fery will head into the American hard-court swing with areas he can improve ahead of the US Open - but that's "exciting", says Tim Henman.

The wild card's surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals has injected a much-needed shot of positivity and given British fans a new name to follow in the Grand Slams - starting at the US Open in New York - live on Sky Sports Tennis from August 30.

The challenge for the 24-year-old now is to acclimatise to his new standing in the game and the loss of anonymity and the freedom that brings with it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arthur Fery reflects on his Wimbledon experience, his massive climb up the world rankings and the tournaments he's planning to play next

The 23-year-old, who has soared to 36 in the world from No 114, was the last player standing in what was an otherwise dismal tournament for the host nation, but he became only the fifth British man this century to reach the second week at the All England Club.

Fery has earned direct entry to a Masters event for the first time in Cincinnati - 13-23 August - before appearing at the Winston-Salem Open from 23-29 August ahead of his debut at Flushing Meadows.

Speaking at Royal Birkdale ahead of The Open, Henman called Fery's dream run at the All England Club "amazing" and "transformational for his career and his life".

The former British No 1 said: "He started the year at 185 in the world, qualified in Melbourne and then has continued to improve his ranking - then getting a wild card at Wimbledon ranked 114 and winning five matches getting to the semi-finals it was an incredible performance - and I think it also shows the fine margins between these top players.

"If you're in the top 250 in the world you're an extremely good player and on your day you've got a chance of beating anyone, so huge for him to be 36 in the world now getting to the other Grand Slams and Masters 1000, so he's got an opportunity to really plan his schedule moving forward."

Ombudsman's half-sister Syndicale makes her racecourse debut in Dunstall Park's Tips For Every Race At raceday-ready.com EBF Restricted Maiden Fillies' Stakes.

Karl Burke's filly, who is by Ten Sovereigns, will have all eyes upon her as she tackles the seven-furlong trip on the tapeta. The Spigot Lodge team have sent three two-year-olds into battle at the track thus far in 2026, with two emerging victorious.

The Cheveley Park-owned Consultation comes here off the back of a decent run at Yarmouth at the end of last month, which has worked out very nicely. Perfect Love - who was bought by the Basher Watts Syndicate for 30,000gns as a yearling - could attract attention. The daughter of Palace Pier will be ridden by Alistair Rawlinson for Mick Appleby, who is closing in on 200 career winners at Dunstall Park.

Horizon Dore and Zarraf lock horns in today's Listed Prix Hubert Baguenault de Puchesse at Vichy.

Sports.title: A pioneer and a superstar, Kevin Keegan’s achievements were extraordinary
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, is the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, was the star of Liverpool’s first European Cup-winning team, a messianic figure at Newcastle United as a player and coach, forging a team so memorable that Fifa’s president wrote to commend him, and was the captain and then manager of the England men’s national team. And yet, as Keegan would ruefully reflect, he will principally be remembered by many for an emotional outburst that precipitated Newcastle’s historic failure in a Premier League title race, a TV interview which presaged the coming era of the modern game.

Keegan’s “I’d love it” rant of April 1996, directed at Alex Ferguson, became a meme before the modern meaning of the word and social media even existed, repeatedly played on Sky Sports and becoming indelibly marked in the minds of multiple generations, many not even born when it occurred. It frequently tops polls as the most memorable moment in Premier League history and foreshadowed an era where digital clips and personality narratives would dominate football coverage.

There is a danger, however, of reducing Keegan’s life to a series of ever-more emotional explosions, of which there were many, such as his punch-up with Leeds United’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield. For that would obscure the extraordinary nature of his achievements and the fact he was arguably the most charismatic modern English footballer; more eloquent than David Beckham and Paul Gascoigne and more passionate than Bobby Moore. He had a rare gift for inspiring players and almost everyone who interacted with him at his best came away uplifted.

Still, Keegan’s meltdown on TV, where he took issue with Ferguson’s supposed “mind games” in suggesting Leeds players would go easy on Newcastle during a tight title run-in with Manchester United, became a defining moment. “Strangers shout ‘love it’ to me from car windows,” wrote Keegan in his autobiography. “Autograph hunters tell me they would ‘love it’ if I could sign their pieces of paper. When I go to charity events I am often asked to sign photographs showing me in that classic pose: headphones on, finger jabbing, blazing eyes. Those pictures tend to be auctioned for a lot more money than the ones where I am playing for England or any of my clubs.”

Keegan claimed to be relaxed about the characterisation, skewed though it was, perhaps because more than any English footballer before he had maximised football’s commercial and media opportunities and accepted the respective bouquets and brickbats that ensued. Even before that meltdown, he would be best remembered by many in the 1970s for his excruciating bike crash on Superstars, a TV show which pitted athletes from different sports against each other in unfamiliar disciplines. Sprawled across the cycle track, Keegan’s bare flesh was ripped red raw by the gravel. Most remember the drama but few recall that, showing characteristic pig-headed determination, he got back on the bike, bloodied and bandaged, for a rematch, which he won before winning the entire contest.

Keegan was born in Armthorpe, Doncaster, to Doris and Joe, a war veteran Durham miner who had migrated south in search of work at Markham colliery. His upbringing echoed Monty Python’s Yorkshiremen sketch, only his memories were authentic, a throwback to a different century. Their terrace house “had a detached outhouse where we washed. Our bath was an old zinc tub and the toilet was at the foot of the garden and we never had electricity until I was 10 and we moved into a council house in Balby.”

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan shares a joke with Alex Ferguson after the rollercoaster 1995-96 season. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan’s ascent to the peak of the game’s elite was unforeseen, few recognising his talent early on, most dismissing him as too small. He always credited Sister Mary Oliver, the nun who ran his Catholic primary school football team and who refereed with a crucifix around her neck, as being as important to him as a mentor as Bill Shankly was. “Kevin’s football must be encouraged,” she wrote in a school report, which gave him immense self-belief.

Doncaster Rovers rejected him and he started work at Peglers Brass Works at 16, playing for their football team but only in the reserves and also for a pub team on Sundays, where he fortuitously played against a Scunthorpe scout, Bob Nellis, who got him a trial at the struggling Third Division club. Keegan referred to himself as a “mongrel” and “weasel” and the “least-talented” Ballon d’Or winner, and despite impressing at Scunthorpe it was still a major shock when Shankly, the man he regarded as a second father and progenitor of his success, took him to Liverpool. Shankly told him: “You’re not just a great player – you’re one of the great players!” It seemed an unlikely boast but Keegan scored on his Liverpool debut and was never dropped thereafter. He would inherit from Shankly comparable motivational skills.

Quick Guide The Keegan years: from player to manager Show 1951 Kevin Keegan is born on 14 February in Armthorpe, near Doncaster. 1968 Begins playing career at Scunthorpe United. 1971 Signed by Bill Shankly for Liverpool at age of 20, initially as a midfielder. 1972 Makes England debut against Wales in November. 1973 Liverpool win the league; Keegan scores twice in Uefa Cup final win over Borussia Mönchengladbach. 1974 Scores twice as Liverpool beat Newcastle 3-0 in the FA Cup final. His first England goal comes against Wales. 1976 Liverpool win the league title and Keegan scores in each leg of Uefa Cup final win against Club Brugge. His celebrity is such he appears on the TV show Superstars, and famously crashes his bike during one of the races. 1977 Another league title for Liverpool, who also win their first European Cup, a 3-1 victory over Mönchengladbach. Keegan moves to Hamburg for £500,000, nearly double the German transfer record. 1978 Wins Ballon d’Or. 1979 Wins Ballon d’Or again as Hamburg secure their first German ‌championship title in 19 years, and first in the Bundesliga era. 1980 Captains England at Euros but they are knocked out in the group stage. Leaves Hamburg to join Southampton for two seasons. 1982 Transfers to Newcastle in the Second Division. Plays final match for England, after 63 caps (31 as captain) and 21 goals. 1984 Helps Newcastle secure promotion in his second season, then retires from playing. Across his club career, he scores 204 goals in 592 ‌appearances. 1992 Takes first coaching role as manager of struggling Newcastle in February. Danger of relegation to the Third Division is averted. 1993 Leads them to the First Division title and promotion to the Premier League in his first full season in charge. 1994 Newcastle finish third in Premier League. 1996 Newcastle finish second in the Premier League, ​despite leading for most ​of campaign – by 12 points at one stage. Season includes famous “I would love it if we beat them” comments when discussing rivals Manchester United on Sky Sports. 1997 Leaves Newcastle and takes over at Fulham for two seasons. 1999 Takes charge ​of England national ‌team in February. 2000 Coaches England at Euro 2000 where they beat Germany but still go out in the group stage. Resigns in ​October after a 1–0 loss to Germany in World Cup qualifying. 2001 Takes over at Manchester City. 2008 Returns to Newcastle but lasts eight months after tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley. Though reclusive, Keegan also had a streak of extrovertism, embracing every aspect of the game’s growing commercial opportunities, from his famous Brut advert to appearances on Top of the Pops, where his single Head Over Heels in Love reached the top 40. Though he enjoyed standing out, he admitted he would never have got away with his trademark bubble perm in the old-school Liverpool dressing room. His wife, Jean, whom he met on the waltzers at the Doncaster St Leger horse racing meeting when she was 16 and he was 19 and to whom he remained married for life, burst into fits of laughter when she first saw it. He had the last laugh, the hairstyle inspiring alarming copycat versions across the football world.

Keegan remained true to what he considered to be his working-class, mining roots, declaring himself a Labour man, annoyed that a staged photo of him feigning to kiss then prime minister Margaret Thatcher on the cheek was interpreted as support for economic policies which had ravaged heavy industry. He was more at home playing head tennis with a later PM, Tony Blair, to whom he was close enough to host at his home for dinner.

View image in fullscreen The then Newcastle manager Keegan chats to the Labour leader Tony Blair in the summer of 1996. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan inherited two mantles from Britain’s greatest players of the 1960s. As George Best, the original footballer sex symbol of the modern era, lapsed into alcoholism and increasing unreliability, Keegan became the more wholesome and dependable commercial face of the superstar footballer in Britain, inundated with deals. For England he effectively became Moore’s successor as captain but at a time when the national team was in decline from his predecessor’s World Cup-winning heights. For Keegan, as the sole outfield world-class player, it was a heavy burden to bear as they missed out on successive World Cup finals.

His first major tournament for his country was the ill-fated 1980 European Championship and his World Cup career amounted to 20 minutes in 1982, a campaign which was disrupted by a back injury and where “my only contribution was a dreadful miss against the host nation to send us home. That moment is probably the only moment of my England career that people remember now.” It would prove to be his last game for England at the age of just 31.

More notable features of Keegan’s England career were his courage in defying IRA death threats to play against Northern Ireland in Belfast, then walking out on the team when Don Revie dropped him shortly afterwards and being arbitrarily beaten up by Yugoslav custom officials prior to a game in Belgrade, a horrific and wholly underserved ordeal that sparked an international incident. His frustration was best summed up in a story he told about the great Dutch player Johnny Rep. Surveying an England team at Wembley in 1977, Rep turned to Keegan and said: “Kevvy, you have problems here: this is the worst England side I have seen.” The Netherlands won 2-0 and, as Keegan recalled, could have scored at will.

Keegan was a pioneering player, negotiating release clauses, unheard of at the time in England, at Liverpool and Hamburg, allowing him to leave if a club met a £500,000 fee, thereby controlling his moves. Leaving Liverpool at what was assumed to be their peak – he had just helped them win their first European Cup in 1977 – to join a team sixth in the Bundesliga was demonstrative of both Keegan’s single-mindedness and capacity to challenge himself. He also quadrupled his salary, reflecting the economic state of English football at the time.

View image in fullscreen Keegan with the ball at his feet for Hamburg in the 1977-78 Bundesliga season. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Hamburg was not an initial success. Jealous teammates held meetings to get him kicked out of the club and, according to Keegan, refused to pass to him. His nadir came at Christmas 1977 when, in a festive-season friendly, unhappy at his plight and frustrated with over-physical treatment from the Lübeck defender Erhard Press, Keegan punched him on the jaw and subsequently knocked him out, receiving an eight-week ban as punishment. Yet, a year later, he won his first Ballon d’Or and went on to lead Hamburg to their first Bundesliga title since 1960.

Keegan embraced Germany, learning the language and was nicknamed “Mighty Mouse”, a tribute to his astonishing strength given his diminutive size. His first daughter, Laura, was born there but his finale, a European Cup final that would have sealed Hamburg’s place in history, was a sad one, ending as it did in defeat to Nottingham Forest. Having won three league titles, two Uefa Cups, an FA Cup and European Cup at Liverpool, the Bundesliga title would be the last trophy Keegan ever won. He was just 29 years old.

Keegan made a typically unconventional choice in joining Southampton, a promising yet small-market team under a talented, persuasive manager in Lawrie McMenemy. Keegan propelled them to a top-six finish and qualification for Europe, but they faded to seventh in the second season and Keegan, disillusioned, made a decision that would define the second half of his professional life.

Newcastle were in one of their periodic financial and footballing crises and in the old Second Division when, with money from brewers Scottish & Newcastle, they persuaded him to join in 1982. His father’s links to the north-east and reverence for Newcastle players such as Jackie Milburn were an emotional pull on Keegan, but one that cost him his England career. The manager, Bobby Robson, didn’t feel it appropriate to pick a second-tier player for England and Keegan, still captain and by far the most iconic national team player, learned from the press he had been “dumped”. He felt “betrayed, hurt and humiliated”.

Crowds doubled at St James’ Park with Keegan’s arrival and Newcastle were promoted in Keegan’s second season, 1983-84, by which point he had already decided to quit playing at the age of 33. Typically impulsive, it was when Mark Lawrenson outsprinted Keegan to dispossess him during an FA Cup tie at Liverpool that he decided he would finish his career at the end of the season.

View image in fullscreen Keegan in action for England in May 1979. His international playing career ended in acrimonious fashion. Photograph: Peter Robinson/Empics Sport/PA

Keegan and family, which now included his second daughter, Sarah, born in 1982, decamped to his Marbella villa and, other than periodic business deals and discussions about a long-held dream to launch a Soccer Circus, he embraced retirement. Yet endless rounds of golf failed to satisfy. The family had moved back to his Hampshire home when Sir John Hall, a dynamic north-east businessman, called in 1992, begging Keegan to help Newcastle avoid relegation to the third tier and potential liquidation. Despite having watched no football for years, Keegan accepted. He threatened to quit after a few games but stayed to keep Newcastle up and promptly announced that he wanted to build a dynasty to rival Liverpool and challenge for the Premier League title.

Most considered that quixotic and yet Newcastle won promotion to the Premier League as champions and with judicious youthful signings such as Andy Cole and Rob Lee, and veteran players such as Peter Beardsley, they came third and sixth in the top flight. So great was his authority, Keegan could even placate angry fans on the steps of St James’ Park when the club sold Cole to Manchester United.

With that money the club signed David Ginola and Les Ferdinand and won nine of their first 10 games in 1995-96, often in thrilling fashion, establishing a seemingly unassailable 12-point lead by January. But a crucial defeat at home to Ferguson’s United in March 1996 and the Scot’s repeated use of psychological barbs seemed to weigh heavy on Keegan as his team’s form disintegrated. A dramatic yet debilitating 4-3 defeat at Liverpool led Sepp Blatter to write to Keegan but the sight of him slumped over advertising hoardings as Liverpool scored a last-minute winner suggested the toll was too much.

Keegan eventually cracked, denouncing Ferguson in his famous TV interview. “You can tell him now, we’re still fighting for this title and I’ll tell you, honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it!” United won the title with four points to spare.

View image in fullscreen Keegan (left) during a Fulham training session at Roehampton in 1999. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Keegan initially seemed determined to rebuild as the club signed Alan Shearer for a world-record £15m and they beat United 5-0 at St James’ Park that autumn, but Keegan quit soon after, outraged that a city banker preparing the club for flotation had issued him an ultimatum to sign a contract. Football’s new era seemed untethered from the idealistic foundational values imbued in him by Shankly.

Keegan seemed done with football until the now-disgraced Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used speculative talks about his much-vaunted Soccer Circus to persuade him to become chief operating officer and eventually manager of Fulham in the third tier. He almost seemed at his happiest as the club accelerated to promotion, but his time was interrupted by a national crisis when Glenn Hoddle was sacked as England manager for making offensive comments about disabled people. The clamour for Keegan to take over was indicative of his popularity with ordinary fans. However, it proved a decision he came to greatly regret, taking in a humiliating Euro 2000 group-stage exit and ending with him resigning in the toilets after an ignominious defeat against Germany in England’s last game at the old Wembley Stadium. It was, he conceded, a job beyond his abilities.

That said, Keegan was happy to take on Manchester City in the old First Division, getting them promoted to the Premier League as champions with 99 points. He remained at the club for four years, an almost unprecedented period of stability at the club at that time. When he finally left City he seemed to be done with coaching and finally launched his Soccer Circus in Glasgow, though it closed after a few years. Yet there was to be one last comeback at Newcastle under the ill-starred ownership of Mike Ashley, which proved a disaster and lasted just eight months.

The idea that a high-minded, old-fashioned football manager schooled by Shankly could coexist with a modern businessman as ruthless as Ashley and his cast of minions running the club always seemed improbable. When he walked away from the job, eventually winning a lengthy and bitter constructive dismissal claim, it was to be Keegan’s last act in football. So acrimonious was the departure that he was only able to return in disguise to attend a function at the club.

The current regime made clear Keegan was always welcome back at St James’ Park. That was after his stage four cancer had been revealed in a series of speaking engagements in May 2026, one of which in Newcastle was, in retrospect, a heartfelt farewell to the fans to whom he had always felt closest. After that draining but exhilarating evening Keegan’s associates reported that he was in high spirits, energised by the reconnection with the fans who loved him most.

It was to prove Keegan’s final goodbye. Football, as he observed, had given him everything except for a happy ending.

Sports.title: Only four years to the next men’s World Cup – what can we expect from the 2030 edition?
Sports.content:
If the 2026 World Cup was the tournament’s largest edition yet – featuring 48 teams for the first time in its 96-year history, being played in three different countries – the 2030 World Cup is going to have an even bigger footprint.

How many countries will host the 2030 World Cup?

Technically three. The tournament is set to be jointly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain, marking the first time the World Cup will be held in more than one confederation and the first time it will visit north Africa.

In addition, though, and in honour of the World Cup’s 100-year anniversary, a special match is scheduled to be held at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, Uruguay – the stadium that hosted the 1930 World Cup final. There will also be one match each in Argentina and Paraguay.

How did this come about?

The bidding process for the 2030 World Cup began in earnest in 2022, with the host to be officially selected at the 2024 Fifa congress. The governing body’s rules for rotating the tournament between continents meant that football federations from Asia (AFC) and North America (Concacaf) were ineligible to host following the Qatar 2022 and North America 2026 bids respectively.

Uefa federations Spain and Portugal – unsuccessful in 2018 and 2022 and ineligible in 2026 – added Morocco to their joint bid in 2023. That same year, Conmebol federations Uruguay, Argentina, Paraguay and Chile launched their joint bid, with a proposed tournament name of “Centenary World Cup”.

In October 2023, the Fifa council unanimously selected the Morocco-Portugal-Spain bid over the South American bid.

And why are South America still hosting some games?

The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, announced that Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay would host one match each to celebrate the centenary of the World Cup “in the most appropriate way”. Uruguay hosted – and won – the tournament’s inaugural edition with Argentina beaten 4-2 in the final. A game will also be played in Paraguay in recognition of the country’s role as the home of Conmebol, the only confederation in existence in 1930.

Fifa has also announced “a unique centenary celebration ceremony”, scheduled to take place in Montevideo the week before the tournament begins on 13 June 2030.

How many teams will take part?

Initially the idea was for it to be 48 teams again, but during this World Cup Infantino raised to prospect of it being expanded with a further 16 nations.

“That’s definitely ​an issue that will be examined and discussed in the relevant committees after this World Cup,” Infantino said. “When organising ⁠a World Cup, it’s important to organise it for the whole world – not just Europe and South America – but effectively the ⁠entire world.

An expansion had already been suggested in 2025 when the Conmebol president, Alejandro Domínguez, put forth an official proposal to expand the number of participating teams to 64 in honour of the tournament’s centennial. “[It] will be unique because 100 years are celebrated only once,” Domínguez said.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

What will it look like?

Spain last hosted the World Cup in 1982, the final of which involved Italy defeating West Germany in the Bernabéu. Co-hosts Portugal and Morocco have hosted various major sporting events, among them the 2004 Euros and the 2025 Afcon.

The 2030 World Cup will take place across 17 host cities – one more than the 2026 edition – with 11 of the proposed 20 stadiums located in Spain. Among the 17 host cities are Marrakech and Tangier in Morocco, Porto and Lisbon in Portugal and Barcelona, Madrid and San Sebastián in Spain.

The main talking point so far?

Without a doubt the inclusion of the centenary match hosts. By rejecting the South American host bid but declaring that Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay would host one match each Fifa ensured that Conmebol would be ineligible to bid for the 2034 World Cup with Asia and Oceania the only two continents able to host. (The 2034 edition has since been awarded to Saudi Arabia, a decision that has been heavily criticised by human rights groups).

And beyond that?

Well, who knows? After the shenanigans of Donald Trump’s intervention and Folarin Balogun’s red card being suspended, could we see the Spanish king, Felipe VI, get involved after an over-zealous Lamine Yamal tackle in the last 64? With these guys in charge, nothing is off the table.

Sports.title: Argentina players face bans as Fifa opens investigation into World Cup final brawls
Sports.content:
Fifa has opened an investigation into the violent scenes that followed Spain’s World Cup final win on Sunday, with several Argentina players facing bans.

Nahuel Molina appeared to strike Spain’s captain Rodri in the stomach as he ran on to the pitch following the final whistle, while there was also a large melee on the halfway line, where Leandro Paredes appeared to grab Eric García by the throat before throwing Gavi to the ground.

Parades was subsequently shown a red card by the referee, Slavko Vincic, who had also sent off Enzo Fernández towards the end of normal time, as well as booking three other Argentina players and the head coach, Lionel Scaloni.

“Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the Fifa World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the Fifa Disciplinary Code (FDC), the Fifa Disciplinary Committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents,” Fifa said in a statement.

Fifa is also investigating Argentina’s conduct after their semi-final win over England, when their players celebrated with a banner proclaiming “Las Malvinas son Argentinas”, which was smuggled into the Atlanta Stadium by supporters.

Fifa prohibits players or teams making political statements, so those involved could be banned.

Sports.title: Gaza celebrates World Cup victory of Spanish team they took into their hearts
Sports.content:
The Spanish football team’s World Cup win has been celebrated in the streets of Gaza, where Spain’s support for Palestinian rights and Israel’s backing for the Argentinian team turned the competition into more than a football showdown.

Gathered at cafes and outdoor screenings, Palestinians defied the risk of Israeli attacks to cheer on a team they had taken to their hearts.

Many waving Spanish flags paid tribute to teenage star Lamine Yamal, who brought a Palestinian flag to celebrations for Barcelona’s La Liga win in May.

“Whoever raises the Palestinian flag deserves to raise the World Cup,” the Gaza al-Irada amputee football team wrote in a pre-game video message for the Spanish team.

Saadi al-Masri, 40 and captain of the amputee team in Gaza, watched the game with friends in a cafe. “I support Spain because we see it as a country that stands with the Palestinian cause and supports Palestinian rights,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Palestinians defied the risk of Israeli attacks to cheer on Spain. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images

Spain has been among Europe’s most vocal critics of Israel’s war on Gaza and state-backed violence in the occupied West Bank. It is pushing for stronger European Union action over human rights violations, including suspension of a broad free trade pact.

When Israel’s defence minister attacked Yamal for raising the Palestinian flag, accusing him of “inciting hatred”, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was quick to defend the young player.

“Lamine has only expressed the solidarity with Palestine that is felt by millions of us in Spain. Another reason to be proud of him,” he said in a social media post.

Israeli support for Argentina was led by Netanyahu, who has cultivated close ties with far-right president Javier Milei, and posted a good luck message for the team ahead of the final.

The Palestinian delegation to the United Nations responded with an image of the Spanish team, under the headline “world champions”.

Even keen fans in Gaza have struggled to keep up with matches during the World Cup. Most of the 2 million Palestinians in the territory live in tent camps after Israeli attacks destroyed their homes, with little access to power or internet connections.

Arkan al-Walaida, 23, went to internet cafes to seek out match highlights each morning during the tournament, looking for short videos on TikTok or Fifa’s official YouTube and Instagram pages.

When she found out on Monday that Spain had won, she was overwhelmed. “Honestly, I felt like I was about to cry from happiness,” she said. “We see their support as a sign of humanity.”

Al-Masri watched the match at a cafe, packed with an excited crowd. “We were very happy when the final whistle confirmed Spain’s victory,” he said, but fear of Israeli airstrikes meant there were no late-night parties.

In early July, an Israeli bomb killed Mohamed al-Wahidi, a Palestinian aid worker who organised screenings of World Cup matches in Gaza.

The strike, just before the game between Egypt and Argentina, also killed brothers aged eight and 10, and a second man. The Israeli military confirmed the attack but said it had not targeted al-Wahidi.

Sports.title: A big red speaker, Louis Vuitton trophy trunks and a tattoo bet – how Spain celebrated World Cup win
Sports.content:
On the night that Spain won their first World Cup in 2010, Rodrigo Hernández was on camp somewhere lost in the woods of Connecticut. He had been canoeing when the selección beat Germany in the semi-final, upset to have missed it, and for the final he convinced one of the supervisors to let him watch, alone, on a mini-laptop in the hut where the staff slept. When Andrés Iniesta scored the winning goal in the 116th minute, he ran off screaming, doing laps of the lake. He was 14.

On the night that Spain won their second World Cup 16 years later, Rodrigo Hernández was back in the US, not so far from there. When Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute, he ran off screaming in a straighter line and accompanied this time: towards the corner where his other family were. And then, when it ended, when the fighting finished too, he collected the trophy, pausing just long enough for Donald Trump to leave centre stage before lifting it, his timing perfect even here.

It wasn’t the only trophy he had, but those could be handed over and this could not. By the time Rodri departed at 9.38pm eastern time, the last man out of the dressing room at the New Jersey New York Stadium, he couldn’t carry them all: walking with him, just ahead, Ladis had to lend a hand. A football team is never just the players, nor even just the coaches. When he departed the dressing room nine minutes earlier, the same happened for Pau Cubarsí. Nuria helped him, their boy: just 19, looking like a kid down here in the stadium in real life but not on the pitch where he’s a leader. Luis de la Fuente was accompanied by Paloma.

Rodri came with the trophy for the tournament’s best player too. Cubarsí had the young player award, Unai Simón the Golden Glove. They also had two World Cups, every Spain player did: a replica of their own in a black Louis Vuitton trophy trunk, not easy to fit under an arm, and another in Lego. Rodri had three: both of those and the cup. They departed laden down, great big plastic bags full, pieces of the history they made. Shirts, in red and yellow and blue and white. Balls, boots. They had cut the net and taken pieces of that too. They had been given rings, NBA style.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino holds a replica of the trophy in the dressing room after Spain’s triumph. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Before the final began, Marc Cucurella had sneaked off towards the touchline and buried a coin in the pitch, like that other left-back Joan Capdevila had done in 2010. Iniesta had been out there, his name chanted, as he showed the cup to the stands. After it, Sergio Ramos brought it back again. Dashing out, excitedly kissing it, he placed it on the plinth for this new generation, achieving the impossible in emulating them, to go and collect. One by one they passed, Borja Iglesias and Lamine Yamal among the most evasive in shaking Trump’s hand, until Rodri took the trophy and lifted it to the sky.

Nico Williams went to find his mum in the front row and handed over his medal. Lamine Yamal had made his way across to Lionel Messi, who was sitting but who stood for him, embracing the boy in the bath, the successor: a rite of passage, an image that will be for ever. The actor Javier Bardem was hugging Iglesias, his new friend and idol. Ferran Torres was talking about a “great liberation”: he had suffered, felt how cruel this game could be, how people could be too, but he said: “Destiny is written: God gives to those who deserve.” And Keyne was, well, Keyne. In the dressing room – the same one, Cucurella noted, where he had been at last year’s Club World Cup – the champagne was cracked open.

It was brief – the flight to Spain was scheduled for 11pm and they wanted to get back – and soon they were on their way again. Behind the screen, along the corridor they came, way down in the depths and the half-light of the stadium. The president, the staff, all the players; the many, many people who made this so. Iglesias carried a bag so big it was like he was a student taking his washing home, and he was struggling to stop that box slipping. In the other hand he wheeled a big red speaker. Now playing: Dirty Cash (Money Talks) by PAWSA & Adventures of Stevie V. Lamine Yamal came, via the anti-doping room, in orange sunglasses, four chains, black cap on backwards. He didn’t wear his medal, but most did, thick discs round their necks. And commemorative shirts, ordered up in case.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Argentina’s Lionel Messi embrace after the match. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Back in Dallas, at a celebration after the semi-final victory, someone had joked to the federation president, Rafael Louzán, that the shirts should say world champions on one side and Finalissima winners on the other, two trophies in one. Tempting, but these bore just the one trophy, “Spain 26” on the back. The war in the Middle East had prevented the Finalissima from going ahead in Doha as scheduled in March and every time another option was offered, Argentina said no, the impression that of a team, a federation, running scared. “Good job we didn’t play,” Emi Martínez had said then, after they scraped past Mauritania in a hastily arranged friendly that filled the hole. “If we had played [Spain] like this …”

Something like this might have happened. Not just because Argentina played like this but because Spain made them play like this. “We gave them a battering,” came the verdict from one of those heading out of the dressing room. This wasn’t just a win; this was more. Has a 1-0 ever been as dominant? There was a moment late in the game, still at 0-0, when the Spain fans chanted: “Look at them! Look at them! How they shit themselves!” and they weren’t wrong. Argentina could not get out all game; as Spain turned the screw, still less, the goal seemingly inevitable; the surprise was that it hadn’t come yet, that there would be just one. When it did it came as a liberation but also an act of irresistible logic.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scores the only goal of the World Cup final. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Torres’s shot was Spain’s 20th. Argentina didn’t manage one until the 115th minute. They didn’t manage any on target, all game. Across 900 World Cup games for which Opta has the stats, it is only the third time that a team has failed to shoot. And this in the final. They had done to Argentina what they did to France and to everyone, choking them. For the whole tournament Spain had an xG against of 0.3 per game. “If my gloves could talk, they would say they didn’t have much work to do,” Simón said. “Many teams depend too much on the back line,” Aymeric Laporte said, but not Spain.

This was the triumph of a collective, of a group; it ended in New York, but it was built in Chattanooga and beyond, over 51 days. It is the triumph of an idea, a conviction and of a coach too: a victory for De la Fuente and the system he leads and the system that made him. He began his coaching career at Deportivo Alavés in the third tier, where he lasted just 11 games. It was November 2011 when he left and he has not had a club job since. For months, no one returned his calls. He was on the dole for a year and a half until he saw an advert for a job: the Spanish federation was looking for a coach for the youth system. He started in the under-17s. He won the European Championship with the under-19s and the under-21s. Then he won it with the senior side; now he has won the World Cup.

“They asked me what there is left to win; we said the next game in September because they’re insatiable,” he insisted afterwards. Simón said: “The manager is outstanding; he has been our leader.” Cucurella, meanwhile, was in trouble. He had promised that if Spain won the World Cup, he would get a tattoo of De la Fuente’s face and now he had to decide where to put it to minimise the damage, the flight home an opportunity to think. Not least to think what a fool he had been.

View image in fullscreen Marc Cucurella is to have a tattoo of Luis de la Fuente’s face after Spain’s win. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

“I said: ‘You made a bad mistake’,” the coach joked. “But it’s not like I am so horrendously ugly that you have to put it somewhere it can’t be seen. And they are men of their word.” For all the laughs, that final line really mattered, and he knows: 10 of them played with him at junior level. The first title he ever won was the Under-19 Euros in 2015. In the middle of his midfield that day was Rodrigo Hernández.

Eleven years on, 16 since he watched Spain’s first World Cup win, motivation sought and identification found in what they achieved, Rodri was back in the US. The embodiment of that idea, a player who approached perfection here, no one played more passes nor made more tackles than him. No one had his weight either, the captain leading Spain out and leading them back too. Like so many of his teammates at a tournament that was an expression of justice and vindication too, he had suffered for this, a torn cruciate ligament overcome.

“It doesn’t matter if you fall, there’s always a reason to get up again,” he said and now he had it right here in his hands. It was 9.40pm when he boarded the bus bound for the airport, carrying the actual World Cup.

Sports.title: Neuer to Neymar: 11 World Cup players who retired from international football
Sports.content:
Manuel Neuer (Germany, 40)

First participated in the World Cup in 2010 before winning the trophy four years later. Germany have had little success since and their penalty shootout defeat by Paraguay marked the end of Neuer’s international career. He initially retired after Euro 2024 but reversed that decision a few weeks before this tournament. “Despite the bitter end, I don’t regret this decision,” he said after his 23rd and final World Cup appearance. The former Germany defender Robert Huth criticised the decision to bring Neuer out of retirement: “I think the big one that really unsettles the squad was the Neuer inclusion. I think [it was] really unexpected, he came late to the table.”

Patrik Schick (Czechia, 30)

Made his World Cup debut this summer having left an impression at Euro 2020. Schick failed to score as Czechia went winless and were eliminated in the group stage. The striker announced his international retirement hours after the final group game. “Today, my national team chapter is coming to an end,” he said. The official Czechia statement paid tribute: “Thank you for every match, every goal, and the pride with which you represented the Czech Republic.”

Guillermo Ochoa (Mexico, 41)

Cemented himself as a fans’ favourite in 2014 when he kept a famous clean sheet against the World Cup hosts, Brazil. His playing time was limited this summer, but he got 12 minutes against Czechia, where he was celebrated by teammates. After full time the manager, Javier Aguirre, said: “The moment he stepped on to the pitch, it overshadowed everything else. He is a world-class legend, and I am incredibly proud of him.” Ochoa later posted: “It was the greatest privilege of my life. Thank you for believing, for always accompanying us. I love you Mexico.”

View image in fullscreen Guillermo Ochoa shows his emotions after Mexico’s exit against England. Photograph: Álex Cruz/EPA

Riyad Mahrez (Algeria, 35)

Having made one appearance at the 2014 finals, Mahrez had to wait 12 years to add to his tally. He scored two goals against Austria before Algeria were eliminated in the last 32 by Switzerland in his final game. Mahrez said: “Representing Algeria has been a dream of mine ever since I was young, to play for my country. It’s been an immense honour and a great source of pride.” A Confederation of African Football’s statement said: “You gave us memories that time can never take away. Thank you, Riyad Mahrez.”

Enner Valencia (Ecuador, 36)

The forward got six goals in as many matches across the 2014 and 2022 finals but was unable to add to that tally for an Ecuador team who lost to Mexico in the last 32. “I’ve played my last match with the national team,” he said in the tunnel after. Ecuador’s official X account showed appreciation to their record scorer: “The GOAT. Super Enner. Thank you for giving yourself to the country and representing it in the best way.”

Nicolás Otamendi (Argentina, 38)

The uncompromising defender played every minute as Argentina triumphed in Qatar, having made his World Cup debut in 2010. Playing time was harder to come by in North America, though he featured in every game bar one, having revealed his intention to retire in March. “It’s my last World Cup, from there I’ll be a fan,” he said. Otamendi’s final home match became a tribute, with Lionel Messi letting him score a penalty at La Bombonera.

Marko Arnautovic (Austria, 37)

This was the striker’s first and last World Cup. He scored twice as Austria reached the last 32, where they were defeated 3–0 by Spain. Arnautovic revealed his departure in an emotional post-match interview, saying: “Playing for Austria was the biggest highlight. It hits me that from now on I won’t see my second family any more.” In a social media post, the Austrian Football Association said: “What a career. What a character. Thank you for everything.”

Sadio Mané (Senegal, 34)

Participated in 2018 but injury ruled him out four years later. Following Senegal’s capitulation against Belgium, Mané released a statement regarding retirement via Senegalese outlet Le Quotidien – although there have been questions about its authenticity – saying: “Know that I sacrificed everything for this flag. I gave the very best of myself and I always fought fiercely for our homeland.” Pape Thiaw was asked about Mané’s retirement in January and replied: “We want to keep him as long as possible … when we say it’s his decision, it doesn’t just belong to him, he belongs to the people of Senegal, and they want to see him carry on.”

View image in fullscreen Sadio Mané has called time on his international career with Senegal. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/FIFA/Getty Images

Craig Gordon (Scotland, 43)

The goalkeeper amassed 84 caps, making his debut in 2004, but did not get off the bench at his first World Cup. “I’ve never wanted it to end, but it must,” Gordon said, calling time on his club and international career. Gordon’s spell was described as “a career unlike any other” by the Scotland national team’s social media account.

Jean Michaël Seri (Côte d’Ivoire, 35)

Made his World Cup debut in his side’s 2–0 victory over Curaçao, his 64th cap. In a social media post, the former Fulham midfielder later said: “After 11 years in the national team, and one World Cup played, I announce the end of my international career today.” Seri received a wealth of tributes below his post. “Congratulations on all that you’ve accomplished with the national team,” replied the captain, Franck Kessié. “Thank you for all these moments shared under our colors.”

Neymar (Brazil, 34)

Announced himself on the World Cup stage with two goals on debut in 2014. Restricted by injury at the current tournament, he managed 55 minutes before Brazil’s exit against Norway and announced his international retirement shortly after full time. “It started here at MetLife Stadium,” he said, referring to his debut against the US in August 2010, “and I finished here. It is now over.” Zlatan Ibrahimovic, working as a pundit for US television, said: “An amazing player, and the skill set he had was just crazy. So, sad moment for Brazilian football.”

Sports.title: Spurs break their women’s transfer record to sign Alice Sombath from Lyonnes
Sports.content:
Tottenham have signed the France defender Alice Sombath from Lyonnes for a club record fee. The price paid for the 22-year-old has not been disclosed but the previous club record, paid for Signe Gaupset in January, was reportedly more than £375,000.

“The league is very competitive, every game is a tough game and that’s what I’m most excited about,” said Sombath. “I saw that Spurs had a very good season last year. My qualities can bring something to the team, even though I know they already have a lot.”

Sombath spent six years at Lyonnes, the eight-time European champions, joining the club after she was signed from Paris Saint-Germain in 2020.

She won the Champions League in her second season, featuring twice and being on the bench in the final, and won five league titles and two Coupe de France titles.

Tottenham’s head coach, Martin Ho, said the defender “fits the profile of what we’re building”. She has already shown real maturity in her performances and we believe she has all the qualities to continue developing into a top player within our environment.

“Alice is an aggressive defender who is comfortable in possession, competitive in her duels and has the ambition to keep improving every day. Those characteristics are really important to us and we’re excited to help her take the next step in her career while strengthening the squad.”

Sombath is Spurs’s sixth signing of the summer, after Shekiera Martinez, Kirsty Hanson, Victoria Pelova, Caitlin Dijkstra and Selma Panengstuen.

The club are delighted to have got these deals done early, allowing for a full pre-season, and that Sombath’s recruitment means they have secured the services of their six priority targets.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tottenham finished fifth in the WSL last season after a disappointing 11th the preceding season. They were four points behind fourth-placed Manchester United, but 19 behind the league winners, Manchester City.

Sports.title: EFL boss who went from top at Christmas to sacked in March takes surprise new job in Belgium
Sports.content:
EFL boss who went from top at Christmas to sacked in March takes surprise new job in Belgium

Former Walsall manager Mat Sadler has made the move to Belgium to become the new assistant coach at Lommel SK.

The 41-year-old, who has penned a 12-month contract at Soevereinstadion, has joined former Bristol City and Sunderland boss Lee Johnson's backroom staff.

1 Sadler was sacked by Walsall in March after losing eight of his last 14 fixtures Credit: Getty

Sadler had been out of a job since March following his sacking at Bescot Stadium.

He spent nearly three years in charge of the Saddlers having been appointed in April 2023.

It was at Walsall where he finished his playing career - returning to the club in 2019 - lasting two seasons.

Across his two spells, he featured in 113 games, before going on to manage them on 161 occasions.

Having guided the club to fourth spot in the 2024/25 season, he then took the League Two outfit to top spot at Christmas last year - with fans dreaming of a return to England's third-tier for the first time since 2019.

But a disastrous run of form led to the West Midlands outfit sitting in 11th place at the time of Sadler's axing, with the club losing eight and drawing four from their previous 14 fixtures.

A new adventure

Sadler is now gearing up for his first role overseas having never played or coached outside of England.

Lommel, who are part of the City Football Group, will be playing in the Belgian Pro League in the upcoming season.

In his first campaign at the club, Johnson guided Lommel to play-off glory.

They will now be competing in Belgium's top-tier for the first time in 23 years.

And Sadler has expressed his excitement at linking up with Lommel as they prepare for a historic season.

He told the club's website: "I'm very pleased to be joining this ambitious club from today.

"From my conversations with Jeffrey [van As - sporting director] and Lee Johnson, I immediately had a very positive feeling.

"And it was great to see that the feeling was mutual.

"I'm really looking forward to the upcoming Jupiler Pro League season and to building something special together with my colleagues."

Lommel chief Van As meanwhile stated: "In our opinion, Mat's profile is the best fit for the ambitions we have as a club and for the way we want to shape our coaching staff."

Sports.title: EFL club sign ex-Chelsea defender Tariq Lamptey two months after having contract ripped up
Sports.content:
EFL club sign ex-Chelsea defender Tariq Lamptey two months after having contract ripped up

Queen's Park Rangers have announced the signing of former Premier League defender Tariq Lamptey on a free transfer.

The 25-year-old, who came through Chelsea's academy, joins QPR just two months after having his contract terminated at Serie A side Fiorentina.



3 Tariq Lamptey is looking to revive his career at QPR Credit: qpr.co.uk

Lamptey moved to Italy last September following his departure from Brighton, but this soon turned into a nightmare.

He suffered an ACL rupture just 22 minutes into his first start for Fiorentina against Como, ending his season in devastating fashion.

The full-back had only made a three-minute substitute appearance in Serie A before that and he didn't play for the club again.



Fiorentina announced in May that Lamptey's contract had been terminated by mutual agreement, leaving him a free agent.

Before his spell in Italy, the Ghana international had played 122 times for Brighton and three times for Chelsea's first-team as a youngster.



Back in town

Now, six years after his departure from Chelsea, Lamptey is back in west London, as it was announced that he has joined QPR.

The move marks the London-born right-back's return to English football, who is set to play in the Championship for the first time.



Speaking to the club after signing, Lamptey said: “I'm excited for the opportunity ahead.

“When I spoke to the gaffer and Christian (Nourry), the project was an encouraging one.

“The team have ambitious goals for this season, so I'm looking forward to it.”

3 Lamptey featured in just two games in his horror spell at Fiorentina Credit: Getty



Having impressed in his early senior career at Brighton after breaking into their first team, Lamptey vowed to get back to his best at Loftus Road.

He added: “I know what I'm capable of and I set myself high standards.

"I had a great start to my career, and I'll keep continuing that.”

Lamptey also shared an update on his ongoing recovery from ACL injury, as he revealed he is close to making a comeback on the pitch.

The defender confirmed: “My recovery has gone well and I’m not too far away now. I’m looking forward to joining with the boys.



“Throughout my football journey I've always been resilient.

“You can't really predict what's going to happen, but you can only put your best foot forward and prepare as well as possible. And that's what I try to do.”

While Lamptey hinted he is close to a return, he is unlikely to make his comeback in time for an exciting clash with his new club.

QPR will face off against his former side Fiorentina in a pre-season friendly on Saturday, when the two teams meet at Loftus Road.

Meanwhile, Lamptey will be hoping to be back in time for the Rs' Championship season opener, away to Portsmouth on August 15.



Putting the past behind

After his time in Italy was wrecked by injury, Lamptey will be hoping to finally return to full fitness at QPR, having endured a nightmare time of things in recent years.

When he left Brighton, he was carrying a knee issue that had kept him out for 123 days in the 2024/25 campaign, while the season before that, he spent a similar length of time in the treatment room for another set of multiple problems.

3 Lamptey was seen as a promising young full-back in his early career at Brighton Credit: AFP

That followed a serious knee injury in 2022/23, which forced him out of action for another 100-day spell.



That wasn't even the start for him in the Premier League though, as two hamstring injuries in 2020/21 kick-started his nightmare, causing him to miss 32 games of the season.

But with the chance to start afresh at QPR, Lamptey will be desperate to return to the form that made him a regular starter in the Premier League when fully fit.

Sports.title: Jhon Duran accused of being a ‘bad egg’ as he joins seventh club aged just 22
Sports.content:
Jhon Duran accused of being a ‘bad egg’ as he joins seventh club aged just 22

Jhon Duran has joined Benfica on loan from Al Nassr - the seventh different club of his young career.

And Aston Villa legend Gabby Agbonlahor thanked Unai Emery for selling the 22-year-old 18 months ago.



3 The Colombian scored 20 times during his spell at Villa Park Credit: Getty

Since making his senior debut as a 15-year-old for Envigado in his home country of Colombia, Duran has represented Chicago Fire, Aston Villa, Al Nassr, Fenerbahce, Zenit Saint Petersburg, and Benfica.

Saudi club Al Nassr splashed out a staggering €77m (£65m) to sign him 18 months against from Villa after scoring 12 Premier League goals across 55 appearances.

He has only played 18 times for the Saudi club - going on loan to Fenerbahce, Zenit and now Benfica.



After joining the Portuguese giants, the striker said: "I am happy! I continue to say that it is the biggest club in Portugal. I am very grateful to be here.

"I have very high expectations of being here. I want to play well, give my all and become champion.



Some Villa fans were left confused last season over why the club would sell the young star, especially regarding depth issues in attack.

He had scored seven goals in 20 games in the first half of the season before his big money exit in January 2025.



However, Agbonlahor, who played nearly 400 times for the club, congratulated the Villa manager for making the decision.

Bad egg

On talkSPORT Breakfast, he said: "When Jhon Duran left Aston Villa, everyone was a little annoyed but the manager did the right thing.

"He left Aston Villa for Al Nassr in January 2025 for £65m. Since then, he’s been on loan at Fenerbahce, Zenit and now Benfica, and there’s a buy-option in the loan of £22m.

3 Duran started strongly in the Saudi Pro League, and was playing alongside Cristiano Ronaldo Credit: AFP



"He’s 22 years of age, in 18 months look at what has happened to him. Sometimes players are bad eggs, and well done to Unai Emery for getting him out."

Jeff Stelling followed up and asked: "Would you have him back?"

Agbonlahor replied: "No. I think he caused carnage in the changing room."

Benfica will pay a loan fee of €6.1m (£5.19m) for the Colombian, while the deal includes a €30m (£25.5m) purchase option.

Within six months of joining Al-Nassr, Duran was loaned to Turkish side Fenerbahce after struggling to settle.



During his time with the Istanbul giants, he netted five times in 21 matches.

3 Marco Silva is the new Benfica manager Credit: Getty

His stint in Turkey was disrupted due to health setbacks, as he was diagnosed with osteoarthritis and had to undergo a 58-day treatment process.

The 22-year-old terminated his loan spell at the club after only six months to head to Zenit St Petersburg until the end of last season.



He made nine appearances and secured two goals with the 12-time Russian champions.

Fresh start with Marco Silva

The move to Benfica represents Duran's fourth switch since leaving Aston Villa 18 months ago.

Benfica failed to qualify for the Champions League despite having an invincible campaign under Jose Mourinho, who left to rejoin Real Madrid.

The 38-time Portuguese champions will hope Duran can bolster their attacking line next season, having also appointed former Fulham manager Marco Silva.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino and FIFA targeting World Cup’s ‘missing country’ amid 64-team expansion plan
Sports.content:
FIFA will discuss expanding the World Cup, in the hope that China, a nation of 1.4 billion people, could qualify in 2030

The next World Cup will be expanded to 64 teams, the president of CONMEBOL has claimed.

In a post on X, Alejandro Domínguez of the South American football confederation appeared to confirm Gianni Infantino's grand plans for a bigger tournament that has angered football purists seemingly fighting a losing battle.

7 The next World Cup will be expanded to 64 teams, CONMEBOL's president has claimed Credit: Getty

Domínguez wrote: "In 2030, the World Cup comes to Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay, a great opportunity for football, to celebrate the World Cup Centenary with a 64-team tournament."

While there has been no official word from FIFA on the matter of expansion, Infantino said earlier this month that soccer's global governing body will discuss a 64-team field once the 2026 tournament is done.

Spain beat Argentina in the World Cup final in New York on Sunday.

This was the first edition to feature 48 teams, and that number appears likely to grow again in 2030.

FIFA is expecting record breaking revenue from the tournament that has just passed in the United States, Canada and Mexico -- and with further expansion, is targeting another massive market.

World Cup expansion plans target 'missing team'

Despite the 48-team field in 2026, China’s national team still failed to qualify.

Politico reports that if 64 teams compete at the next edition, there is 'implicit hope' from FIFA of pulling in the Chinese team and its huge market of soccer-obsessed fans.

Hong Kong University Professor Xu Gouqi told the outlet that a 'running joke' in online soccer forums in the country is that China still might not qualify despite an expanded field.

"Chinese are not allowed to discuss many things in social media," Xu said in an interview.

"But you can criticize the Chinese men’s football team with no consequences. It’s still a safe place."

7 China were beaten 7-0 by Japan in qualifying for the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty

7 Chinese soccer fans have had little to get excited about Credit: Getty

China has a population of approximately 1.4 billion people, but their soccer team hasn't given fans much hope of a World Cup run.

They have appeared just once, at the 2002 tournament hosted in South Korea and Japan.

Despite a respectable performance against Costa Rica 24 years ago, China lost all of their group games without scoring a goal, and finished with a goal difference of 0-9.

In the qualifying stage for the 2026 World Cup, the team was beaten 7-0 in one particularly tough game against regional power Japan.

China also lost to Indonesia and drew with Singapore, two other teams that didn't qualify.

There are currently no Chinese players in the top tiers of any of Europe’s professional leagues, which suggests the nation would struggle on the big stage.

7 No players from China play in any of Europe's top leagues Credit: Getty

7 Fans across the nation still tuned into the World Cup final Credit: Getty

Despite far from encouraging signs, Xu told Politico that a 'world class football fan base' remains in China.

He remains optimistic that China can qualify, and even win, the World Cup in the coming decades.

Should that happen, the country would be swept by a whole new level of soccer obsession which, according to Politico, would be a FIFA marketer’s dream.

Even Donald Trump, who became one of the biggest stories of this summer's tournament, has joked the US and China could co-host a future edition.

7 Trump has joked the US and China could co-host an expanded World Cup Credit: Getty

"Gianni also had another idea. He said we could do it -- China and the United States the next time," the president said.

"So you have a nice short flight in between games... the players would love that."

What has Gianni Infantino said about expanding the World Cup to 64 teams?

While it appears FIFA's expanded World Cup would target a forgotten soccer nation like China, Infantino has insisted the change would allow many smaller countries to participate on the global stage.

The 2030 tournament will be hosted by newly-crowned champions Spain, Morocco and Portugal, as well as in the three South American nations noted by CONMEBOL president Domínguez.

7 FIFA believes an expanded World Cup would give smaller nations a better chance of qualifying Credit: AFP

"This is certainly an issue that will be looked at and discussed in the relevant committees," Infantino told Swiss broadcaster Blue Sport on July 12, while speaking on expansion.

"When you organize a World Cup, it's important that you organize it for the whole world.

"It's not just Europe and South America, but the entire world, effectively. Every nation should be able to dream of taking part in the World Cup.

"We can see that the quality of the teams is extremely high, and it's getting higher and higher everywhere in the world.

"If you don't give smaller countries the chance to participate in the World Cup, they also lose the incentive to keep improving."

Stay up to date on all things World Cup across our talkSPORT platforms - subscribe to our YouTube channel for the latest news, opinion, exclusive interviews and our daily unfiltered, unscripted show 'The S* Word, from 8am ET.

Sports.title: Blame FIFA, not the USA, as $14bn 64-team World Cup angers football purists in losing battle
Sports.content:
An expanded 64-team World Cup feels inevitable, after the overwhelming success of the 2026 tournament. It will be hard for football to push back vs Gianni Infantino.

Blame FIFA, not the USA, as $14bn 64-team World Cup angers football purists in losing battle

The old game is gone and it is not coming back.

That's been the case for decades and the overwhelming success of the biggest World Cup in history will only embolden Gianni Infantino in his global football push.

4 Gianni Infantino is pushing for the World Cup to be even larger Credit: Getty



With the USA (and Canada and Mexico) pulling off a 104-match tournament that featured 48 teams bouncing across three countries, FIFA could fast track a push for further World Cup expansion in time for the next tourney in 2030.

It was initially expected that Infantino and Co. would at least hold off until a 2038 World Cup that is still waiting for a host country.

"In 2030, the World Cup comes to Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay, a great opportunity for football, to celebrate the World Cup Centenary with a 64-team tournament," CONMEBOL president Alejandro Domínguez posted on social media.

"We are working to ensure that the 2030 World Cup is held with 64 national teams in homage to the Centenary of the World Cup. International football grows when it opens up to the world.



"The expansion to 48 teams demonstrated that greater participation generates more opportunities, boosts the development of football, and turns the World Cup into a true global celebration. The Centenary offers us a historic opportunity to Dream Big. May the World Cup be the greatest celebration that football has ever known."

Cape Verde provided athletic inspiration across the globe this summer, highlighting the positives of expanding the playing field.



But some Group Stage matches lacked intensity as the 2026 World Cup progressed, while the performances of Panama, Iraq, Qatar, Jordan, New Zealand and Curacao were reminders that bigger isn’t always better for the beautiful game.

"This (64-team) proposal was maybe even more surprising for me than you," UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin said in April 2025. "I think it is a bad idea."



Yet even with UEFA increasingly at odds with FIFA, a 64-team tourney feels like a question of ‘when,' not ‘if.’

Infantino saturated the World Cup with America in 2026, topped off with a Super Bowl-like halftime show and 'hydration breaks' that raked in TV advertising cash, and were similar to the quarter system used by the NFL and NBA.

4 Momentum is building for the World Cup to expand to 64 teams Credit: getty

4 Fans packed stadiums and paid record ticket prices Credit: Getty



"It was like everything American got put into the World Cup, when some of that wasn't needed," Gabby Agbonlahor exclusively said Tuesday on talkSPORT Breakfast.

But money talks louder than ever in global football, and Infantino recently stated that FIFA could top $15 billion in revenue across the 2023-2026 World Cup cycle.

When you have Ted Lasso, BTS, Madonna, Shakira and Justin Bieber willingly on your side -- even if the halftime show was junk -- FIFA's financial steamroller is harder than ever to stop.

"Spectacular success," football finance expert Kieran Maguire exclusively told talkSPORT Breakfast, while discussing the 2026 World Cup.



"In 2022 in Qatar, around about $8 billion (in revenue). It's estimated that this World Cup -- with the increase in the number of matches, with the increase in the size of the average capacity of the stadium, and, of course, the pricing -- you put those three things together and we're talking $14 billion.

"The winners only got $40 million. So all of that money is effectively recycled back to FIFA."

4 Messi might have played in the last 48-team World Cup Credit: Getty

Infantino can also bat down overexpansion criticism with overwhelming numbers.



For all of the concerns that shadowed the 2026 World Cup before the first match was played, FIFA answered the negativity by setting an all-time attendance record as 6,810,966 fans packed stadiums in the USA, Canada and Mexico.

“The American dream, Mr. President, came to reality," said Infantino, while standing next to Trump. "We united the world."

The next big step is a 64-team World Cup that improves the math for the knockout rounds and shines a spotlight on more Cape Verdes.

"This is certainly an issue that will be looked at and discussed in the relevant committees after this World Cup," Infantino told Blue Sport.



"When you organize a World Cup, it's important that you organize it for the whole world. It's not just Europe and South America, but the entire world, effectively. Every nation should be able to dream of taking part in the World Cup.”

With a potential revenue intake of $15 billion staring FIFA in the face and Saudi Arabia already on the World Cup calendar in 2034, it will take a unified pushback to prevent a 64-team expansion that suddenly feels imminent.

Infantino understands what's obvious after the triumph of 2026.

Football won't get smaller, especially on a global scale.

It will only keep growing, no matter how badly the old-school purists long for the faded days that no longer exist.

Sports.title: When does the summer transfer window shut? Deadline day info amid spending spree
Sports.content:
When does the summer transfer window shut? Deadline day info amid spending spree

The summer transfer window is well underway, with big-money business being completed left, right and centre.

But clubs are going to have to make sure they get all of their signings over the line by the time the deadline comes around.

2 Santos to Man United has been one of the biggest deals of the summer Credit: Getty

Already this summer, there have been multiple record-breaking £100million-plus transfers made in the Premier League.

Elliot Anderson has joined Manchester City, Sandro Tonali has signed for Tottenham and Morgan Rogers is set for Chelsea.

However, time will feel like it's quickly running out for all clubs to get their deals done as the deadline gets closer...

When does the transfer window shut?

The transfer deadline in England is set for Tuesday, September 1.

For the last two windows, the closing time was set for 7pm, but the time will now return to its original later deadline.

It means the summer window closes at 11pm on September 1.

Clubs can submit deal sheets before the deadline to give themselves a two-hour grace period to complete transfers.

This deadline is in place for the Premier League and EFL.

In the WSL, the window closes at 11pm on Thursday, September 3.

And that's the same day as the Scottish Premiership, but in Scotland, the deadline is going to be set for 5pm rather than 11pm.

2 England star Anderson has joined Man City for a record-breaking fee Credit: Getty

When is the deadline across Europe?

For LaLiga clubs, their summer window shuts at a similar time to in England, with the deadline set for September 1 at 10:59pm.

In Italy and Serie A, clubs have until 8pm on the same day.

As for the Bundesliga, their deadline is Monday, August 31 at 7pm.

When does the winter transfer window open?

Once the summer deadline shuts, clubs will not be able to do any more business until the winter window opens.

In England, transfers will be possible again from January 1, 2027.

The window will run for a month, closing again on February 1 at 11pm.

Meanwhile, in the WSL, the winter window will open on January 4 and close exactly a month later on February 4.

And in Scotland, their window will open on January 5, closing at 5pm on February 4.
