World.title: Amid U.S.-Iran war, Houthi rebels threaten to blockade another key strait
World.content:
Amid U.S.-Iran war, Houthi rebels threaten to blockade another key strait

toggle caption Mohammed Huwais/AFP via Getty Images

TEL AVIV — The Houthis, a Yemeni Shiite militia which is aligned with Iran, have announced a naval blockade of a key waterway, the Bab Al-Mandeb Strait.

In a video statement, a Houthi spokesperson said the blockade was in retaliation for strikes from Saudi Arabia on a major airport in Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

The Houthis have accused Saudi Arabia of hitting the airport while an Iranian official was traveling through it earlier this month.

Bab Al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and it lets Saudi Arabia, one of the biggest oil producers in the world, get millions of barrels of oil a day out to the open ocean for export.

Sponsor Message

Bab Al-Mandeb has become even more important for Saudi Arabia now that the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed off by the U.S.- Iran war.

Any potential Houthi blockade of the strait would rattle energy markets already shaken by the war in Iran and would likely raise energy prices further.

The blockade would also test Gulf states' resolve to counter Iran and Iran-aligned groups in the Middle East, including the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia condemned the blockade in a statement. The Houthis said in response that the Saudis were a "criminal" regime.

The Houthi rebels are designated by the U.S. State Department as a terrorist group.

Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and the United Arab Emirates have been exploring the idea of building new oil pipelines or expanding existing ones to move oil overland instead of by sea, but those pipelines could take years to build.

U.S. and Iran trade fire – again

The U.S. and Iran traded fire for a 10th consecutive round of strikes overnight.

U.S. Central Command said late Monday it struck Iranian military command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and air defense systems.

Iran's state news agency IRNA said it targeted three U.S. bases hosting American military personnel and equipment in Kuwait last night.

Sponsor Message

The fighting is now at its most intense level since the war began in February.

The Pentagon on Monday confirmed the identities of two service members killed by Iranian attacks in northern Jordan last Friday and said another still remains missing.

The Pentagon later disclosed a third service member was killed in Iraq.

That brings the death toll of the war in Iran to at least 17 service members killed. The Pentagon says 427 people have been injured to date. Iran's government says about 3,000 people in Iran have been killed in the war.

But a U.S. military official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, confirmed with NPR that the Department of Defense has been slow-walking information on casualties.

Just this week the Pentagon spokesman admitted after questions from journalists that 100 service members have been injured in the last two weeks. He said the vast majority recovered quickly and went back to work.

Lebanon's president to meet Trump in the White House

A separate ceasefire between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon is still holding, despite ongoing Israeli strikes on people and sites in Lebanon that Israel claims are Hezbollah-affiliated.

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun is scheduled to meet President Trump in Washington D.C. on Tuesday, in the first state visit to the United States since 2009.

His visit comes at a critical time. A sweeping roadmap for peace between Lebanon's government and Israel signed in June would see the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah. But that is preconditioned on Israel withdrawing from the large amount of Lebanese territory it has occupied since earlier this year.

So far, the timeline for any Israeli withdrawal has been unclear, and about 400,000 Lebanese people remain internally displaced because of Israeli occupation or destruction of their homes.

NPR's Quil Lawrence contributed reporting.

World.title: Amid nurse shortage, a school in the South rolls out the welcome mat for men
World.content:
Amid nurse shortage, a university rolls out the welcome mat for men

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter sent every weekday morning.

Men are largely missing out on one of the hottest professions in the U.S. right now: nursing.

For registered nurses alone, the Labor Department projects there will be 189,000 job openings each year for the next decade. But only 1 in 8 nurses are men.

There have long been efforts to rewrite the script around nursing — to push back on the idea that it's women's work. Now, the economy is helping, too.

Sponsor Message

With diminishing opportunities in male-dominated industries like manufacturing and software engineering, nursing has emerged as a stable alternative and a solid pathway to a middle-class life.

Nursing students at the University of Alabama at Birmingham are already experiencing what it's like to be in demand.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Ethan Stinson will graduate next month and go straight into a job in the psychiatric unit at the university hospital.

"I feel like it's really easy to get a psych job if you're a nurse," he says. "They're hunting people all the time."

His classmate Hatim Nasser, whose family had wanted him to study computer science, has a job lined up in the university hospital's heart and lung transplant intensive care unit.

At a time when many of their peers are unsure of what's next, the students are happy their skills are in demand.

"We're grateful for it," Nasser says.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

A nursing school in the South leads the way

No doubt, stereotypes about men in nursing still abound. But slowly, they're being eroded.

At the University of Alabama at Birmingham, close to 1 in 6 nursing students are men, outpacing the national average. And nearly 1 in 5 faculty are men. In some specialties within the university hospital, male nurses are nearly as common as female nurses.

Sponsor Message

"I don't really feel like nursing isn't for men or anything like that. When I go to the hospital, I see guys all the time," says nursing student Amiri Saadiq, who's headed for a job in the bone marrow transplant intensive care unit.

For years, the nursing school has been intentional about creating a welcoming environment for men. It features male students on all its marketing materials. It sends male and female nurses into high schools to recruit students. There's an employee resource group for men in nursing at the university hospital.

Professor Curry Bordelon says all of this makes a difference.

"We're never going to flip the entire iceberg. But I can get one little ice cube at a time out of it," he says. "And when you do that, you're opening up that opportunity for change."

toggle caption Andi Rice//for NPR

A different landscape in the 1990s

Things were very different three decades ago when Bordelon was getting his start in what he calls "small-town Louisiana."

Men made up only 4% of nurses back then. Bordelon first learned about nursing through his aunt, who was a nurse. He was her practice patient.

Out of high school, he worked as a volunteer firefighter and found himself drawn to the medical calls.

From there, he enrolled in a nursing program at a local community college. He remembers his first day, looking around. There were about 90 students in his first class. Just three of them were men. He recalls the instructor telling the guys that the only reason they were there was to satisfy a quota.

"That, to me, was sort of a wake-up," he says. "It was a — 'I want to find my right fit where I can strive.'"

Getting help from someone who looks like you

Bordelon found a more welcoming environment at a different nursing school. Then, he found his calling: working in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), where male nurses are extremely rare.

Sponsor Message

He says fathers in the NICU would sometimes get defensive when they saw him talking to their wives about breastfeeding. But he made a point to include them, too.

"'I'm here to support the entire family unit,'" he says he would tell them. "'Which means — Dad, would you like to do skin-to-skin?'"

That simple action — holding a baby to one's bare chest — is incredibly important for the baby's long-term success, Bordelon says. Not to mention, it prepares fathers for the transition home.

Bordelon is certain that having more male nurses everywhere could improve health outcomes. Studies have found that patients respond better to healthcare providers who look like them.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Nursing student Nicholas Seay, who is Black, has already experienced this during his clinical rotations. He finds older Black men often look relieved when he walks into the room. At times, they seem more at ease talking with him than with the nurse he's shadowing.

"I think they're happy to see [a] familiar face," he says.

Seay has also experienced the opposite: female patients who are not comfortable with him at their bedside. In those situations, he steps aside.

"If I was a woman, I don't know if I'd want a male student in the room either, so I really can't be mad," he says.

"Permission" to be in nursing

Even in the cocoon of the university setting, stereotypes persist.

For one, male nurses are often mistaken for doctors. Chris Jones, a graduate student pursuing a dual master's degree in nursing and business administration, says it happens when he enters patients' rooms, as well as elsewhere in the hospital.

"They would give me the resident discount in the cafeteria, and it's a good discount," he says with a laugh. "I've had to correct them."

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

And because nursing requires patience and compassion — traits traditionally seen as feminine — there are people who assume all male nurses are gay.

Sponsor Message

Bordelon knows persistent stereotyping gives some men pause.

"A lot of times, men need permission to be in the nursing field," he says.

He's happy that popular shows like The Pitt depict men in all kinds of healthcare roles, including nursing. And, he says, the fact that the jobs pay well doesn't hurt. The national median wage for registered nurses tops $90,000 a year.

Jones, who was the first in his family to go to college, says one reason he became a nurse was so that he'd be able to take care of himself.

"And if I wanted to start a family one day, too, that I could do that as well," he says.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

In recent years, nursing has become more technologically advanced, another draw for men, says Steven Parsons, a cardiovascular operating room nurse and adjunct instructor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

Robots are frequently used in lung surgery and sometimes in heart surgery, he says. A robotics team that he was a part of was majority male.

"You've got guys that are kind of interested in that mechanical stuff," he says.

Still, for others, the motivation for going into nursing is personal. Connor Aderholt, a former college baseball player, says he and his brother both decided to pursue careers in nursing after observing the compassionate care their grandmother received after a stroke.

"In that vulnerable moment — in our family's vulnerable moment — it made me realize, this is what I want to do, to deal with these tough situations that people have to deal with," says Aderholt. "To be that calm in the storm for other people."

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Moving the needle faster

This fall, Bordelon will assume leadership of the American Association for Men in Nursing, a national advocacy group. He knows there's still much to tackle.

"Will we ever be 100% gender neutral? I don't know that," Bordelon says. "Can we help move the needle a little faster? Sure, there's opportunities for that."

Sponsor Message

He and a colleague at Purdue University School of Nursing recently scored a big win: getting men's health officially designated as a nursing specialty. Beyond urological issues, Bordelon argues, there are many other factors that drive a shorter life expectancy for men.

"We have women's health nurse practitioners. We potentially could have men's health nurse practitioners," Bordelon says. "That's our dream. That's our goal."

World.title: A homeless man was charged with a felony for camping. He's one of the first
World.content:
A homeless man was charged with a felony for camping. He's one of the first

toggle caption Erica Lynn for NPR

NASHVILLE, Tenn. — In the burgundy booth of a diner, John Lozier leaned in, lowered his voice and asked his friend a question he's carried for nearly two weeks.

"Joe, we haven't talked about when they arrested you," said Lozier, 73.

The man across the table shrugged. Dark sunglasses obscured his gaze. The plastic-sheathed menus still lay open on the table.

"They tased you?" Lozier pressed.

"Yeah," said Joseph Lamont Williams, 49, taking a swig of coffee.

When he refused to leave the Nashville public park where he has lived for the past several years, Williams became one of a handful of homeless people in the country to be arrested and charged with a felony for camping on public property.

Sponsor Message

Eleven states have passed homeless camping bans over the last four years, according to the National Homelessness Law Center. In the two years since the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public, more than 300 municipalities have joined them. Supporters of these laws say they enable public officials to enforce rules that already exist and provide incentive for unhoused people to seek shelter. But opponents call the laws cruel and say that an arrest record only makes it harder for those experiencing homelessness to secure a job or a home.

toggle caption Erica Lynn for NPR

The maximum penalty for felony camping in Tennessee is six years in prison. Williams pled to a lesser charge and was released from jail after nine days.

"The slickest thing was asking me if I knew what I was pleading to," Williams said. "I'm just trying to plead to get out of here."

Lozier, a neighbor and retired social worker who befriended Williams years ago while walking his dog through South Inglewood Park, said he picked him up from jail. He thought it might be nice if Williams saw a familiar face, one who could take him where he wanted to go next.

Williams didn't want to go to a hotel or a shelter or a different part of town. He told Lozier to take him back to his spot in East Nashville.

By nightfall, he was settling back in under the picnic pavilion.

More states are passing anti-camping laws

Williams was one of two people arrested in the park on June 28 and charged under Tennessee's no-camping law — the only one in the country to make sleeping on public property a felony.

Though the law was passed in 2022, advocates for the unhoused say they have never before seen it used like this.

Sponsor Message

Lindsey Krinks, co-founder of Open Table Nashville, a nonprofit homeless support organization, said it's another escalation by officials after years of policies aimed at pushing homeless people out of public view.

"Welcome to the city of Nashville, where luxury condos are going up every few blocks, and everyone living in their shadows are being left out of the progress and sometimes freezing to death or getting heat stroke and dying on our streets," Krinks said.

toggle caption Erica Lynn for NPR

Homelessness in Nashville has been on the rise, according to the city's Homelessness Planning Council, which in December 2025 estimated that roughly 4,300 people experience homelessness in the city, an uptick of more than 30% in less than a year.

Nationally, homelessness has dipped slightly after reaching record levels in 2024. But chronic homelessness has grown, according to 2025 data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. HUD's most recent tally of chronically homeless people in the U.S. found more than 155,000.

Camping bans differ from state to state — some enable the state to level penalties against cities that refuse to enforce the ban; others make it easier for law enforcement to involuntarily commit people experiencing homelessness — but the broad strokes are the same. No camping, or sleeping, on public property.

Many state legislators have taken inspiration, or even borrowed legislative language, from the Cicero Institute, a conservative think tank founded by tech billionaire Joe Lonsdale. Lonsdale is a co-founder of Palantir, whose data mining software has been used by local and federal law enforcement, including the CIA and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Cicero has called for more measurable accountability and ways to push homeless people, under threat of arrest if necessary, to engage with agencies that provide various social services, including shelter space, mental health and addiction treatment and somewhere to sleep in state or county-run campsites.

toggle caption David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images/Bloomberg

Devon Kurtz, who oversees Cicero's homelessness and public safety policy efforts, has been a vocal critic of the longstanding program model known as Housing First, saying it is ineffective. Housing First, which has long been promoted by experts and homeless outreach workers, aims to get unhoused people into stable housing before attempting to address any other needs, such as mental illness and drug or alcohol addiction.

Sponsor Message

Earlier this summer, Cicero supported a law in Louisiana that bans public camping by making it a misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $500 fine and six months in jail. Those charged could forgo jail time if they agree to enter into a program geared toward substance abuse or mental health treatment, the law says. But they could end up on the hook for paying the state back for the costs of such treatment — either in cash or by performing unspecified labor.

North Carolina's legislature also passed a bill outlawing public camping and allowing any resident or business owner to sue the state if an encampment was not cleared within five business days. The bill was vetoed by Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, though lawmakers in the Republican-controlled legislature have vowed to force the law through.

"My hope is that no one is ever convicted under any of these camping bans," Kurtz said. "The intention is not to jail people. I've also said, however, that sometimes, at the margins, it is essential that law enforcement has the ability to jail them because it can save lives."

In Tennessee, Krinks, of Open Table Nashville, said the state has made it easier to clear homeless encampments.

Nashville's oldest homeless enclave, Old Tent City, was disbanded last year. The area along the Cumberland River where more than 100 people once lived is now encircled by fences and no-trespassing signs. Krinks said the encampment had been there since the 1980s.

Krinks has seen more security cameras installed around public parks and benches ripped out of the ground in downtown Nashville. The no-camping felony, she said, only makes things more dire for the city's homeless community.

"Punishing people and using police to address homelessness only makes the crisis worse, and it prolongs people's experience of homelessness," said Krinks, who also helped start the statewide coalition Housing for All Tennessee. "Most people I know experiencing homelessness are so hungry for freedom, for agency, for their dignity to be seen and recognized and understood. Jail erodes every aspect of a person's agency."

Sponsor Message

A changing neighborhood

If you ask Williams how long he's been living in the park, he'll say he doesn't think of it that way. It's not living, he says. It's a place he goes to stay because he doesn't feel like he has anywhere else.

Williams has been offered a bed at a Nashville shelter. He's been approached by service providers over the years. But he doesn't trust those organizations, and doesn't want to leave the neighborhood he considers his own. Instead, he sleeps sprawled across the wooden picnic tables, heats his food up in the sun and does pullups on the monkey bars at the playground.

But the park is not home. Home is the aging public housing complex just up the hill; that's where he grew up. Williams can see it from the picnic benches. No one lives there now.

East Nashville is a historically African American community that has rapidly gentrified over the last two decades and lost many of its Black residents.

"It has changed so much," said Williams, who is Black. "The color boundaries, let's keep it real, that's changed. Putting more, better housing and stuff like that around. Knocking some old ones down."

toggle caption Erica Lynn for NPR

About three months ago, Alex Bilbrey, 33, moved into a house on a lot just across the street from the park. He said he was drawn to the neighborhood, in part, because of the green space — the hiking trails, the wildlife, the pavilion and picnic tables and grills, the playground that he could see from his front door.

Bilbrey noticed the man living under the pavilion, he said, but didn't think much of it.

"I've lived around homeless people before. It's no big deal," Bilbrey told NPR. "But when it becomes a big deal, and I start to see stuff..." His voice trailed off.

Sponsor Message

After dark, Bilbrey said, the park transforms: Cars pull in and out with suspicious frequency, he said. Bilbrey said he's seen men and women have sex out in the open and has found drug paraphernalia on the ground near the jungle gym.

Bilbrey said he contacted his city council representative and suggested they contact Open Table Nashville to come out and help. Later, he called the police. Open Table has no record of being contacted about this case prior to Williams' arrest.

Last month, prosecutors charged Williams with two felony counts of camping and one misdemeanor charge of evading arrest. According to charging documents, Williams attempted to flee after police officers told him they had a warrant for his arrest. That's when he was tased.

Alissa Heydari, a court-appointed attorney who represented Williams in the camping case, said the arrest "makes what is already a very difficult life situation for Mr. Williams harder and worse."

Williams pled guilty to the misdemeanor charge and was sentenced to time served. Prosecutors dropped the two felony counts on the condition of his plea, Heydari said. He was released from custody on July 6, nine days after his arrest.

As far as Cicero is concerned, this is the law working as it should.

"I understand the way it seems a bit ineffective that he ended up right back where he was," Kurtz said. "But even insofar that he is back in that park, the fact that whatever encampment he had created … was cleared, that park is safer. Him being in that park is actually safer."

Bilbrey doesn't think it has changed much. The same shady cast of characters has been showing up again, he said, night after night.

Back to where it began

Williams said he doesn't ruminate on what could happen if he got arrested again.

Sponsor Message

He doesn't want his mind to wander into dark places, he said, or think about what it was like to be behind bars.

Instead, he has returned to his routines: Going on long walks. Making up songs to pass the time. Breakfasts with Lozier.

toggle caption Erica Lynn for NPR

On a recent Friday, they hit the diner. Williams didn't need to read the menu. He always knows what he wants; it's called the lumberjack.

The description reads: "For those who may not see a meal soon."

His plate, stacked high with pancakes and eggs and sausage and bacon and home fries and Texas toast, was clean before Williams got up to leave.

Outside, it was raining. But Williams wanted to walk back to the park. He knows the way; he's lived there his whole life.

World.title: Why Trump is threatening new 50% tariffs on Canadian exports right now
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It may appear that U.S. President Donald Trump's move to hit many Canadian products with new tariffs of 50 per cent came out of the blue, but there are clear signs of what's driving the tactic.

Monday's announcement comes as the U.S. pushes for significant changes to the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), changes that would lock any Canadian trade concessions into the text of a trade deal.

The Trump administration wants to wipe out as much of Canada's leverage in those CUSMA talks as possible.

Some of that leverage comes from eight Canadian provinces banning the import and distribution of U.S. alcohol products — one of the trade irritants the White House said triggered the new 50 per cent tariff.

The U.S. escalation is a big deal but is not unexpected, says Brian Clow, who advised former prime minister Justin Trudeau on Canada-U.S. relations.

"It's not a surprise to the people in government and people who've been watching this closely because they've known for a while that the U.S. may turn up the heat on us," Clow told CBC's Power & Politics on Monday.

WATCH | What you need to know: Trump plans new 50% tariff on Canadian goods | Duration 4:30 U.S. President Donald Trump plans to slap 50 per cent retaliatory tariffs on a new list of Canadian products including wine, hockey sticks and dairy products.

Government should 'react calmly'

While Trump announced the new tariffs in presidential proclamations he issued on Monday, they aren't scheduled to take effect until Aug. 19.

That dangles a carrot to Prime Minister Mark Carney, suggesting Canada could escape the stick of the new tariffs if the government simply capitulates to the U.S. on its demands within the month.

Clow warns the government against responding rashly to the threat.

"They have 30 days, so they should take that time, react calmly, not rush into any quick judgments or decisions here and think about their next steps," he said.

The alcohol boycott has had a visible impact on the U.S. industry. According to U.S. Census Bureau figures, it has resulted in a $360 million US drop in wine exports to Canada in 2025 from the previous year, along with a $150 million US drop in spirit exports.

But retaliation for that boycott is just one of three ostensible reasons U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer gave for the new tariff threat.

"Canada has taken U.S. alcohol products off Canadian shelves, given better market access to dairy products from the European Union, and has put a cap on U.S. vehicle exports to Canada from companies reshoring to the United States," Greer said in a statement.

The tariffs would apply to nearly $20 billion US worth of Canadian goods, according to Greer's office. That's roughly five per cent of the value of Canada's exports to the U.S. in 2025.

WATCH | No need to panic, says auto parts official: 'We shouldn't panic' over Trump's new tariffs, says auto parts association head | Duration 13:59 U.S. President Donald Trump signed proclamations on Monday that impose new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports next month. Power & Politics speaks with president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association Flavio Volpe on how these tariffs would affect Canada.

Milk, wine, whisky… and wigs

The U.S. has listed nearly 500 product categories impacted by the new tariffs, some of which clearly relate directly to trade irritants with the Canadian dairy sector and the provincial alcohol boycotts.

Canadian milk products, wine and whisky are all targets for the 50 per cent duty.

But dozens of products seem chosen at random, with no clear link to the stated trade barriers. Circular saw blades, candles, envelopes, hammers, Christmas decorations, synthetic wigs and plastic cups are among the items that face the 50 per cent tariff.

Some appear to make the list for their status as quintessentially Canadian, including hockey equipment and down jackets.

The list of products facing tariffs to "offset Canadian discrimination against the commerce of the United States with respect to motor vehicles" does not include any motor vehicles or auto parts.

WATCH | What's behind Trump's new threat of 50% tariffs: What will this new wave of tariffs do to U.S.-Canada relations? | Duration 9:25 U.S. President Donald Trump is moving to impose 50 per cent tariffs on many Canadian exports. The rate is five times higher than the current tariff imposed on a limited selection of Canadian products. It's a move that deputy chief of staff to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Brian Clow, tells Power & Politics is going to continue to negatively affect the relationship between the two countries.

"When a country designs a list like this, they go after where they can inflict maximum pain but also suffer the least amount of damage on their own economy," said Clow.

Canadian exports of crude oil, potash and critical minerals are explicitly exempted from the tariff. That's a clear sign that the Trump administration doesn't want to trigger even more of a price increase at the gas pumps than was caused by the war with Iran, nor does it want to hamper U.S. farmers' access to fertilizer or the defence industry's access to military-grade material.

Still, the move would both broaden the scope and increase the size of existing U.S. tariffs on Canadian products.

Currently, the U.S. has a 10 per cent blanket tariff on all goods from Canada.

However, products that comply with the rules of origin in CUSMA are exempt, and that means the vast majority of Canadian exports enter the U.S. tariff-free.

The new tariff would be five times higher and CUSMA-compliant goods would not be exempt.

Never-before-used U.S. law

Trump is imposing the tariffs through a section of a 1930 trade law that has never before been used by a U.S. president.

John Veroneau, senior counsel with Washington, D.C.-based Covington and Burling law firm who also served as a trade official in the George W. Bush administration, says the section was intended to ensure trading partners don't give some countries preferential tariff rates that put the U.S. at a disadvantage.

"It is ironic, to say the least, to use this authority to impose tariffs to retaliate against tariffs that were imposed in response to actions taken by the U.S.," Veroneau told Reuters.

WATCH | Assessing the potential impact of Trump's newly threatened tariff: Trump to impose new 50% tariff on some Canadian exports | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 14:55 U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday imposing 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian exports. The tariff is in response to Canada's 'retaliation and discrimination' against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol, according to a senior Trump administration official.

Trump has threatened to impose new or increased tariffs on Canadian products several times over the past year, but hasn't actually followed through.

He threatened unspecified tariffs on Canada last week over smoke from wildfires, 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian-made aircraft in January, a 100 per cent tariff on all Canadian goods if Canada made "a deal with China" that same month, and an additional 10 per cent tariff on Canadian goods last October in response to a TV ad by the Ontario government.

For those who think Trump will once again chicken out, take note that he issued all those threats on social media or in comments to reporters. This time, he's formalized the threat in official White House proclamations.

He also announced the new tariff plan one day after appearing alongside Carney at the FIFA World Cup final.

Perhaps the timing is a coincidence, or perhaps Trump and his officials realized that slapping high tariffs on the U.S.'s second-largest trading partner while jointly hosting a soccer tournament watched by billions around the globe would be bad optics.

World.title: Trump's escalating trade war puts pressure on premiers with U.S. booze bans as they gather in P.E.I.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's surprise escalation in his trade war with Canada puts renewed pressure on the premiers — most of whom have pulled American booze from liquor stores — as they descend on Charlottetown for their annual summer meeting.

The White House announced on Monday that it will impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of goods in response to what a senior administration official described as Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy and its discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

It upends the tone and focus as the Council of the Federation gathers along the harbourfront starting Tuesday — not far from where the Fathers of Confederation discussed uniting the colonies in the face of American threats some 160 years ago.

Sources said the agenda this week is quickly changing in light of Monday's news; there will now be a virtual meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney Tuesday to discuss Trump's latest salvo. Premiers will also hear from Indigenous leaders Tuesday.

Carney was already scheduled to travel to P.E.I. on Thursday for a face-to-face meeting with the premiers.

Speaking Monday to reporters following a dinner with his counterparts, B.C. Premier David Eby suggested nobody is talking about putting booze back on the shelves. Every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan has banned the sale of U.S. alcohol in retaliation to his previous tariffs on things like the auto sector, steel and aluminium.

The boycotts have been seen as a bargaining chip in the ongoing trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S. and have become an irritant for the Americans as U.S. exports of wine, beer and spirits to Canada plummeting.

"At this point I just feel sorry for Americans. You know, if you're picking fights with Canadians, then you don't have a friend in the world," Eby said.

"I can't make sense of what the president is doing, nobody can."

He also said he has asked staff to contact the U.S. Embassy to have his government's statement marking the two countries' friendship removed from the U.S. 250th birthday website.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Canada should hit back against the latest measures. The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is one of the largest alcohol retailers in the world.

"I'll never stop fighting to protect Ontario. If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," he posted on social media Monday.

American products were pulled off the shelves of the LCBO, one of the largest purchasers of alcohol in the world, last year in response to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

The new tariffs, set to come into place in 30 days, would apply to a variety of Canadian imports, "ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement," the official said. Energy, potash, critical minerals and fish would be exempt, but other products that until now have been allowed into the U.S. tariff-free under terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) would be hit.

This follows the White House's announcement earlier this month declining to extend CUSMA, triggering what are expected to be tough negotiations on amending the continental pact.

Before Monday's news, premiers had listed health care transfers, energy development, economic growth and the wildfires destroying swaths of northern Ontario as priorities for their meetings.

In 2023 the federal government, under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, hiked the annual Canada Health Transfer by five per cent for five years. With the transfers reverting back to three per cent increases come March 2028, the provinces are beating the drum for more federal funding.

"It's very important that before we expand responsibilities, for example, do more on dental care or do more defence spending, that we do honour our commitments to Canadian citizens of providing quality public health care," Quebec Finance Minister Eric Girard told CBC's Power & Politics last week.

Referendums off the official agenda

The meetings also come ahead of what could be internal tests to Canadian unity.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is going ahead with a series of referendum questions in October — including whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or commence the legal process of holding a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

The question of Quebec independence has also been resurrected, with Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon promising to hold a referendum on separation if he secures a mandate in the fall provincial election. While St-Pierre Plamondon's party has been dominating in the polls over the last year, recent surveys suggest the race is tightening.

In an interview late last week, New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the referendums aren't on the official agenda, "but there are also conversations that we have around the coffee pot or as we're moving in and out of different discussions.

"We were one of the four that set Canada up and I believe very firmly in the beauty of this nation from coast to coast to coast and New Brunswick will do whatever we can to keep our country strong and united," said Holt.

World.title: How the outbreak of an intestinal parasite in the U.S. unfolded
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Federal and state authorities in the U.S. have been investigating cases of illness from an intestinal parasite.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that contaminates food that has come into contact with human feces, such as when produce is irrigated or washed with contaminated water.

Cyclosporiasis, the infection caused by the parasite, most commonly causes diarrhea, but some people can experience other gastrointestinal symptoms and dehydration. Symptoms usually start within a week of ingesting the parasite, doctors say.

The illness usually does not spread from person to person.

As of July 20, more than 30 states have reported illnesses, with about 100 hospitalizations to date and no deaths. The true number of infections is likely much higher given that many people recover without seeking medical treatment and that there is lag between when symptoms start and reporting.

Public health officials say they are not currently investiagting any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

The parasite can stick in the nooks and crannies of berries, food scientists say. (Frannyanne/Shutterstock)

Foods imported to Canada that have been linked to the Cyclospora parasite include:

Basil.

Cilantro.

Raspberries.

Blackberries.

Mesclun lettuce.

Snow and snap peas.

Pre-packaged salad mix.

This is how the current outbreak south of the border unfolded and how Canadian health officials reacted.

May 13, 2026

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says this is when the first illnesses from the C yclospora parasite started.

June 30

Michigan state health officials say as of this date, more than 170 cases have been reported across several counties compared with around 50 cyclosporiasis cases per year typically.

July 8

The Public Health Agency of Canada says it is not investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada and tells CBCNews the parasite is not commonly found on food and is not in drinking water here.

"In the spring and summer, there is usually an increase in Cyclospora infections linked to consuming fresh fruit and vegetables imported from other countries," a spokesperson for PHAC said in an email.

July 16

The FDA and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with state and local partners, investigate a multi-state outbreak of Cyclospora illnesses linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.

WATCH | A food scientist explains Cyclospora: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Illnesses start occurring between May 13, 2026, and July 13, 2026. Michigan analyzes food exposure details from 190 of the cases of people who reported eating at Taco Bell and shared these findings with CDC.

The FDA says its traceback investigation to try to find the source converged on a single supplier of iceberg lettuce from Mexico used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill.

Meanwhile, health officials in Alberta say they're investigating an uptick in cyclosporiasis. But the province said no connection has been made between the Alberta illnesses and the American outbreak.

July 17

Taylor Farms de Mexico, which provided shredded iceberg lettuce used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill, is flagged by the FDA as a supplier. The company announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

Health officials in Quebec say that since the beginning of the year, 85 cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported, compared to 30 cases in 2025 for the same period (average of 32 cases annually between 2022 and 2025).

"As in previous years, most Quebec cases are thought to be linked to travel exposure, primarily in Mexico," a spokesperson for Quebec's Ministry of Health and Social Services said in an email.

No Quebec cases appear to be associated with the outbreak in Michigan, they said.

July 18

On July 17, the FDA said Taylor Farms de Mexico, based in Guanajuato and also known as Taylor Fresh Foods, announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

A recall notice put out by Taylor Fresh Foods includes Marketside-brand iceberg lettuce products available at Walmart in the U.S.

July 19

The FDA points to the complexity of detecting Cyclospora, saying its laboratory experts concluded a new sample of shredded lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico tested positive for Cyclospora during import examination at the U.S.-Mexico border. This ended up being a false positive, the FDA said.

July 20

On social media, FDA officials clarify there is still "overwhelming epidemiological data" supporting a large voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.

The Public Health Agency of Canada says is still not currently investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

World.title: Man shot days after Halifax officials asked to take security action at 'dangerous' park
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An overnight shooting at a city-run park across from a Halifax emergency shelter occurred days after municipal officials were urged to take security action to prevent risky behaviour from escalating in the green space, CBC News has learned.

The 1 a.m. shooting on July 12 has deeply affected staff and residents at Metro Turning Point, the city’s homeless shelter for men, according to a statement from Shelter Nova Scotia, which operates the 30-bed facility.

Shelter employees and a person in the area rushed to "keep the injured individual alive until paramedics arrived," said Linda Wilson, CEO of Shelter Nova Scotia, in a statement. The 39-year-old man, who sustained gunshot wounds, was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, said police.

Employees also supported another person who came inside the shelter seeking safety, said Wilson.

Metro Turning Point is directly across the street from Amalamek Way park. (Paul Poirier/CBC)

Dartmouth councillor Tony Mancini, who worked alongside Wilson as a director on Shelter Nova Scotia's board, praised the people who acted "heroically."

"Staff are trained and told not to leave the grounds," he said. Even though the park is not on shelter property, "like good Nova Scotians and Haligonians, when someone's in need, most jump into it and they jumped into it."

The creation of the park — along with a network of realigned roads, safer pedestrian crossings, and high-density lots — was the culmination of reimagining the Cogswell district, one of the city's largest building projects.

Shelter Nova Scotia participated in the district's planning process "over the past decade, and consistently raised concerns related to the design, location and after-hours impacts of the public park" across from the shelter, Wilson said.

It was built anyway, and opened last fall.

The park features a gazebo, picnic benches, a water fountain, raised garden beds, and artwork. The green space is tucked in between the Halifax Water treatment plant and the shelter.

The street was also dramatically altered. Previously, the shelter was highly visible on busy, multi-lane Barrington Street. The road is now a one-way side street with a bike lane called Amalamek Way.

Drug use, partying, fighting and "behaviour that's really inappropriate and dangerous" have been happening in the park at night, said Mancini.

For several months, the non-profit organization incurred the cost of security at the park to the tune of approximately $40,000 to $50,000, he said, even though the property is owned by Halifax Water and leased to the city.

Tony Mancini is a Dartmouth councillor. He previously served on the board of Shelter Nova Scotia. (Mark Crosby/CBC)

When it became clear that two security guards were required to "safely manage the environment," the city took over responsibility, said Wilson.

Halifax brought in security at the end of March, which "seemed to calm things," and withdrew it on May 22, said Mancini.

In July, after problems resumed, Mancini said Wilson sought his help out of frustration. He quickly organized a meeting with the city's parks and recreation department, the community public safety office, Halifax Water, shelter staff, and Virginia Hinch, the councillor for north-end Halifax where the park is located. The city agreed to look into installing fencing with a gate.

Five days after the meeting, there was gunfire in the park.

The suspect fled the scene on an electric scooter after the shooting. Halifax Regional Police continue to investigate the incident, which they do not believe was random.

Overnight security at the city's expense has now been reinstated and police patrols have increased. The plan is to build a fence with a gate to be locked at night. If it continues to be hazardous, removing the park is an option, said Mancini.

Coun. Virginia Hinch represents Halifax Peninsula North. Hinch says she's not surprised Amalamek Way park was the scene of a shooting. (Elizabeth Chiu/CBC News)

Hinch, in her first term as councillor, regretted that the shelter's concerns "fell on deaf ears."

She hopes extra policing and community safety programs will make a difference. She said her district, which stretches from downtown to the city's North End, is home to more than 30 agencies that provide social support including a safe injection site, the needle exchange program, the provincial Department of Community Services, and one of the city's two remaining encampment sites.

Erecting a fence around the park will only move the problem, she said.

"I'm concerned about this community as a whole, to be honest."

World.title: Carney slammed over lack of Gordie Howe bridge opening deal details
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Opposition MPs are expressing increasing frustration over the lack of details about how a deal between the U.S. and Canada to open a long-awaited major border crossing will work, with several calling on the federal government to release a copy of the agreement. Both the Conservatives and NDP have now written to the Liberal government demanding more information about the pact to open the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe International Bridge, which Canada paid for in full. "Canadians are asking for full transparency regarding the costs of this project and the text of the recent Canada-U.S. agreement," NDP MP Heather McPherson, the party's critic for international trade, wrote Monday. "We find it unacceptable that your government has refused to answer questions about this project." The Prime Minister's Office did not respond to a request for comment Monday. Under the original crossing agreement signed more than a decade ago, Canada was set to recoup the costs using toll revenues and then would split the revenues with the state of Michigan. Earlier this month, the Canadian government announced that it had struck a fresh deal with the U.S. to open the bridge connecting Windsor and Detroit on July 27. The statement said the new pact includes provisions around toll management and investment of some profits into an economic development fund for 15 years. It provided few other details. Various spokespeople for federal offices declined at the time to answer questions seeking more details. In the week that followed, Prime Minister Mark Carney offered reporters seemingly contradictory information about the deal — a deal that followed weeks of uncertainty after the bridge's June opening was delayed. Carney and Gregor Robertson, the housing and infrastructure minister, initially said the new pact included a plan to split "net profits" from tolls evenly between Canada and the economic development fund — which Carney has said will go toward the U.S. side of the border. It's unclear how there would be any profits over the next 15 years to split after debt repayments, which Carney said would come first. But on Thursday, he said the split would be of "net revenues" after operational costs, such as maintenance and toll booth staffing. He also said the previous crossing agreement remains in place. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has said the split of net revenues will happen before Canada's debt payments — seemingly contradicting the prime minister's earlier comments. "Our share is before interest and principal," Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick posted on social media. "This is the Art of the Deal in action." The text of the agreement does not include a provision related to Canada's debt repayment, according to Bloomberg News. On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Carney about the differing explanations of the agreement. Prime Minister,

Canadians are not stupid.

Stop speaking in riddles. Stop contradicting yourself in the same breath. Just own up that you signed a deal to hand over half the profits on a bridge, that was 100% built with Canadian tax dollars, before getting repaid.

Release the… https://t.co/DXcRRK7k8z —PierrePoilievre "Yesterday, while answering questions about the deal, you made directly contradictory statements about what you’ve given away," Poilievre wrote. "First, you said, 'It's not splitting the tolls of the bridge.' Then you continued, 'It is an agreement for 15 years to split net revenues.' "But you just said you would not be splitting the tolls, so which is it? Are the Americans getting a cut or not?" Poilievre also questioned Carney's descriptions of when and how Canada's debt would be repaid. The NDP's letter, sent to Robertson and Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, criticized the government's refusal to explain how the bridge's net profits will be calculated, " especially given reports that Canada and the Windsor community may receive fewer benefits from this project than our U.S. counterparts. "Moreover, Canadians are learning more details about this agreement from U.S. sources rather than our own government," McPherson continued. "Canadians paid for this bridge and deserve to know the details."

World.title: The pyramid is back: Dance Moms is getting an unauthorized parody musical
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A trip to the Abby Lee Dance Company meant tears, tutus and grown women fighting over whose eight-year-old deserved the front row.

The 2010s reality show Dance Moms followed an elite group of young dancers — and their dramatic mothers — as they trained and competed under intense pressure.

But the real main event of the Lifetime reality hit was always Abby Lee Miller: a woman who built a career out of ripping apart little girls' chassés and ranking them best-to-worst on a pyramid every single week.

Some of Miller's chastising lines included "save your tears for the pillow" and "I wasn't put on this Earth to make her feel special," among many others.

Now, nearly seven years after the show ended, the show is getting the parody musical treatment

Titled The Pyramid: An Unauthorized 'Dance Moms' Musical, the show now in development all started with a simple question: What if Dance Moms was made into a musical?

That's what college friends James Stryska and Isabelle Grace Blankenship asked each other while wandering through a Goodwill thrift store in Greensboro, N.C., several years ago.

Now they're the show's music and lyrics team, alongside a crew of fellow Dance Moms fans to help them bring the show to life.

What started as a college project turned into their first original song, My Little Kendall, which they posted in 2023 on TikTok. The video racked up more than five million views. The huge response wasn't just coming from fans. Former Dance Moms cast members showed up in the comments with their support.

"It was a really great feeling," Blankenship said. "We were like, 'Oh my gosh, Christi's reaching out, Jill's reaching out.'"

The viral moment also caught the attention of L.A.-based producer Logan Clark, who worked on Dance Moms during its original run. Tye Blue, director and co-creator of Titaníque, another hit parody musical built around Céline Dion, joined as creative producer.

Abby Lee Miller, centre, and dancers Kendall Vertes, left, and Jojo Siwa, right, walk onstage to accept the favourite reality award for Dance Moms during Nickelodeon's 28th annual Kids' Choice Awards on March 28, 2015, in Inglewood, Calif. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Scrolling through TikTok, Clark said he stumbled across the video and immediately saw the potential.

"I kind of sat up and I was like, 'Oh my God ... this could actually happen.'" he said, describing himself as the Dance Moms' "pseudo-husband" back in the day.

As the show's talent co-ordinator, he'd often help get the girls where they needed to be, manage schedules and even handle day-to-day emergencies around their homes — like clogged toilets.

For him, a musical made sense. Dance Moms was supertheatrical — a group of talented young dancers, a whole lot of drama and of course, Abby Lee Miller's pyramid. Miller herself even showed up to an early showcase to offer support.

"Dance Moms was introduced right when social media was taking off," Clark said. "It kind of ran so everybody else could walk. I think for generations it will stay in pop culture."

Craving 'that old school ridiculousness'

And that staying power is real. Long after the cameras stopped rolling, Dance Moms never disappeared. Miller's jabs became viral sounds on TikTok. Old arguments between moms and kids became clips and new audiences became obsessed with the chaos years after it originally aired. Search for the show on TikTok and you'll find more than one million videos.

"It's the perfect kind of show to be clipped for TikTok," comedian and pop culture critic Ashley Ray said. "You see one weird moment and suddenly you're asking, 'Why is this woman yelling at children?'

"I think people sort of crave that old school ridiculousness, that level of drama."

Dancers Maddie Ziegler, left, and Siwa attend Nickelodeon's 2016 Kids' Choice Awards at The Forum on March 12, 2016, in Inglewood, Calif. The two went on to have breakout careers after Dance Moms wrapped. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)

The show's stars continue to make headlines, too.

Maddie Ziegler went from Sia's breakout music-video muse to Hollywood actor, starring in films like My Old Ass and Fitting In.

JoJo Siwa went from a kid-pop star with a multimillion-dollar hair bow empire to a viral personality, shocking fans with her "bad girl" rebrand, claims of originating gay pop and later nabbing a spot on Celebrity Big Brother, where she fell for a Love Island alum.

And Miller stayed in the headlines, too. In 2016, she pleaded guilty to bankruptcy fraud in Pittsburgh, Pa., and spent eight months in federal prison.

Back to the top of the pyramid

Ray says the show stuck around because it captured something that feels familiar to younger generations on social media: constant competition.

"Every week now, everyone gets to create their own pyramid."

Whether it's ranking celebrities, debating who is "flopping" or deciding who deserves the spotlight, Ray said the internet has taken on the same culture of public scrutiny that made Dance Moms so compelling.

The creators behind the new parody musical know audiences will come for the quotes and chaos — and promise them. But they also want to showcase the relationships behind the scenes.

"It's a love letter," Blankenship said. "The show is centred around … mother-daughter relationships and the intricacies."

"We're not trying to make a show that's just all jokes," Stryska added. "These are real people with real experiences."

The team is documenting their progress on social media and crowdfunding the project, with the goal of taking Dance Moms back to the top of the pyramid and onto the stage.

World.title: Kashechewan First Nation evacuees await water testing results to return home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Evacuees from Kashechewan First Nation, who have been away from their homes for more than six months, are now awaiting water testing results to learn if it’s safe to return to the fly-in community.

Officials with Health Canada are in the community collecting water samples after the local water system was successfully flushed with chlorine dioxide.

The Cree community located near Ontario's James Bay coast, has been in a state of emergency since Jan. 4 due to issues with the water treatment plant.

More than 60 people tested positive for a parasite called cryptosporidium that can cause gastro-intestinal issues such as nausea, diarrhea and vomiting.

Tyson Wesley, the First Nation's executive director, said after repairs were completed at the water treatment plant, flushing the system with chlorine dioxide was the final step.

Wesley said that process took longer than expected because the solution was also pumped through fire hydrants and people’s home plumbing to ensure any parasites still in the system were killed.

“We found 30 per cent of the houses had deficiencies in their sinks and their tubs,” he said. “So that’s something that we had to get teams in to fix.”

Tyson Welsey is the executive director of Kashechewan First Nation. (Jamie Pashagumskum/CBC)

Wesley said it will take at least a week before water samples from the remote community can be transported to a Health Canada facility and tested for pathogens.

If the federal agency determines the water is safe to drink, Wesley said Kashechewan’s 1,700 evacuees will be able to return home.

Those evacuees have been living in hotels in several Ontario cities and towns, including Timmins, Kapuskasing, Cochrane, Kingston and Niagara Falls.

Because other First Nations in the northwest are in a state of emergency due to wildfires, however, Wesley said it could take more time to book flights and get evacuees home.

He added that the long evacuation has taken a toll on people’s mental and physical health.

“We're hoping that the government and our funders that support mental health programming can provide more support as we're returning home,” he said.

Annual flooding risk

Kashechewan is at risk of flooding every spring from the Albany River, and some of the community evacuates every year.

Chief Hosea Wesley has called on the provincial and federal governments to move forward with plans to relocate the First Nation to higher ground.

The federal government promised in 2019 to move Kashechewan about 30 km to the south to a location known as "Site 5" within 10 years.

Indigenous Services Canada announced last year that it was approving around $8.4 million to undertake detailed planning studies for the relocation of the community.

World.title: Scale of Calgary-wide search for missing 11-year-old boy 'very rare,' police say, as search enters 5th day
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. As the search for a missing 11-year-old boy entered its fifth day on Monday, Calgary police said the scale of the city-wide search is "very rare," with hundreds of officers and volunteers involved. At a news conference on Monday, police said roughly 500 people have assisted with the search, covering approximately 6,500 kilometres. "This is absolutely not typical for a missing person file," Calgary police acting Staff Sgt. Scott Guterson said. "Searches of this degree are very, very rare in Calgary." Guterson asked the public to continue checking their yards, garages, open vehicles, RVs, sheds, pools or anywhere else a child would go. "We're going to keep hoping that he is alive, and we're going to keep acting as if he is alive, to bring him home as soon as humanly possible." Police released new CCTV footage of the boy they say was captured Thursday at 12:34 p.m. from a business adjacent to McKnight Boulevard and Centre Street N.W. The video was captured prior to previously released footage, Guterson said, in hopes that it will aid with the search. WATCH | Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy: Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy | Duration 2:26 On the fifth day searching for Parker, police released a video of the boy recorded Thursday at a business in the area of Centre Street N.W. and McKnight Boulevard. Investigators also gave an update on the scope of the search. As of Monday, police have received and assessed 150 tips from the public, and are reviewing more than 100 hours of CCTV, residential security camera and dashcam footage. Police are asking anyone with information about Parker's location, or who may have CCTV or dashcam footage, to call 403-266-1234 or reach the police's evidence submission portal. When he went missing on Thursday, Parker was seen shirtless, wearing grey shorts, black Skechers shoes and black noise-cancelling headphones. He’s four feet 11 inches tall and weighs approximately 90 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Guterson said Parker is autistic and functions at a two- or three-year-old level. An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) Police ask that any Calgarians choosing to search on their own do not interfere with police operations. They also ask any volunteer searchers to be mindful of the heat, so they do not end up requiring attention that could divert first responders from the search for Parker. Guterson advised the public that if they come across Parker, they should not engage him, but instead call police. He said they believe the boy is non-verbal, and gets agitated when strangers approach him. Police say Parker's family has expressed that he loves Disney music, so officers have been playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles driving in search areas. We know Parker loves Disney music, so officers are playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles in the search area in the hope that it may help draw his attention and encourage him to come out if he is nearby.

This search remains our highest priority. We'll continue… pic.twitter.com/kGAw6R7uMI —CalgaryPolice Child last seen on Thursday After Parker was seen Thursday at his day home in the 0 to 100 block of Connaught Drive N.W. between 11:08 and 11:41 a.m., the boy was seen in the Thorncliffe neighbourhood between 12:30 and 1 p.m., Guterson said. Clothing that’s believed to belong to Parker was found at noon Thursday in the 0 to 100 block of Northmount Drive N.W., police said. An emergency alert was broadcast on Saturday afternoon for Parker. Although police previously said the case did not meet the threshold for an Amber Alert, as foul play is not suspected, Calgary police said the provincial government made an exception in this case. "We are hopeful that expanding the awareness through the Alberta emergency system will generate new information that may help us locate him," said acting Insp. Rod MacNeil . On Saturday, police released a CCTV photo of the boy, captured when he was last seen on Thursday on the 5000-6000 block of Travis Crescent N.E., in hopes it might aid in the search. WATCH | More CCTV footage of Parker: CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary | Duration 0:27 Footage released by the Calgary Police Service on July 19, shows missing 11-year-old, Parker, walking past a home on Travis Crescent N.E. on Thursday, July 16, 2026. On Sunday, police released additional CCTV footage of the boy taken at 12:52 p.m. Thursday in the 5500 block of Travis Crescent N.E. They had released a similar photo the day prior, in hopes it might help the search. Police also said Sunday that search efforts are being increasingly focused on areas connected to Parker's last known movements. Guterson said police know the boy likes water and part of their search has been to check whether he's near bodies of water. He said Parker tends to lock doors behind him, meaning people searching their properties should take the time to check behind doors even if they're locked. Family issues statement In a statement, Parker's family said they have been living "every parent's worst nightmare" since he went missing. "Every hour that passes without knowing where he is or whether he is safe has been incredibly difficult for us," the family said in its statement, sent out by CPS on their behalf shortly after Saturday afternoon's emergency alert. The family implored people to continue searching their properties for Parker. "Parker experiences the world in his own way. He may not respond when his name is called, and he can become frightened when approached by people he does not know," the family said. "Parker is deeply loved, and he is missed immensely. We just want our son home." An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) CPS said it is aware of AI-generated, altered and unverified images of Parker or his whereabouts circulating online, and cautioned the public against viewing or sharing the content. "Unverified images, videos and claims can create confusion, spread misinformation and divert investigative resources away from credible leads that may assist in locating Parker," CPS said in a social media post on Monday. Situations like this warrant emergency alert, advocate says For Calgary mom Stephanie Karas, Saturday afternoon's emergency alert came far too late. "We've gotten alerts for tornadoes that have not touched down. We've gotten alerts for less, so I don't know why there wasn't," she said. Karas, a mother of two children with autism, says she's lobbying the municipal and provincial governments to create an emergency alert protocol specifically for situations like this. "Why isn't there something for vulnerable youth and adults that aren't equipped?" Karas said. WATCH | Why there are calls to expand Amber Alerts as police search for autistic Calgary boy: "It's long overdue, so somebody's got to start it," she said. "And if the people of Calgary have to start it and are motivated behind Parker, then that's what we'll do." MacNeil said Calgary police indicated to the province that "it may not be a true Amber Alert, but we need to reach as many Calgarians as we can in such a short amount of time." "The government stepped up right away, made that exception and we were able to get that alert out," he said. In a statement to CBC News, the provincial government said it "worked closely with CPS to assess the situation and determined that this measure to increase the public’s awareness of this missing child in these extremely particular circumstances was important."

World.title: I’m 60 and ashamed that my husband is aging better than me. Am I too vain? | Ask Rebecca
World.content:
Article content

I turned 60 recently, and I’m embarrassed to be writing this because it feels so vain. My husband seems to be getting more attractive with age. He’s five years older than I am. He started working out regularly a couple of years ago, eats healthy, and is in great shape. My friends even tell me how handsome he is. I know I should be happy about that, and I am. The problem is that when I look in the mirror, I don’t feel the same way about myself. I see someone who’s aged in ways I wasn’t expecting. Some days I barely recognize the person staring back, and it’s made me more self-conscious than I’d like to admit.
