World.title: Merz turns resignation of party bigwig to his advantage
World.content:
The reshuffle is attractive to Merz because Spahn was sometimes an obstacle to him: The 46-year-old former health minister was not only an internal party rival who at times pushed back against his plans, but was also disliked by the more left-wing politicians amid his coalition partners in the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

With Spahn gone, Merz can choose a new CDU parliamentary leader to settle down the coalition. A cabinet reshuffle also allows him to make a political reset before crucial regional elections in the fall, in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is expected to perform well and could even secure an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt in September.

Merz’s spokesman Stefan Kornelius said the chancellor was now weighing his next move.

“There are always possibilities — that is, they exist, or they are seized upon, or they are not seized upon — and once a decision has been made, I think [the chancellor] will let us know,” Kornelius told reporters. “The process is underway.”

Merz and fellow high-ranking conservatives are expected to come up with a concrete proposal over the coming days.

Following a CDU leadership meeting on Monday, conservative lawmakers were asked to prepare for a gathering in the Bundestag on Wednesday next week — despite the ongoing summer recess — to elect a new parliamentary group leader, according to a message sent to lawmakers and seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Four drone strikes in four days hit tankers carrying Kazakhstan's oil
World.content:
In four days, four tankers meant to transport crude oil produced in Kazakhstan were attacked by drones while loading at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal in the Black Sea.

 

The foreign and energy ministries of Kazakhstan condemned the attacks, stating that they undermined global energy security and the economic interests of CPC member countries.

"We regard such attacks as an unacceptable infringement upon the economic interests of the Republic of Kazakhstan, as well as deliberate acts aimed at destabilising lawful international trade and global energy markets and undermining the security of global transport and logistics supply chains," the Kazakh foreign affairs ministry said in a statement.

According to the ministry, the attacked ships were “civilian vessels engaged in the legitimate commercial transportation of oil.”

Astana has demanded that all attacks cease and has asked partner countries to condemn them as well.

The attacks are widely attributed to Ukraine, which has mounted repeated drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure throughout the full-scale invasion with the aim of cutting one of Moscow's largest sources of revenue funding its war machine.

CPC itself has not formally attributed responsibility for any of the incidents. Ukraine has not publicly claimed the strikes.

The timeline of attacks

The Nordic Zenith tanker was attacked on Friday while empty and en route to the CPC marine terminal, where it was scheduled to load Kazakh oil. The strike caused a fire, which the crew extinguished. No casualties were reported.

On Sunday, tankers ASIA, sailing under the flag of Liberia, and NISSOS IOS (Marshall Islands) were attacked while loading at the CPC terminal. As a result of the attack, a fire broke out on both vessels, which the crews managed to extinguish.

According to the Kazakh ministry of energy, Single Point Mooring (SPM) facilities were not damaged, and no oil was spilt.

On Monday, CPC reported another drone attack on Cameroon-flagged civilian tanker NELSA, which was loading at SPM-1. The hit caused a fire and 22 crew members were evacuated. The tanker stayed afloat, while an oil spill was prevented, according to authorities.

“At present, crude oil loading operations at the terminal have been suspended pending a full assessment of the consequences of the incident,” the Kazakh energy ministry said.

Kazakh foreign ministry added that the attacks were a "deliberate" breach of previously agreed-upon procedures for exchanging information about civilian ships coursing in the Black Sea.

The ministries said that Astana reserved the right to seek compensation under international law.

Four-fifths of Kazakh oil flows through CPC

The CPC is Kazakhstan's main oil export route, transporting crude from the country's largest fields — Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak — through a 1,510-kilometre pipeline to the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk for shipment to international markets.

The route handles more than 1% of global oil supply and around 80% of Kazakhstan's oil exports, making it a critical artery for the Eurasian country's economy. Prolonged disruptions could reduce export revenues, lower tax receipts and place additional pressure on Kazakhstan's budget and currency.

According to CPC, the consortium shipped approximately 70.5 million tonnes of crude in 2025, more than three-quarters of which belonged to foreign shareholders. Major producers using the pipeline include Chevron, ExxonMobil, KazMunayGas, Eni and Shell.

The CPC press service reported that the oil to be loaded onto the attacked ships was coming from the Tengiz and Kashagan fields.

"We emphasise that this is already the fifth act of direct aggression against a purely civilian CPC facility, which is protected by international law," CPC stated.

They also noted that the company is not under any sanctions and plays an important role in global energy security.

The CPC members include Russia, the US, Kazakhstan and several western European countries.

World.title: Lebanese army begins deployment to southern regions after Israel deal
World.content:
The Lebanese army announced on Tuesday that it had begun deploying to an area in the south, one of three "pilot zones" outlined in a deal with Israel to disarm Hezbollah.

 

The announcement came with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun visiting Washington, which brokered the deal with Israel.

Israel invaded Lebanon during its recent war with Iran-backed militants Hezbollah, and it has continued to occupy parts of the country despite a ceasefire agreement in place.

To date, Israeli troops have only controlled the outskirts of one of the so-called pilot zones, with their occupation of other areas yet to be addressed. The Lebanese military already has a presence in the other two pilot zones.

Lebanese army soldiers stand at a checkpoint in Froun village, southern Lebanon, Thursday, July 16, 2026 Mohammed Zaatari/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

"Military units began deploying this morning to Zawtar al- Gharbieh" in the Nabatieh region, the army said in a statement.

The announcement comes as Aoun prepares to meet with his US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday to wrap up his four-day visit, aiming to bring about long-term calm in the war-torn country after months of war and occupation.

Joseph Aoun's landmark meeting with Trump comes as Lebanon and Israel continue to hold rare direct talks mediated by Washington. Lebanon hopes they will result in Israeli troops withdrawing from large swaths of their southern regions, but talks have not yet produced tangible results on that front.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has previously asserted that he had no intention of removing Israeli troops from the region, arguing that in the absence of a domestic front against Hezbollah, IDF forces will maintain their presence to secure northern regions of his country.

A Lebanese army soldier stands at a checkpoint in Froun village, southern Lebanon, Thursday, July 16, 2026 Mohammed Zaatari/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Lebanon and Israel announced a “framework agreement” on 26 June, setting a plan for IDF forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon as well as the disarmament of Hezbollah, which for decades had a strong presence in the area.

It also laid out steps toward an eventual peace arrangement between both countries, which have never held formal diplomatic ties and have been nominally in a state of war for nearly 80 years since Israel’s establishment.

The US State Department announced on Monday that operations in three villages deemed part of a “pilot zone” had begun, without giving details on what that entailed.

Lebanese women pass by houses that were destroyed in Israeli strikes during the war with Hezbollah in Froun village, southern Lebanon, Thursday, July 16, 2026 Mohammed Zaatari/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Two of the three villages, Froun and Srifa, are not under Israeli military control and the Lebanese army is present there, while Israeli forces are present in part of Zawtar al-Gharbieh.

The Lebanese army in a statement said it was preparing for Israel to withdraw from Zawtar al-Gharbieh and that it had begun deploying troops to the area Tuesday.

The Israeli military said it “will adjust its force posture in one of the pilot areas in order to enable the Lebanese Armed Forces to carry out their mission,” without specifying the location. A spokesperson for the IDF added that withdrawals have not yet begun and did not specify a timeline of when that is planned to take place.

World.title: Anger mounts in Italy after Moroccan man dies under police restraint while pleading for help
World.content:
Human rights campaigners, protesters and Italian politicians expressed outrage after a man died while under police restraint as he pleaded for help in Bologna.

 

Abderrahim Fakir, a 42-year-old from Morocco who moved to Italy when he was five, died on Sunday while being forcibly held down by two police officers, according to a video shared widely on Italian media.

In the video, Fakir,who reportedly suffered from heart issues and asthma, repeatedly calls out "aiuto, aiuto, basta" ("help, help, that's enough") as the officers sit on him and ambulance workers look on.

After he stops moving, the police bind his ankles together.

Only after a moment or two do they and the ambulance workers check his vital signs, the video shows.

Called to the scene by local residents concerned by Fakir's erratic behaviour, the police officers had told the ambulance personnel that he was "having a psychiatric episode", according to media reports.

The incident has been likened to George Floyd's murder in the United States six years ago, and also prompted comparisons with tactics used by the US's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) under President Donald Trump.

Political division over officers' conduct

The incident triggered a protest in Bologna on Monday in which participants called for "justice and truth for Fakir".

Opposition parties also denounced the police officers' conduct. Senator Ilaria Cucchi, whose brother died in custody in 2009, said she was sickened by the "solidarity and thanks" expressed to police after such an "inhumane act".

Cucchi, a member of the opposition Greens and Left alliance (AVS) party, slammed far-right Meloni and her coalition government, saying their "policies seeped in hatred and racism" have fostered a climate of violence.

Francesco Boccia, head of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD) in the Senate, told the Repubblica daily that "if the right wants to import the ICE model, this is the wrong country for it. We have democratic antibodies".

Meanwhile, Italy's far-right Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini defended the police, while Galeazzo Bignami, head of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy party in parliament's lower house, praised the officers' "professional conduct".

Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi told state television network Rai1: "Whoever makes insulting remarks against the police shows they have no trust in our law enforcement nor in our justice system (and) should look into what happened."

Prosecutors in Bologna have opened a probe and have requested the officers' body cam footage.

What is the 'legal shield' and why nobody has been named as a suspect in the Fakir case

Pending the results of the autopsy and the examination of witness statements and footage by the judiciary, a so-called "legal shield" has been activated for six people: the two officers and the four medical workers involved. This was confirmed by Justice Minister Carlo Nordio.

In an interview with Corriere della Sera, Nordio rejected the idea that there is any ICE‑style model in Italy, saying: "The expression “legal shield” suggests an immunity that does not exist. What is avoided is the automatic entry in the register of suspects, which has become a kind of conviction in advance. It is now up to the judiciary to assess whether grounds of justification do or do not exist."

The legal shield applies to cases where conduct potentially amounting to a criminal offence may have been committed in the presence of a ground of justification, such as self‑defence or the fulfilment of a duty. There is therefore no formal investigation with individuals entered in the register of suspects, but a preliminary verification phase.

Information obtained so far shows that the officers used pepper spray to neutralise Fakir before pinning him to the ground, but the man had wounds to his head and face. How he sustained them has not yet been determined.

The autopsy will be crucial in establishing how the 42‑year‑old died: prosecutor Domenico Ambrosino and chief prosecutor Paolo Guido are working to appoint a committee of specialists. The suspected offence is manslaughter.

World.title: Three wounded in strike on Ukraine-bound LPG tanker off Romania in the Black Sea
World.content:
A strike on a ship in the Black Sea carrying propane to the Ukrainian port of Reni wounded three crew members and forced everyone onboard to evacuate, according to a statement by Romania's President Nicușor Dan on Tuesday.

 

"Last night, the LPG tanker Gas Lisbon, flying the Liberian flag, was struck outside Romanian territorial waters, approximately 20 nautical miles off the Romanian coast," said the Romanian leader in a post on X.

“Shortly after the incident, two vessels from the Romanian Agency for the Salvage of Human Life at Sea proceeded to the scene and evacuated the entire crew, including the three injured members. All were brought safely to shore.”

Dan added that that state authorities have been mobilised and tasked with conducting investigations to determine the exact “circumstances, causes and responsibilities” related to what he called a “serious incident”, which he believes to be “most likely” a crime perpetrated by Russia.

The vessel was en route to the port of Reni in Ukraine, located on the Danube River next to the border with Romania. The ship had departed carrying more than 3,790 tonnes of propane from the Egyptian port city of Alexandria, and the strikes reportedly caused a major fire on board the vessel.

Rescuers and paramedics walking at a docking area in Tulcea, Romania, after an LPG tanker ship sailing towards a Ukrainian port caught fire, Tuesday, July 21, 2026, ISU Tulcea via AP/ISU Tulcea via AP

Russian attacks continue to pummel Ukraine

Meanwhile, Russian attacks are continuing to pummel Ukrainian cities on a daily basis as the Kremlin looks to ramp up pressure and shows no signs of letting it up its war, well into its fifth year.

Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin carried out strikes on multiple cities overnight into Tuesday. Earlier, Ukraine’s Air Force said it had intercepted 46 of 58 drones fired across the border from Russia, in what is its latest barrage of an intensified offensive.

In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, firefighters put out a fire following a Russian air attack in Sumy, Ukraine, Tuesday, July 21, 2026 Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP/Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP

They added that the attacks targeted many areas, including Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson and the industrial eastern Donbas region, which has been majority occupied by Russia for years, and makes up roughly 22% of the country.

Attacks in Kherson killed one regional administration employee, according to local officials, while another woman sustained what were described as “fatal injuries”.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, authorities say strikes in Chernihiv and Sumy caused major fires to erupt, prompting local response teams to intervene and put out the blazes.

In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, firefighters put out a fire of residential building following a Russian air attack in Sumy, Ukraine, Tuesday, July 2 Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP/Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP

Ukraine strikes back

Kyiv has also launched its own counteroffensive operations, with Ukrainian media detailing that attacks on Russia’s western city of Lipetsk caused fires to break out at industrial facilities in the early hours of Tuesday.

Lipetsk Regional Governor Igor Artamonov said that a fire had broken out, noting that authorities have launched an investigation to determine the causes, though declined to confirm that an attack had taken place.

A Ukrainian soldier practices military skills at a training ground near the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, Saturday, June 20, 2026 Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian 65 Mechanized brigade

The complex in question is the NLMK steel plant, located about 400 kilometres east of Ukraine’s border, and is Russia’s largest steel producer, accounting for approximately 20% of the country’s steel output.

Ukrainian media say the plant supplies steel to companies involved in missile production for the Russian military.

World.title: Iran's IRGC claims attack on Amazon's main data hub in Bahrain
World.content:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has claimed on Tuesday that its Aerospace Force targeted and "destroyed" the central data infrastructure of the US company Amazon in Bahrain using several cruise missiles.

 

The IRGC also said in a statement released by its public relations office that "US air defence systems and radar installations in the Bahraini areas of Muharraq and Riffa were also targeted" in the attack.

Bahraini and US officials, as well as Amazon, have not yet responded to the claim.

The reported strikes come as direct military confrontations between Iran and the US have continued for the tenth consecutive day despite diplomatic efforts and exchanges of messages between the two sides.

As the US has intensified its attacks on Iranian infrastructure, Tehran has warned that if such attacks continue, it will target facilities and infrastructure in regional countries that are made available to or used by US forces.

US President Donald Trump has vowed to make Iran pay “many times over” for the recent deaths of three US soldiers in Jordan and Iraq.

In the same statement, the IRGC said the attack was carried out in response to what it described as "yesterday's US military aggression against the under-construction, civilian facilities in Darkhovin."

At the same time, Iran's Permanent Mission to the International Organisations in Vienna issued a statement calling on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United Nations Security Council to condemn the US attack on the under-construction Darkhovin nuclear power plant.

The IAEA has also said it is reviewing reports of the attack but has not yet issued an independent assessment of the incident.

World.title: One in five EU jobs classed as vulnerable and Spain tops the list, report says
World.content:
"A multidimensional phenomenon encompassing income inadequacy, employment insecurity and lack of workplace rights," is how Eurofound defines employment vulnerability for living and working conditions.

 

In its latest report, the tripartite EU agency providing knowledge to assist in the development of better social, employment and work-related policies, found that 18.8% of jobs across the EU, close to one in five, fell below the bar on at least one of those definitional dimensions in 2021, the most recent year with comparable income data.

However, the direction of the trend is encouraging.

Vulnerability climbed from 21.4% in 2009 to 23.8% in 2014 in the wake of the financial crisis, driven by a surge in involuntary temporary and part-time work, before declining steadily from 2016 onwards to below its pre-crisis level.

That chimes with the agency's overview of its 2024 working conditions survey, published in April, which reported gradually improving job quality in Europe alongside persistent divides.

A very uneven map

Spain has the highest vulnerability rate at 29%, followed by Portugal and Luxembourg at 25% and Italy at 24%, while Hungary (17%), Malta and Bulgaria (both 18%) record the lowest levels.

Data from 2021 is unavailable for Cyprus, Czechia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania and Sweden, therefore those countries were excluded from the study.

The nature of the problem differs as much as its scale.

In continental countries such as Germany and Austria, and across central and eastern Europe, low pay is the dominant driver, accounting for nearly three quarters of vulnerability in Bulgaria in the report's 2019 breakdown.

Elsewhere the culprit is insecurity as involuntary temporary and part-time work dominates in Mediterranean and Nordic states, and contributes 56% of the total in Ireland, the highest share in the EU.

Luxembourg's surprising position near the top reflects the fact that pay is measured against each country's own median income.

Who carries the risk

Women, young workers, migrants, Roma, people with disabilities and LGBT+ individuals are all disproportionately likely to hold vulnerable jobs, held back by discrimination, care responsibilities and, for migrants, legal hurdles and unrecognised qualifications.

Education offers powerful protection.

For example, in Hungary, 58% of workers with low levels of education are vulnerable against just 6% of graduates.

So does time, as each additional year in the labour market cuts the risk by one percentage point, roughly 20% over a 20-year career.

Youth vulnerability can be striking, with 59% of young Danish workers vulnerable in 2015 against 11% of adults, although in Nordic countries it is largely a transitory phase on the way to stable jobs.

The cost of stacking disadvantages

Vulnerability in a single dimension is not a sentence to a bad working life, and such employees sometimes report better outcomes than their secure colleagues, on work intensity for instance.

"It is the accumulation of multiple vulnerabilities that consistently leads to negative outcomes," the report finds, listing poorer prospects, limited access to training, less autonomy and unpredictable earnings.

The toll is mental rather than physical as highly vulnerable workers show higher rates of anxiety and depression, even though they are less likely to report work-related stress.

Although that reads counterintuitively, it is precisely what the survey data show, and the report presents both findings without attempting to reconcile them as the causes for that increase in anxiety and depression are evidently not work-related.

With the European Commission's Quality Jobs Act under consultation, Eurofound argues that flexibility must be preserved without letting atypical work erode standards, and that rules are only as good as the labour inspectorates enforcing them.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: How India's youth-led 'Cockroach' movement challenges Modi
World.content:
What started as a satirical protest against exam leaks in India has grown into a wider movement voicing young Indians' anger over jobs and education.

Riot police fired tear gas and used batons in New Delhi as tens of thousands of supporters of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) marched towards India's Parliament on Monday (July 20).

Police in the Indian capital said 60 protesters and 118 police officers were injured in the clashes between demonstrators and security forces. Mobile internet was suspended in parts of the city, including around the Jantar Mantar protest site, during the violence.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Earlier this year, authorities canceled the high-stakes NEET medical entrance exam over a leaked question paper, affecting millions of students and sparking outrage across India.

What is India's Cockroach Janta Party?

The CJP began as an online campaign in May and rapidly evolved into a Gen Z street movement, giving a voice to a generation frustrated by unemployment, shrinking opportunities and a failing education system.

The protesters attempted to march toward India's Parliament Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

The youth-led "Cockroach" party is now posing an unexpected challenge for Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, prompting a response that combines political outreach with police action.

Modi's rivals have also tried to step in and take advantage of the youth's frustrations.

"Is this how a government behaves? Using tear gas and baton charges against students? This is a worthless government," Renuka Chowdhury, an MP from India's opposition Congress party, told DW.

Lessons from earlier protests in India

The CJP movement gained fresh momentum over the weekend after veteran reform activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose three-week hunger strike has become a symbol of the protests, was forcibly taken to a hospital by police.

It is not the first time India has experienced major protest movements. Hunger strikes, famously used by Mahatma Gandhi, remain a common and peaceful form of protest in India.

India Against Corruption (IAC) led by veteran activist Anna Hazare, managed to mobilize millions in 2011 and reshape the country's political landscape. A decade later, yearlong farmers' protests forced Modi to repeal controversial farm laws. However, a 2023 Olympic wrestlers' protest over allegations of sexual harassment achieved few of their goals, despite widespread sympathy.

Analysts say the CJP lacks a nationwide organizational network, which the farmers had at their disposal. Yet like the IAC movement, it has tapped into a broader public mood.

"This protest is different because it reflects a much broader cross-section of Indian society," said Yamini Aiyar, an analyst and senior visiting fellow at Brown University. "They are expressing their frustration with a country whose long-atrophied education system has left them with very little hope of a better future."

"Like the IAC movement, it has drawn the middle class onto the streets," Aiyar told DW. "But this is a far more coercive political environment. From the anti-citizenship protests to the farmers' movement, citizens have increasingly looked beyond political parties to hold governments to account."

Police response sparks backlash among Indian protesters

This week's clashes have done little to quell the anger among India's Gen Z.

"Like many young people across India, I am angry about a lack of jobs and an education system that crushes my aspirations. Even though my family supports the BJP, I managed to get away," Rukmini Singh, a student from Meerut, told DW.

"This was an attack against our children. I saw many young boys and girls hurt and bleeding. They will never forget it but the courage these people displayed gives me hope," Vasundara Singh, a teacher from Bihar, told DW.

As during the farmers' protests, leftist parties and student organizations have become visible on the ground, helping mobilize supporters and giving the movement organizational backing.

"After 50 years, youth have occupied the road to parliament," political activist Yogendra Yadav told DW. "This energy by the students shows that the path to parliament goes through the streets. It is remarkable."

Can CJP mobilize India's villages as easily as its cities?

The surge in protest numbers forced the government to engage with the movement after weeks of dismissing it.

Alongside the police action, senior ministers opened talks with CJP leaders. Home Minister Amit Shah met cabinet colleagues while Health Minister J P Nadda held discussions with representatives of the movement.

"We will decide on how best to address the students' demands," a senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP, told DW on condition of anonymity.

Most CJP support appears to come from students and India's urban middle class. The BJP's strongest electoral base remains in rural India and smaller towns, where the CJP has yet to prove that its message resonates with young voters.

However, some experts believe that the CJP will do just fine beyond India's urban centers.

"This movement is likely to resonate beyond India's cities because the aspirations of young people in small towns and villages are no different," political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan told DW.

India's 'cockroach' protests meet with batons and tear gas To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"For a generation that saw education as the route to a better life, the failure of the education system has become a deeply political issue," she said.

"Young people in rural India no longer see farming or traditional occupations as their only future. Whether the CJP itself survives is another matter, but the anger and frustration it has tapped into have the potential to reshape politics."

'The anger is now directed at the government'

A movement focused on India's cities may generate headlines without altering the BJP's political fortunes. But if the CJP spreads to rural youth, it could become a much broader political challenge.

"I don't think this will remain an urban movement," said commentator Apoorvanand.

"People constantly move between villages and cities, and those who witnessed the police action will carry those experiences home," Apoorvanand told DW.

"The anger is now directed at the government. Whether it becomes a broader political movement depends on the CJP's ability to widen its appeal."

For now, the CJP has already achieved something unusual. It has transformed satire into sustained street mobilization, forced the government into talks, and ensured that the concerns of India's young people remain firmly in the national spotlight.

"This is a long fight. We will have to engage in a very long struggle for this. Because you have to change an entire system, the nexus of that system is very deep-rooted," said Saurav Das, CJP's chief spokesperson.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Italy: Protests in Bologna over death of immigrant in police custody
World.content:
Demonstrators are demanding answers over the death of 42-year-old Abderrahim Fakir. Local authorities have urged calm while the investigation is underway.

A day after police and protestors clashed in the northern Italian city of Bologna, local authorities on Tuesday urged residents to remain calm and await the results of an official investigation into the death of Abderrahim Fakir.

"They killed my brother in cold blood, I want justice," Fakir's sister Khadija told reporters following his death in the city's Pilastro neighborhood on Sunday.

What do we know about the death of Abderrahim Fakir?

According to Italian media, Fakir came to Italy from Morocco at the age of 7 with his family, and they settled in Bologna. He ran a cleaning business and was a legal permanent resident of Italy. He was in Pilastro visiting friends, family members reported.

Bologna Police have said that they were called to the neighborhood on Sunday morning, responding to a call about a man causing damage to a vehicle.

Officers said that it was some 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) when they arrived, and that they tried to subdue Fakir with pepper spray before holding him down and handcuffing him when he continued to be aggressive.

In a video widely circulated online, Fakir can be seen repeatedly calling for help and struggling to breathe before he stops moving. His family told Italian media that he had a history of asthma and heart problems, that he was married and not known to have any previous run-ins with authorities.

Protests in central Bologna

On Monday, a demonstration was held in Bologna's famous Piazza del Nettuno. Italian news agency ANSA reported that some protestors chanted anti-police slogans and one threw a firecracker, but that demonstrators were largely peaceful.

ANSA added police responded with tear gas and water cannons.

Italy's two main police unions have accused activists of using social media to conduct online witch hunts against police based on incomplete footage of the event and said that dozens of officers were injured in clashes with protestors.

Local authorities have urged calm, saying a thorough inquiry is being carried out. Bologna Police have said they plan to release the bodycam footage in full to investigators.

Bologna health authorities have said they are also launching an investigation into how long it took to arrive on the scene.

Police released smoke canisters to disperse protestors Image: Michele Lapini/REUTERS

How have lawmakers responded?

Mayor Matteo Lepore of the center-left Democratic Party (PD) also urged residents to await the full picture, but said you could tell that "something clearly went wrong."

"You cannot die like this," he said, appearing alongside some of Fakir's loved ones. At the same time he expressed his confidence in the rule of law in the city and that the truth would be borne out.

He thanked a niece of Fakir for calling for "respect, truth, and justice, not revenge."

Italy's far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has also called for the full truth to come to light, but accused online agitators of fomenting "hatred against the police."

World.title: Why the youth jobs crisis is becoming global
World.content:
Young people in much of the world face growing competition for entry-level jobs as graduate numbers rise, hiring slows and AI-driven disruption adds uncertainty to career prospects.

The youth job crisis that first became obvious in China points to major economic and social problems that governments and businesses need to address.

Last year, unemployment, weak job prospects and a general lack of economic opportunities drove young people onto the streets in Kenya, Peru, Nepal, Indonesia and the Philippines.

This year, concerns about youth unemployment have added fuel to protests in South Africa and Morocco. In India, they helped give rise to the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that started as a satirical social media project but quickly gained national attention.

China's youth unemployment problem

Youth unemployment refers to the share of young people, typically aged 15 to 24, who are actively seeking work but cannot find it. The rate is usually higher than overall unemployment because young people have less experience and networking opportunities, but that gap is widening in a growing number of countries.

China became an early example of the problem as university enrolment and graduate numbers grew faster than job creation, contributing to anxiety, long job searches and underemployment during a period of weaker economic growth.

In May, the official unemployment rate among ​urban 16 to 24-year-olds in ‌China was ​15.6%, according to Reuters news agency based on National Bureau of Statistics data.

While this represents the lowest level ⁠in 11 ​months, it remains three times higher than the overall unemployment rate of around 5%. Since 2023, the Chinese youth unemployment figures exclude the millions of university students, making comparisons with older data harder.

Is AI reshaping entry-level job opportunities?

China is not the only country with weak growth, slowing upward mobility, or a sense of intergenerational inequality.

In other countries, technology, sluggish hiring and rising competition have also weakened the link between a university degree and a secure white-collar career.



Besides the growing number of graduates, another factor eating away at confidence is the fear that artificial intelligence (AI) could turn into a massive entry-level job destroyer. Experts are not yet clear about its impact.

A decade after Brexit, youth in Britain want the EU back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"In the UK, new postings for graduate jobs have fallen faster than for non-graduate jobs, and many of these roles are highly exposed to AI," said Golo Henseke, an associate professor in applied economics at University College London.

His research has shown that "where firms have taken up AI faster, employment of 15 to 24-year-olds has grown more slowly, while prime-age employment holds up." But for now, the AI-effect is small compared to the regular business cycle.

Sara Elder, a youth employment expert at the Geneva-based International Labour Organization (ILO), agrees. AI may be one of the current drivers of stagnating youth employment, but she considers other factors more important.

Right now, economies are not dynamic and job creation is just not keeping pace with the number of young people seeking jobs, says Elder.

"This is then exacerbated by the tendency of employers to raise hiring criteria in ways that make it more difficult for young people with little job experience to get their foot in the door," said Elder.

What type of jobs are impacted where?

Without these entry-level jobs, young people may never get the experience they need for better jobs. Consequences could be lower consumption, lower home ownership rates and delayed family formation — not to mention widespread frustration.

Currently across Europe, there is no broad youth jobs crisis, says Henseke, who specializes in education, labor markets and human resources.

Since 2022, the share of young people not in employment, education, or training has increased in only a handful of European countries like Austria and Germany and fallen in much of southern Europe.

"Youth unemployment is not new to Europe either," said Henseke. "It was severe after the financial crisis, and the biggest improvements since have been in the countries that struggled most then."

Youth employment growth is strong in Latin America, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, even if the quality of jobs is low, says the ILO's Sara Elder Image: Stefan Sauer/dpa/picture alliance

But the ILO found that between 2023 and 2025 youth unemployment rates rose in eight of the world's 11 regions, like East Asia, North America (the US and Canada), Southeast Asia and the Pacific.

Opportunities for young people have declined in manufacturing, construction and the service sectors, in particular.

"Jobs for young people in high-skilled knowledge-based technical areas, like science, engineering, health and information and communication technologies, have fared better, showing continued growth in most countries," said Elder.

Dream job abroad? It could be a trafficking trap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What can be done about entry-level jobs?

In Germany, a survey this spring by consultancy EY found that students are much less optimistic about finding suitable work after graduation than they were two years ago. Job security now also ranks ahead of salary as their top priority when choosing an employer.

This leaves lots of room for improvement. Policymakers and employers will need to make big investments to create decent jobs and "support young people's school-to-work transitions," said Elder.

Golo Henseke is cautious about blaming young people's skills. "It is very unlikely that today's graduates are less capable than those who left education just a few years ago, and the skills employers want have not changed overnight."

"More than anything, what would help is economic growth," concluded Henseke.

Edited by: Andreas Becker

World.title: China, Philippines clash in South China Sea ahead of ASEAN meeting
World.content:
China and the Philippines traded accusations after a violent altercation between navy personnel in the disputed South China Sea. The incident heightened tensions ahead of a major diplomatic summit in Manila.

Sailors from the Chinese and Philippine navies faced off with oars and batons in the disputed South China Sea, with Philippine officials saying that one of its sailors suffered a head injury as a result of the altercation.

What did Beijing, Manila say about the South China Sea confrontation?

The latest confrontation took place on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, a contested area where the two countries haverepeatedly clashed before. The Philippines keeps a military presence in the area aboard the grounded warship BRP Sierra Madre.

Manila said that Chinese Coast Guard personnel had assaulted Filipino sailors as they approached the outpost.

China quickly rejected this narrative. Beijing's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the "Philippine side provoked the incident first," by approaching the Chinese vessel in small rubber boats, but then "turned around ​and made counter-accusations, distorted the facts and engaged in malicious ​hype."

On Tuesday, China summoned the Philippine ambassador in Beijing to lodge its complaints, with the Philippines quickly following suit with the Chinese counterpart in Manila.

Disputed South China Sea remains a flashpoint

The Second Thomas Shoal is part of the Spratly islands, a disputed archipelago in the South China Sea.

The Spratlys are key to Beijing's claim of the entire South China Sea, a key global trade route. Beijing maintains its claim to the waterway despite a 2016 ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague that there is no legal basis to its argument.

China has repeatedly demanded the removal of the outpost on the BRP Sierra Madre, and surrounded the atoll with its ships in a tense territorial standoff that has dragged on for years.



Philippine island on edge amid fear of China-Taiwan conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US, Australia condemn China ahead of ASEAN gathering

The incident came just ahead of a meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) which was set to begin on Tuesday with foreign ministers of the eleven member states and external partners.

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who was in Manila for the summit, denounced Beijing on Tuesday for what she called "destabilizing and dangerous conduct" during the standoff.

Wong, during a visit to the headquarters of the Philippine Coast Guard, also announced a support package for the agency totaling 10 million Australian dollars ($6.7 million) for drone technology.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Manila on Tuesday morning ahead of the ASEAN summit Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

The US State Department also issued a statement criticizing China's actions, saying its "troubling pattern of provocations against the Philippines' legitimate maritime operations undermines regional peace and stability."

"We stand with our Ally, the Philippines, and commend the professionalism and restraint shown by Philippine navy personnel in this incident," the statement read.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in the Philippine capital on Tuesday morning, and has indicated he was open to meeting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who is also attending the ASEAN summit.

World.title: Afghanistan: Deadly flash floods hit Nuristan province
World.content:
Some 20 people have been killed and more than 80 injured, with the city of Parun hit particularly hard. A lack of infrastructure and the effects of climate change have left the country vulnerable to natural disaster.

Eastern Afghanistan was struck by flash floods that left at least 20 people dead, 80 injured, and over 100 missing, authorities confirmed late on Monday.

Yousaf Hammad of the National Disaster Management Authority said that a rescue mission was underway to locate the missing and bring them to safety if possible.

"Unfortunately, severe floods today in Parun city and several other areas of Nuristan province have caused heavy loss of life and property among our fellow citizens,” Hammad said, stressing that there had been severe damage to people's homes, farmland, and public facilities.

"We urge all citizens to stay away from flood-prone areas and zones at risk."

A spokesman for the Taliban government in Kabul added: "We pray for those who lost their lives in this incident and for a speedy recovery for the injured."

Why Afghanistan is vulnerable to floods

A variety of factors have left Afghanistan particularly vulnerable to extreme weather events. Decades of conflict, followed by the removal of foreign investment after the return of the Taliban in 2021 has left prevention infrastructure in poor condition, where it exists at all.

Deforestation, a struggling economy, and the effects of climate change have compounded these issues.

More heavy rain, thunderstorms, and extreme winds were predicted to continue in 10 of the countries 34 provinces in the coming days, Taliban officials said.

World.title: How heat waves are messing with your sleep
World.content:
Residents across Europe have struggled to sleep during the latest record heat waves. But as the planet continues to warm, sleep deprivation could create an epidemic of mental and physical ill-health.

During the June heat wave that brought record temperatures to western Europe, around 65% of adults in the UK struggled to sleep, according to a recent poll. Near half of those lost three or more hours sleep a night.

Sleep disruption is an inevitable consequence of longer and hotter summers fueled by human-made climate change. As the fastest-warming continent that is heating at more than double the global average, Europe is a sleep loss hot spot.

In the German state of Saxony in June, a weather station reported a tropical overnight minimum temperature of 29.4 degrees Celsius (85 degrees Fahrenheit).

Such overnight extremes are now 100 times more likely due to climate change caused primarily by burning fossil fuels, notes World Weather Attribution, a global scientific body analyzing how climate drives weather extremes.

Climate change disrupts sleep

Heat-driven sleep loss has only recently been recognized as an important indicator of how climate change affects both physical and mental health.

A global team of researchers collated 165 million nights of data from nearly 318,000 users of wearable and under-mattress sleep trackers to monitor the impact of rising temperatures on sleep. In a paper published in July , they showed that when nighttime temperatures rise from around 12 C to 27 C, people face about a 40% higher chance of sleeping less than six hours.

Humans can't maintain cognitive function, memory or emotional balance when they sleep less than seven hours a night, noted Ty Ferguson, a research fellow at Australia's Adelaide University who studies the potential health and social impacts of climate-driven sleep disturbance — but wasn't part of the July study.

Europe's heat wave: The worst is yet to come To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to impacting mood and attention, disrupted sleep can increase diabetes risk, depression, heart disease and even obesity, according to Ferguson.

'Sleep essential for immune function, mental health'

"Sleep is a fundamental physiological necessity essential for human immune function, mental health, and daily well-being," said Bowen Chu, a researcher at the School of Atmospheric Sciences at Nanjing University in China who co-authored a March study on the potential economic impacts of climate-driven sleep erosion in children.

Parisians cool off at a local fountain in June amid temperature extremes Image: Mustafa Yalcin/Anadolu/picture alliance

Unlike traditional climate impact research focused often on extreme weather events, understanding sleep loss "allows scientists to quantify the gradual, day-to-day, and cumulative effects of ambient temperature rise on the everyday lives and health of global populations," Chu told DW.

"Temperatures are also rising faster at night than during the day," notes Kelton Minor, an associate professor at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark whose research team, along with the World Sleep Society, has called for a global sleep task force to better understand and prepare for sleep depletion in a hotter world.

Nights are getting hotter in part because clouds absorb heat and send it to Earth after dark — unlike daytime when they reflect sunlight. Researchers have found that cloud patterns are changing in ways that amplify global warming.

'Quietly accumulating' sleep decline underreported

Sleep loss is probably underreported as a climate impact since it "doesn't produce a dramatic single event — no headline death toll, not as visible damage," noted Kim van Daalen, an environmental epidemiologist at the University of Cambridge and co-author of a recently published paper on "Sleep loss in a warming world."

"It accumulates quietly, night after night, which makes it easy to miss in coverage that tends to focus on acute heat wave deaths or hospitalizations," said van Daalen of the subtle impacts of sleep deficits.

"Heat-related sleep loss is likely to widen existing health and socioeconomic inequalities," said van Daalen. Children may struggle with concentration, learning and emotions, while "greater cardiovascular and metabolic strain" is being placed on older adults and people with chronic illnesses when sleeping less.

Europe's heat wave deepens strain on elderly, homeless To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Chronic sleep loss driven by high temperatures is associated with decreased labor productivity, reduced learning efficiency, potentially an increased risk of traffic accidents, and heightened long-term healthcare burdens on society," said Chu of the broader societal impacts of sleep interruption.

"Poor sleep makes it harder to work, learn, care for others and maintain good health," he said, adding that low-income households are more exposed because they live in poorly ventilated homes or cannot afford cooling.

Both lower-income populations within wealthy nations and residents of lower-income countries may be up to three times more vulnerable to the impact of heat on sleep, according to Minor.

This is explained by "lower access to air conditioning and other economic lifelines that can keep the heat out," he said, pointing to "houseless individuals trying to sleep on the streets, migrants in sweltering tents, incarcerated populations in searing hot prison cells, infants in scorching bedrooms, as well as pregnant and new mothers already struggling to sleep."

People cooling off at a spray mist fountain in Warsaw, Poland in late June Image: Jaap Arriens/Sipa USA/picture alliance

What are the solutions?

Even in a scenario where nations achieve net zero emissions, adaptation to climate-driven sleep loss will be an ongoing necessity since temperatures will take decades to fall, noted Ferguson.

Increased access to fans or air conditioning, lighter and breathable bedding, greater building insulation, and limiting heat-trapping concrete in cities are some of the ways climate-related sleep decline can be mitigated, he explained.

More green spaces and solar-radiation reflective surfaces, along with passive cooling building designs that utilize window shades and improve ventilation, will be vital structural solutions, according to Chu.

Adjusting schedules to avoid work during extreme heat waves will also be fundamental to adaptation measures that help maintain sleep duration in a hotter world, he said.

These solutions will be especially important in European countries like Germany that traditionally have little air conditioning, for example, compared to the US or Australia, notes Minor.

"Adapting the approximately one third of our lives that we spend sleeping to nighttime warming already warrants European policy prioritization and adaptive innovation," he said.

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

Pistorius says Germany wants to secure influence on KNDS Image: Political-Moments/IMAGO

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said on Tuesday that Germany wants to secure its influence over tank maker ​KNDS in some way.

"We ‌want to keep this ‌key ​technology within Germany's control — on an equal footing with ​our partners from France," he said, while visiting a company site in the central city of Kassel.

"Which shape this ⁠will ​take will ​be subject to discussions ​and decisions over ‌the next few weeks," he ​said.

Pistorius said the company was of the highest importance for the defense and economy of Germany.

KNDS, which produces German Leopard-2 and French Leclerc battle tanks, is currently owned half by the French state and half by the German Wegmann Group.

In early July, it postponed a planned stock market flotation that had been set to enable the German government to take a 40% stake in the company.

The German government has said it remains committed to the project despite the postponement, which the company said was due to "unfavorable market conditions."

An agreement was struck with France to ensure both states would hold equal shares of 40%, with 20% to be floated publicly, according to the news magazine Spiegel.
