07/21/2026 July 21, 2026 Rahul Gandhi demands Modi's resignation for 'destroying the future of India's youth'

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has called for Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah's resignation over Monday's police crackdown on youth protesters.

Gandhi and other members of his Congress party, including his sister Priyanka, held a demonstration outside Modi's official residence in New Delhi on Tuesday afternoon.

The protest comes after the Indian parliament was adjourned over disruptions for a second day in a row on Tuesday, as the opposition demanded a discussion on paper leaks and other issues within India's education system.

"We have marched to PM Modi's house to demand answers from him for the brutalities against young students yesterday," Gandhi said on X

"The Government doesn't want to take any accountability or does it want to have a debate on it in Parliament. PM and HM must resign for destroying the future of India's youth," he added.

World.title: El empresario Julio Martínez se ratifica ante el juez al señalar a Zapatero por el rescate de Plus Ultra, pero afirma que no sabe con quién habló
World.content:
El empresario Julio Martínez Martínez ha ratificado este martes ante el juez José Luis Calama, instructor del caso Plus Ultra en la Audiencia Nacional, el escrito que envió el lunes al magistrado para señalar a José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero como la persona que “marcaba los pasos a seguir” en las gestiones que desembocaron en el rescate de 53 millones de euros que la compañía aérea recibió del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez tras la pandemia de coronavirus. Varias fuentes presentes en el interrogatorio inciden en que el imputado, que ha declarado durante cerca de tres horas tras imprimir un giro de guion a su estrategia y ofrecerse a “colaborar” con la justicia, ha implicado al expresidente en los trabajos para la aerolínea, pero ha sostenido que él no sabe si el antiguo jefe del Ejecutivo intermedió ante alguien para agilizar la ayuda.

Como ya avanzó en el escrito enviado a la Audiencia Nacional, Martínez Martínez solo ha contestado este martes a las preguntas del magistrado (que lo ha interrogado durante alrededor de una hora y cuarto), de la Fiscalía Anticorrupción y de su propia defensa. El administrador de la consultora Análisis Relevante no ha querido responder a las acusaciones populares, encabezadas en este sumario por el PP. La cita ha comenzado con las cuestiones del juez Calama. Y después ha llegado el turno del ministerio público, representado por la fiscal Elena Lorente.

Fuentes jurídicas señalan que Martínez ha contado al juez que él empezó trabajando para Plus Ultra ante la administración de Venezuela y que, más tarde y tras la pandemia, extendió su labor a España. Según estas fuentes, el empresario ha recalcado incluso que aterrizó en al país sudamericano gracias al exlíder socialista, donde llegó a tener como interlocutora a la entonces vicepresidenta del Estado chavista, Delcy Rodríguez. A ella también la conoció a través del propio Zapatero, según ha apostillado.

El empresario ha venido a perfilar al expresidente como una persona que canalizaba sus contactos a través de Análisis Relevante y otras sociedades, mientras que él era solo un mero transmisor de las directrices que iba marcando el exdirigente socialista. En esta línea, según las fuentes consultadas, el juez ha llegado a calificar a Martínez Martínez como una especie de “correveidile”.

El empresario ha contado que Análisis Relevante cobraba por los informes y las gestiones de Zapatero, y luego él pagaba al expresidente. Como ya expuso en el escrito entregado el lunes, Martínez Martínez ha explicado que cuando el rescate de Plus Ultra empezó a ser cuestionado, la consultora y la aerolínea acordaron diferir el pago a lo largo del tiempo y que parte de esas cantidades se facturaran a otras sociedades del empresario. “En total, la cuantía abonada en concepto de honorarios por mediar en la obtención de la ayuda pública ascendió, aproximadamente, al 1% de la cantidad obtenida conforme a lo acordado”, especificaba el documento remitido al instructor José Luis Calama.

Julio Martínez Martínez ha entrado en la Audiencia Nacional sobre las 08.45 de este martes, acompañado de su abogada María Dolores Márquez de Prado. El empresario ha llegado al tribunal dispuesto a ratificar el escrito enviado un día antes al juez José Luis Calama, donde apuntaba directamente contra el expresidente y mostraba su disposición a “colaborar y contribuir al esclarecimiento de los hechos”. “En su faceta de consultor, era Rodríguez Zapatero quien marcaba los pasos a seguir”, incide el documento firmado por el dueño de Análisis Relevante.

“Zapatero quedó fuera del accionariado [de Análisis Relevante] y órganos formales de la empresa, pero era quien la lideraba y decidía todas aquellas cuestiones de estrategia y captación de clientes”, ahondaba el escrito de Julio Martínez Martínez, que también implicaba al exlíder socialista por el rescate de la aerolínea. Una maniobra que inflige un enorme daño a la defensa del exlíder del PSOE, que se desvinculó ante el juez de las ayudas a Plus Ultra. De hecho, en las últimas horas, el exjefe del Ejecutivo ha recibido más severos golpes, propinados por dos directivos de la compañía aérea. El presidente Julio Martínez Sola y el director financiero. Ambos le han atribuido gestiones para favorecerles en la obtención de los 53 millones de euros de dinero público obtenidos durante la pandemia.

World.title: Última hora de la actualidad política, en directo | El Ejecutivo mantiene la confianza en Zapatero: “La actuación del Gobierno de España en el rescate de Plus Ultra fue correcta”
World.content:
El Ejecutivo de Ayuso sitúa a Zapatero como la “autoridad moral del PSOE” y cree que el final del Gobierno “está marcado”

El consejero de Presidencia, Justicia y Administración Local de la Comunidad de Madrid, Miguel Ángel García Martín, ha situado al expresidente del Gobierno José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero como la “autoridad moral del PSOE” y ha señalado que el “final” del Gobierno central “está marcado”.

Lo ha expresado este martes ante los medios de comunicación desde la Viceconsejería de Justicia y Víctimas al ser preguntado por el caso Plus Ultra en el día en el que el juez de la Audiencia Nacional, José Luis Calama, tiene previsto interrogar este martes como investigado al empresario Julio Martínez, socio de Zapatero.

En la víspera, aseguró que el expresidente del Gobierno “marcaba los pasos a seguir” y admitió una comisión del 1% por intermediar en el rescate de 53 millones de euros concedido por el Ejecutivo a la aerolínea en la pandemia. “Ayer conocíamos el testimonio de Julio Martínez, que viene a demostrar que tenemos a un expresidente del Gobierno que ha utilizado su cargo para montar una trama que ahora se está investigando. Y creo que esto es gravísimo”, ha subrayado García Martín. En este sentido, ha remarcado que es “la primera vez en democracia” que un expresidente del Gobierno está “imputado” y que “va a tener que dar explicaciones de todo lo ocurrido durante los últimos años”.

“Estamos viendo, y esto ya es insoportable, que todo lo que toca el sanchismo lo convierte en corrupción. Recordamos que Rodríguez Zapatero era esa autoridad moral del PSOE. Si esta era la autoridad moral que tenía, ¿cómo será el resto de dirigentes de un partido que ha hecho de la corrupción su forma de hacer política?”, ha lanzado.

El consejero ha aseverado que el Ejecutivo central se encuentra en el “periodo de descuento” y que “cuanto antes” el presidente, Pedro Sánchez, “tiene que darse cuenta de que está solo y que no le apoya absolutamente nada y nadie”. “Tiene que abandonar el cargo y convocar elecciones para que sea un gobierno honrado de verdad el que pueda asumir los retos y tomar las riendas de un país como España. El final del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez está marcado desde hace muchísimo tiempo”, ha aseverado.

Considera que esta legislatura “nunca tuvo que comenzar” porque comenzó “apoyándose en los odiadores de España y en los que dieron un golpe de Estado desde Cataluña”. “Han sido siete años, pero especialmente estos tres últimos años, donde hemos visto que lo único que ha traído Sánchez a nuestro país ha sido la corrupción”, ha añadido.

García Martín ha insistido en que no quieren “corrupción generalizada” en España y al que “lo ha traído, que es el presidente Sánchez”. Por ello, le ha pedido que “se dé cuenta de que está solo y de que solo queda que él se dé cuenta de que está solo, de que todo lo que ha rodeado es corrupción”. “No podemos seguir ni un minuto más con un presidente y con un gobierno que nos ha traído la corrupción de Estado de este país”, ha concluido. (EP)

World.title: Una perspectiva insólita para pasar revista a medio siglo
World.content:
Miguel Prieto y Reyes Lluch son, desde hace 50 años, lectores de EL PAÍS. El abogado y la promotora cultural, ciegos y trabajadores de la ONCE, muestran en esta entrevista un ángulo diferente sobre cómo ha cambiado España y cómo lo ha contado este diario

Durante muchos años, Miguel Prieto (Sama de Langreo, Asturias, 1961) y Reyes Lluch (Tortosa, Tarragona, 1957) leyeron EL PAÍS con los ojos de otros. Amigos, compañeros o familiares les prestaban la voz para recorrer juntos unas páginas que terminarían formando parte de su educación sentimental. Hoy ambos son lectores autónomos, la revolución digital ha traído eso: accesibilidad. Entre una escena y otra han transcurrido cinco décadas de historia de España; la evolución de un país que, también él, gracias a la labor de instituciones como la ONCE, aprendió a mirar de otra manera a las personas con discapacidad.

Prieto, abogado, procede de la cuenca minera asturiana, se crio en ese ambiente metalúrgico de obreros con afilada conciencia social, aunque la suya, cuenta, no vivió el despertar hasta que ingresó en la facultad. Al poco de nacer comenzaron sus severas dificultades de visión, obstáculo que no frenó un día a día agitado, donde las pasiones del niño y luego del joven se disfrutaban con absoluta intensidad. Como el ciclismo. Dicen de él que fue un buen fondista, y lo cierto es que los aficionados a la bicicleta le deben un hito fundamental: gracias a Prieto, la Vuelta Ciclista a España incluyó en su recorrido la subida al Angliru. A sus manos llegó el reportaje de una revista de principios de los noventa: ‘Atrévete con el puerto más duro de España’. Prieto, por supuesto, quiso subir a testarlo, altímetro digital y lupa al cuello, para alcanzar a leer el registro de datos. Tras su experiencia, en 1997 envió una carta que llegó al patrón de la Vuelta: tenemos el Mortirolo español —en referencia a ese puerto alpino que supone una de las etapas cumbre del Giro. En 1999, el Angliru hizo su debut en la gran ronda española, y el resto es historia.

Habla

Miguel Prieto Licenciado en Derecho Aficionado al ciclismo: gracias a él, se incluyó la subida al Angliru en la Vuelta Ciclista”

EL PAÍS fue la voz de los jóvenes que en la Transición adquirieron conciencia política. Un diario con pensamiento, hondura y plumas imbatibles. Miguel Prieto. Licenciado en Derecho

La tarraconense Reyes Lluch encontró desde niña en la música la forma de expandir esas fronteras que las dificultades visuales parecían querer imponerle a su mundo. Estudió guitarra, y también piano y canto. Participó activamente en aquella vida cultural catalana que, en los años de la Transición, suponía el mejor síntoma para creer en un resurgimiento cierto. Y convirtió después eso que había nacido como vocación en profesión. En mucho más, en realidad, dado que Lluch consagró su carrera a promover que las artes sirvieran como herramienta de participación: gracias a ella, unos 1.600 actores y actrices ciegos o con discapacidad visual se han subido a las tablas de un teatro. Su palmarés es largo, aunque en él brilla con fulgor especial un premio Max.

Pregunta. ¿Dónde estaban el 4 de mayo de 1976, cuando salió el primer número de EL PAÍS? ¿Cuál fue su primer contacto con el diario?

Prieto. En ese momento vivía en Asturias, en Sama de Langreo, en los valles mineros, y estaba cursando primero del Bachillerato Unificado Polivalente, el BUP. Lo empecé justamente en septiembre del 75, y ese noviembre murió Franco, así que fíjate qué curso más movidito. Pero en mayo de 1976 yo era estudiante, no muy preocupado o interesado en la actualidad, tan solo en el deporte. Sí recuerdo, sin embargo, que había ejemplares de EL PAÍS en sitios para mí emblemáticos. Porque en el Langreo en el que crecí (me fui con 22 o 23 años) la conciencia social era muy avanzada. El obrero o el metalúrgico que trabajaba duramente en sus turnos de mañana, tarde o noche luego se iba a leer periódicos y libros a lo que se llamaba entonces el hogar del productor, lo que luego serían las casas del pueblo. No era un mero local sindical, era una construcción con bibliotecas, cines, la gente jugaba al dominó o las cartas. Y, bueno, pensemos lo que significaron en la España de aquella época de transformación política. El diario EL PAÍS comenzaba a ser moneda de curso común, la gente lo llevaba bajo el brazo; a medida que pasaban los años se consolidaba como una voz diferente a las hegemónicas de la época. Prendía en los jóvenes, en esos que adquirían conciencia política, como fue mi caso, en la universidad.

Lluch. En mayo del 76 yo era una niña de 17 años que vivía en Tortosa (Tarragona) y todo mi grupo de amigas estaba preparándose para tener un futuro. Ese era nuestro interés. Queríamos un país más abierto, poder hablar de muchos temas. La publicación de EL PAÍS fue un soplo de aire nuevo, de libertad. Mis amigas lo leían y charlábamos, era una gran forma de análisis y debate. A mí me encantaba la sección de Cultura, porque yo era estudiante de música clásica, estudiaba guitarra y me encantaba leer las críticas de Enrique Franco. Cuando teníamos oportunidad, íbamos a escuchar conciertos: clásica, jazz, cantautores. EL PAÍS se ocupaba de hablar de los géneros emergentes. También prestaba atención a la literatura que nos interesaba, siempre nos fiábamos de sus recomendaciones sobre nuevos títulos publicados, libros interesantes, de sus críticas, leer su sección de Internacional... A mí que me gustaba muchísimo viajar, te abría las miras: siempre fue muy interesante cómo la enfocó el periódico. En Cataluña hablábamos dos idiomas, castellano y catalán, y mi familia, gracias a esa perspectiva que ofrecía, siempre trató de inculcarnos el valor de aprender otras lenguas y comunicarnos con gente diversa: fue una ayuda para tener la mente más abierta.

Reyes Lluch Promotora cultural Experta en teatro, música y artes plásticas: ganadora de un premio Max

Las dificultades de acceso a los medios escritos de las personas ciegas empezaron a solventarse con la prensa digital Reyes Lluch. Promotora cultural

Aquellos primeros años consolidaron una relación que se mantendría durante décadas. Para Prieto, EL PAÍS representaba una forma rigurosa de acercarse a la actualidad, con un periodismo de profundidad que encontraba difícilmente en otros medios. Lluch, por su parte, fue ampliando sus intereses desde las páginas culturales hacia los artículos de opinión, convencida de que una democracia madura necesita confrontar ideas y no únicamente consumir titulares.

Con el tiempo también cambió la manera de leer. Para ambos, la llegada de la edición digital supuso una transformación radical: la apertura definitiva de una puerta hacia la autonomía que durante décadas había permanecido, como mucho, entreabierta. Prieto la vivió como una evolución natural del periódico hacia otro ecosistema informativo. Lluch, en cambio, la recuerda con hondura: ya no dependería de nadie para leer. Esta evolución tecnológica la resumen fuentes de la ONCE: “En cuanto aparecieron los diarios web, las personas ciegas pudieron hacerse con distintos dispositivos que leían en alto aquello que estaba escrito en la pantalla para que pudiera escucharse. Había incluso aparatos que traducían los artículos a braille. Hoy, hay periódicos como EL PAÍS que, directamente, ofrecen la posibilidad de que una IA transforme en audio con una voz lineal y poco interpretativa —como prefieren las personas ciegas— cada uno de sus artículos”.

Si, como lectores de EL PAÍS, existe un día que ambos recuerdan con precisión fotográfica, es el 23 de febrero de 1981.

Pregunta. El 23-F es un día importante en la historia del diario, que lanzó una edición especial esa misma noche. ¿Qué estaban haciendo ese día y cómo recuerdan la actuación de los medios de comunicación?

Prieto. Eso lo tengo grabado en la memoria. Era lunes, yo estaba estudiando segundo de Derecho. Tenía que preparar un examen de derecho civil, justo ese año que se aprobó la ley del Divorcio. Yo entonces era una persona muy implicada. Cuando se publicó EL PAÍS reivindicando el estatus democrático de aquella España que daba un pasito para adelante y otro para atrás, con balbuceos, con atentados de ETA, el Grapo, la Triple A, atentados fascistas… significó muchísimo. La apertura vino enredada en mucha confusión. El martes 24 de febrero la mitad de mi clase quería entrar y seguir con las asignaturas como si nada; y la otra mitad señalaba el momento crucial de la historia que vivíamos. El gesto de EL PAÍS nos enseñó qué tipo de prensa necesitaba un proyecto de progreso con el que nos sentíamos representados.

En la imagen, la música y promotora teatral Reyes Lluch toca la guitarra.

Lluch. El 23-F me pilló volviendo del Conservatorio de Tarragona a Tortosa. Mi hermana, que vivía en Tarragona, me había acompañado al tren; yo subí al vagón y, como el resto de los que estaban ahí sentados, no me enteré de nada. Fue cuando por fin llegué a casa cuando fui consciente del tremendo golpe de Estado. Mis padres estaban en Valencia, tuvieron prácticamente los tanques en la puerta: fueron horas de mucha incertidumbre, de miedo, pendientes de la radio y la televisión. Hasta que salió el Rey. La edición especial de EL PAÍS, defendiendo la democracia y las libertades, el pacto constitucional, nos dio tranquilidad, nos ofreció la certeza de que nuestro país iba a continuar por la senda de la democracia.

Tanto Prieto como Lluch llegaron muy jóvenes a la ONCE y han permanecido en la organización una vida entera. Prieto se mudó a Madrid con 23 años y, desde el principio, mostró interés por participar en el asociacionismo que prestaba ayuda a las personas con discapacidad. Fue director adjunto del área de Juego de la ONCE y, actualmente, gestiona la unidad de Juego Responsable. Lluch, armada sempiternamente con una guitarra que no ha dejado de tocar, fue durante años responsable de Promoción Cultural de la ONCE: ha impulsado más de 40 grupos de teatro, con más de 45 montajes anuales de media; y también ha prestado apoyo a cientos de iniciativas literarias, musicales y de artes plásticas.

El diario deportivo AS daba cuenta en este reportaje de la hazaña de Miguel Prieto como descubridor del Angliru.

Ambos, cuando se paran a analizar el presente de España y cómo lo afronta la prensa, coinciden en el complejo desafío al que se enfrenta el periodismo de hoy, ese que, dice Prieto, de pronto da igual cabida a influencers que a buenos columnistas. Prieto echa de menos la profundidad intelectual, aquella sensación de que cada artículo ayudaba a comprender la realidad y no solo a reaccionar ante ella. Para Lluch, el mal mayor es la radicalización ideológica, la composición de informaciones donde, en su opinión, se percibe ya un sesgo intencional. La tarraconense lamenta la creciente polarización del debate público y reclama medios capaces de preservar la independencia y de favorecer una conversación democrática realmente fructífera, basada en el respeto a las opiniones diferentes.

Cinco décadas después, ambos se mantienen fieles al mismo periódico, a un diario EL PAÍS hoy global. Quizá por eso insisten tanto en el valor de la información con contexto, en la preservación del pensamiento crítico. Tras medio siglo, el objetivo no ha cambiado: están convencidos de que el periodismo todavía tiene la obligación de hacernos comprender mejor el mundo.

World.title: Me he mudado de San Fernando a Gijón, ¿puedo aplicar la exención por reinversión en vivienda habitual?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. He adquirido una vivienda en Gijón antes de vender la que tenía en San Fernando (Cádiz), con un incremento patrimonial de 38.000 euros. ¿Puedo deducir el importe de adquisición de la nueva vivienda considerándolo reinversión en vivienda habitual a pesar de haberla comprado un año antes? Ana M. Carbajales

Respuesta. Partimos de la base de que tanto la vivienda de San Fernando (Cádiz) como la de Gijón tienen la consideración de vivienda habitual. En ese caso, sí podría aplicarse la exención por reinversión en vivienda habitual, siempre que se cumplan los requisitos previstos en la normativa del IRPF. La ley permite acogerse a esta exención tanto cuando la nueva vivienda se adquiere después de vender la anterior como cuando la adquisición se realiza con carácter previo.

En concreto, la reinversión puede efectuarse dentro de los dos años anteriores o de los dos años posteriores a la transmisión de la vivienda habitual. Por tanto, si adquirió la vivienda de Gijón un año antes de vender la de San Fernando y ambas tienen la consideración de vivienda habitual, podrá beneficiarse de la exención por reinversión.

No obstante, la exención no depende únicamente del importe de la ganancia patrimonial obtenida (38.000 euros), sino del importe total obtenido en la venta de la vivienda. Para que la exención sea total, deberá reinvertirse la totalidad del valor de transmisión, es decir, el importe obtenido en la venta una vez descontado, el capital pendiente del préstamo hipotecario que gravaba la vivienda si lo hay y los gastos e impuestos asociados a la operación. Si la cantidad reinvertida es inferior, la exención será parcial, en proporción al importe efectivamente reinvertido.

Respecto a la declaración del IRPF, la exención debe aplicarse en el ejercicio en el que se produce la venta de la vivienda, ya que es en ese momento cuando se genera la ganancia patrimonial.

En definitiva, si la vivienda de Gijón fue adquirida un año antes de la venta de la vivienda de San Fernando y se cumplen el resto de los requisitos legales, podrá beneficiarse de la exención por reinversión en vivienda habitual al presentar la declaración del IRPF correspondiente al ejercicio en el que transmitió la vivienda de Cádiz.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Lo que no puedes perderte si vas a Asturias de vacaciones este verano
World.content:
Varios caballos en la laguna de Sobia, en el concejo de Teverga (Asturias).

Restaurantes, pueblos, playas, naturaleza y prerrománico en un destino ideal para ver el eclipse solar del próximo 12 de agosto

Sería injusto reducir los atractivos de Asturias a su clima fresco en verano. Pero es cierto que, en los últimos años, el imparable aumento de las temperaturas ha hecho que el Principado se haya convertido en la opción elegida por muchos para pasar las vacaciones. Asturias batió en 2025 su récord de turismo rural con 304.979 visitantes, según los datos que publicó el pasado mes de febrero el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Quienes elijan esta comunidad este verano, tienen muchas opciones para disfrutar de la naturaleza más allá de los Picos de Europa —aunque siempre merecen una visita— y para perderse por sus pueblos y aldeas. Además, Asturias también será un enclave estupendo para contemplar el eclipse total de sol del próximo 12 de agosto, ya que será total en toda la comunidad, como explica nuestra guía. Si estás planeando un viaje, estas son algunas de nuestras recomendaciones.

World.title: Frost in July: Twente records a midsummer first for Netherlands
World.content:
Parts of Twente woke to a touch of ground frost on Tuesday, something never before recorded in the Netherlands at the height of summer.

A temperature of -0.1° was briefly measured at 10 centimetres above the ground at around 5.30am, broadcaster NOS reported. According to weather bureau Weeronline, ground frost had never previously been recorded in the Netherlands between July 20 and August 21.

Since meteorologists began measuring ground temperatures in 1971, ground frost in July has occurred just nine times. The coldest reading, -1.6°, also came in Twente, on July 4, 2019 – a month that went on to produce the opposite extreme, with the hottest temperature ever measured in the Netherlands, 40.7° in Gilze-Rijen, following three weeks later.

Ground frost is slightly more common in June, and in 1955 frost was even recorded at the standard measuring height of 1.5 metres, when Witteveen in Drenthe registered -0.8°.

World.title: Dutch ban on Israeli settlement goods to start on September 22
World.content:
The Netherlands will ban the import of goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements from September 22, foreign minister Tom Berendsen has told MPs.

The cabinet announced the trade ban in May but had not yet set a date, broadcaster NOS reported. A majority of MPs called last year for a national ban on the import and transit of goods from illegal settlements in territories occupied by Israel.

The measure covers not only imports but also trading in settlement goods, and Dutch companies operating abroad will have to comply. Activities aimed at getting around the ban are prohibited as well. The measure will apply for three years in principle.

The Council of State raised no objections to the ban in an urgent advisory opinion, although it expressed doubts about how enforceable it will be, a concern the cabinet itself acknowledged when the measure was announced.

The government has repeatedly pushed for an EU-wide ban, but there is insufficient support among member states. Belgium, Spain and Ireland have already introduced sanctions at national level.

Last month, a report by legal organisation Global Echo found that the Netherlands is the top destination for Israeli settlement produce entering the EU market.

The building of settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights is a violation of international law, and according to the United Nations, settlers are systematically guilty of violence and intimidation against the Palestinian population.

“We want to prevent Dutch society, through its economic activities, from contributing to an unlawful occupation and the maintenance of illegal settlements,” prime minister Rob Jetten said when the ban was agreed in May.

World.title: Eindhoven students build world’s first solar-powered ambulance
World.content:
Students at Eindhoven University of Technology have unveiled what they say is the world’s first solar-powered ambulance, designed to bring medical care to remote regions where poor roads and a lack of fuel or electricity put healthcare out of reach.

Stella Juva, presented on Tuesday, was developed in a year by Solar Team Eindhoven, a group of 23 students. Solar panels on the roof power both the motor and the medical equipment on board, and on a sunny day the vehicle is expected to cover 715 kilometres without needing any charging infrastructure.

But how does a solar vehicle fare in one of Europe’s cloudiest countries? “The Dutch weather, to say the least, is not Kenya’s,” team manager Mathijs van Gerven told DutchNews after the launch. The ambulance’s 50 kWh battery stores solar energy so it can keep powering its equipment, and its own motors, without interruption, he explained.

Unlike a traditional ambulance, which transports patients to hospital, Stella Juva is designed to bring care to people, allowing healthcare providers to carry out blood tests, screen for diseases such as tuberculosis and malaria, administer vaccinations and perform pregnancy ultrasounds.

The students developed the vehicle with international health organisations including Amref Health Africa, formerly known as the Flying Doctors. “In remote areas, healthcare workers sometimes travel great distances by bicycle, and reliable energy is not a given,” Femke Maurits of Amref’s Dutch branch said in a statement.

Energy is essential, she said, for keeping vaccines cooled and running medical equipment.

Kenya test

In August the team will take Stella Juva to Kenya, starting with a kick-off at Amref International University attended by officials from the Dutch embassy and Kenyan diplomats. The vehicle will then be tested at two field locations, where healthcare scenarios, such as the treatment of tuberculosis patients, will be simulated.

“Three of our team members have been chosen to drive Stella Juva – they were the first to test her,” Van Gerven told us. “We will see who gets to drive the first Kenyan metres, but I reckon they will all want to go first.”

Afterwards, the ambulance will tour events across the Netherlands, and possibly Europe, to encourage companies and healthcare providers to take the concept further. For production at scale, the team is looking to industry.

“If 23 students are able to do this in just one year, think about what is possible if technological companies and social organisations collaborate,” Van Gerven said.

World.title: Lorries ignoring Merwedebrug ban face €500 fines
World.content:
Roads agency Rijkswaterstaat is installing traffic cameras on the damaged Merwedebrug near Gorinchem to enforce a ban on lorries, with fines of up to €500 for drivers who ignore it.

The bridge on the A27 has been closed since Saturday to freight traffic after an inspection found the bridge’s steel was weaker than expected in several places, and that it could no longer guarantee the structure would hold under heavy traffic.

The roads agency issued an urgent appeal to trucks to avoid using the bridge but many are still driving over it.

An NOS reporter on the scene counted dozens of trucks in half an hour, including vehicles with Dutch license plates.

The new ban will now be enforced via cameras which will automatically read the license plates. Enforcement will be done together with the police and the public prosecution service. Fines can be as high as €500.

Cars, vans, motorbikes, buses and emergency vehicles can still use the Merwedebrug. Freight traffic is being diverted via the A16 and the A2.

World.title: Deaths linked to online medicines prompt national study
World.content:
The addiction research institute Trimbos is starting an investigation into “self-medication”, people buying medicines online without consulting a doctor, it has told broadcaster NOS.

The study has been commissioned by health minister Sophie Hermans, who is worried about injuries and even deaths linked to medicines sold online.

Drugs bought online can be dangerous, according to Laura Smit-Rigter, national coordinator of drug monitoring and policy at Trimbos. “It could involve counterfeit medication,” she told NOS. “In that case, the dosage or composition of the product could be completely different. And that can be life-threatening.”

In 2025, two men who ran a webshop called Funcaps, which sold fake and illegal medicines to the general public, appeared in court in connection with the deaths of at least 27 people.

Funcaps sold a range of substances, among them bromazolam, a sedative, O-DSMT, an opioid painkiller, and 2F-ketamine, an anaesthetic. The products came with no package inserts or usage instructions, and sales were pushed with discount deals and sample packs.

Trimbos wants to find out how many people are buying medicines online and why they turn to the internet instead of going to their doctor.

World.title: Big firms hired 13,500 refugees and asylum seekers last year
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Large companies in the Netherlands hired 13,500 refugees and asylum seekers last year, in an effort to plug staff shortages in sectors such as logistics, hospitality and technical trades.

The figures come from Tent Nederland, a coalition of 51 major employers including Philips, IKEA, ABN Amro, Unilever, Arcadis and Randstad, and were reported by NU.nl. The jobs include both permanent positions and work via staffing agencies.

Tent Nederland was set up in April 2025 as the Dutch arm of the Tent Partnership for Refugees, a global network of large companies founded by Chobani boss Hamdi Ulukaya.

The organisation puts employers in direct contact with refugees, partly through regional job fairs organised with local councils and the refugee settlement agency COA.

Companies are finding it easier to reach refugees, director Hélène van Melle told NU.nl, including asylum seekers, who have been able to work year round since a court scrapped a 24-week annual limit at the end of 2023.

“Employers initially had great difficulty getting in contact with these people,” she said. “But within a year we are seeing that companies are open to taking on asylum seekers.”

Government target

Some firms are recruiting refugees by their own initiative. Construction group Heijmans, which is not a Tent Nederland member, has taken on 60 refugees with residence permits over the past two years.

The hirings fit with government plans to get 75,000 more refugees and promising asylum seekers into paid work by the end of 2030. Work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen wants 60% of new arrivals to have a proper job within five years of being given a residence permit.

Refugee employment has long lagged the rest of the workforce, although CBS figures published in May show new arrivals are finding work faster than a decade ago.

World.title: Fake emergency calls send armed arrest teams to teenagers’ doors
World.content:
Public prosecutors and police are warning about the rise of “swatting” in the Netherlands, in which hoax emergency reports are used to send heavily armed arrest teams to an unsuspecting and innocent person’s home.

The phenomenon, which originated in the US, “is now happening more often here too, especially among young people,” public prosecutor Linda van den Oever told broadcaster NOS.

Swatting can be an act of revenge after an online row, a way of shocking people or a means of coercion, the public prosecution service (OM) said. Contact often begins on gaming or chat platforms, where trust is built up before sensitive information, in extreme cases nude photographs, is used to put victims under pressure.

In May, an arrest team turned up at night at the home of a 17-year-old girl after fake reports were made to police when she refused to send nude photos, she told the AD. Her address had been shared in a chat group after she refused to carry out orders.

Threats of swatting are increasingly common in so-called Com groups – short for “community”, online networks in which violence is glorified, the OM said.

The threats are used to coerce victims, while carrying out a swatting can serve as an initiation: “If you send a SWAT team after someone, you are allowed into the group,” Van den Oever said.

Digital community police officer Malek Kariebo told NOS making a false report is a criminal offence and takes police away from real emergencies.

“You know nothing about it,” he said, “and suddenly an arrest team is standing at your door, wrongly.” Police assess whether reports are genuine, but a claim that there is a firearm in a house has to be taken seriously.

There are no exact figures on how often swatting happens, but several cases are under way and a growing number of suspects in the Netherlands have been identified, the OM said.

World.title: They are off: 108th edition of the Nijmeegse Vierdaagse begins
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmeegse Vierdaagse, or four-day walk, kicked off at 4am on Tuesday.

More than 45,000 walkers from more than 70 countries are taking part in this year’s event, with marchers covering up to 50 kilometres a day.

The first day takes participants across the Waal Bridge into the Betuwe region, into the town of Elst. It is known as “Blue Tuesday” and the centre of the Elst is decorated in blue with walkers welcomed by bands and spectators.

Each day, the marchers will take different route through Gelderland, Brabant and Limburg. They can choose to walk 30, 40 or 50 kilometres a day.

The Vierdaagse was first held in 1909, when 306 mostly military participants set out from 10 army garrisons around the country, an initiative of the Dutch League for Physical Education amid fears that the rise of motorised transport would erode soldiers’ fitness.

The event moved permanently to Nijmegen in 1925 and has been skipped only in 1914 and 1915, during the Second World War and in the coronavirus years. The 2006 edition was called off after the first day, when two walkers died in extreme heat.

Marchers will get lucky with the weather, which is forecast to be between 20° and 22° degrees in the afternoon, slightly lower than average. The next four days will mostly be sunny but with occasional showers on Wednesday and Thursday.

The age of participants has been steadily declining. For years, walkers were mostly 60 plus but this year 20.5% of walkers are in their 20s. They only accounted for 7.5% of marchers in 2016.

The march ends on Friday in Nijmegen. At the finish, the walkers are welcomed by thousands of spectators and showered with flowers.

World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland up 30% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Ukraine’s foreign minister has called on "Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians” after an incident in which a man was filmed shouting xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian girls on a bus in Poland. The perpetrator has been detained https://t.co/AfGCNqtJbj — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Figures from Poland’s government, which is a coalition ranging from left to centre right, have also condemned recent incidents of hate towards Ukrainians. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called last week’s incident in a bus “disgusting” and warned of the potential “disastrous consequences” of inciting national hatred. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. However, PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek accused the government of “cynically exploiting” the incident in Bielsko-Biała “for political purposes”. He said it was, in fact, Tusk and Kierwiński who were “responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, hailed the fact that “the entire political class” in Poland had condemned the incident on the bus and expressed hope that the recent wave of attacks is a “temporary symptom” that “will pass”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Two Polish far-right activists have been charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business providing services to immigrants. World.title: President vetoes legal rights for same-sex couples in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to sign an agreement granting them certain rights. The proposed law would have marked the first time that Poland had recognised same-sex relationships in domestic law. However, Nawrocki argued that such a move would threaten the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. The measures in question were approved by both houses of parliament in May and June with the support of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The proposed law would have allowed couples, both same-sex and opposite-sex, to enter into a new type of contract, signed before a notary and then submitted to the registry office. It would have granted them some of the rights available to married couples, including joint property and tax settlement, access to their partner’s medical information, exemption from inheritance and gift taxes, and the right to decide about their partner’s burial if they died. However, the two main opposition parties – the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) – voted against the legislation, and Nawrocki himself also made clear that he intended to veto it. The government’s majority in parliament has approved a bill that would grant same-sex partners some of the rights available to married couples. However, President Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has made clear he will veto the law https://t.co/hx8viUN6QH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 29, 2026 On Friday morning, the president confirmed he would not be signing into law the two bills passed by parliament that would have introduced the new system. He said that the measures would effectively “introduce civil partnerships through the back door”, and that such partnerships are “intended to replace or substitute the institution of marriage”. “As the guardian of the constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the special status of marriage defined in article 18 of the constitution as a union between a woman and a man, placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” he added. Nawrocki also argued that the proposed measures were contrary to the principles of social justice because they would have granted such couples some of the privileges of marriage but without all of the same obligations. He also noted that the proposed new type of contract could be terminated far more easily than a marriage. “Marriage, which best secures family stability, cannot become one of many equally valid options offered by the state administration,” declared the president. “The family is a community fundamental to the survival of the nation.” However, Nawrocki added that, as he has previously said, he remains open to legislation that would grant loved ones rights relating to healthcare and various administrative issues. But only if it “does not create an alternative to marriage” or “introduce ideological changes to family law”. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision was condemned by Tusk, who called it “an expression of contempt toward people and their right to happiness and a normal life”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, accused the president of “turning his back on the two million Poles living today in informal relationships”. However, she pledged that “the veto will not halt social change”. If such change “cannot go through the door, then [it will go] through the window”. Kotula noted that Poland has already begun legally recognising same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union member states, after being ordered to do so by the European Court of Justice. While “not all benefits are yet available” to such couples, “this is something that I intend to deliver”, she added. Prezydenckie weto to wyraz pogardy wobec ludzi i ich prawa do szczęścia i normalnego życia. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 However, the government’s ability and willingness to take such action, even when it cannot be vetoed by Nawrocki, is hampered by internal disagreements over the issue within Tusk’s coalition. The Left (Lewica), from which Kotula hails, and Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party are generally in favour of strengthening LGBT+ rights. But they have met with resistance from more conservative elements in the coalition, in particular the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). The measures vetoed today by Nawrocki were already a compromise within the government: earlier plans to introduce same-sex civil partnerships were watered down to instead simply allow same-sex couples to sign a contract granting them certain rights. However, opinion polls show that the Polish public itself is in mostly in favour of recognising same-sex relationships. State research agency CBOS last year found its highest-ever level of support for the introduction of civil partnerships, with 62% of Poles in favour. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. World.title: Ukrainian teen indicted by Poland for working on behalf of Russia to stir historical tensions
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have indicted an 18-year-old Ukrainian accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tensions between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of slogans in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which massacred Poles during World War Two. Among the sites where he placed graffiti were a monument to Polish victims of those massacres (pictured above), as well as a memorial dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. If found guilty, the suspect could face up to life in prison. The history of the UPA has been at the heart of an ongoing diplomatic dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv. However, the actions in this particular case took place in 2024 and 2025, before the current crisis emerged. Prokurator z dolnośląskiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego we Wrocławiu akt oskarżenia przeciwko Illii K., któremu zarzucono popełnienie 47 przestępstw związanych z działalnością dywersyjną i sabotażową na rzecz obcego wywiadu. 45 zarzutów dotyczy umieszczania na… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 16, 2026 The suspect in the case was detained in August 2025, shortly after graffiti glorifying the UPA had appeared on a monument in Poland honouring victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles. On Thursday, prosecutors announced that they have issued an indictment against the suspect, whom they named only as Illia K. under Polish privacy law. He is accused of 47 crimes in total. Of those, 45 are for “acts of subversion and sabotage for the benefit of foreign intelligence, consisting primarily of writing slogans in Ukrainian on the facades of buildings and in memorial sites with the text ‘Glory to the UPA’ and red-and-black flags attributed to the UPA “, prosecutors said. Those actions “were aimed at inciting hatred on national grounds, deepening antagonisms between Poles and Ukrainians, causing social unrest and creating a sense of helplessness of state authorities”. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. The issue has recently flared up again after President Volodymyr Zelensky in late May named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. Russia has also long sought to exploit such tensions, and Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) notes that Illia K.’s actions were carried out “at the request of the Russian security services”, which were seeking to “incite conflicts between the Polish and Ukrainian nations”. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 In addition, Illia K. also faces one charge of participation in an organised criminal group and another of preparing for an act of subversion or sabotage that would have involved flying a drone over Poland’s Armed Forces Day parade in Warsaw last year, which was attended by President Nawrocki. Prosecutors note that the accused “acted for financial, not ideological, reasons”. He was paid for his actions in cryptocurrencies. That is typical of the so-called “disposable agents” Russia increasingly uses, who are amateurs – often young Ukrainians or Belarusians – hired and paid through messaging service Telegram. The suspect has been held in pretrial detention since he was arrested by the ABW last year. If found guilty, he could face up to life in prison. Prosecutors say that, although Illia K. initially admitted to the charges against him, he later decided to change his stance and has pleaded not guilty while exercising his right to remain silent. The head of Poland's security services has appealed to Ukrainians, the country's largest immigrant group, not to be tempted to earn money by acting as Russian agents. Russia regularly recruits Ukrainians in Poland to carry out espionage and sabotage https://t.co/aa5UUWWBrx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2025 Poland has in recent years detained, charged and in some cases convicted dozens of agents accused of carrying out espionage, sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” on behalf of Russia and its ally Belarus. In March, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism (ICCT) reported that Poland is now the “primary focus of Russian activity” when it comes to sabotage. In June, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski warned that Moscow is “waging a full-scale cognitive war against us” and that there is a “Russian fifth column” operating in Poland. Russia is “waging a full-scale cognitive war against us”, Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has warned. He also said that there is a “Russian fifth column” operating in Poland https://t.co/wsmZSvYnzN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Volkswagen hires 100 sheep to cut grass at Polish solar farm as experiment in agrivoltaics
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Carmaker Volkswagen has deployed a herd of 100 sheep to keep grass under control at a solar farm that powers one of its factories in Poland, providing a greener alternative to mechanical mowing. The project, which is being run in partnership with a local university, will also contribute to research on agrivoltaics, the name given to the use of land for both solar generation and agriculture. Scientists will assess the impact of the practice on animal welfare and the wider ecosystem. In 2016, Volkswagen opened a major plant near Poznań, Poland’s fifth-largest city. The facility employs around 3,000 people and mainly produces VW’s Crafter van. In 2023, the company opened a solar farm next to the plant. On sunny days, its 31,000 photovoltaic panels can power the whole factory, though over the year as a whole it supplies around 25% of its electricity. Volkswagen has now announced that, earlier this year, it welcomed around 100 sheep to the solar farm. They are grazing on the 27 hectares of land around the panels as an alternative to mechanical mowing. “The animals adapted very well to the new conditions,” says Justyna Nowak-Gajek, the owner of the flock. She explains that the sheep are splitting into smaller groups and “grazing peacefully”, whereas herds that feel unsafe tend to stick closer together. Meanwhile, scientists from the Poznań University of Life Sciences (UPP) are studying the impact of the project on the animals’ welfare and behaviour, as well as the functioning of the entire ecosystem. “We are checking, among other things, whether shade created by the panels reduces heat stress in animals, improving their comfort and living conditions,” says Joanna Składanowska-Baryza from the university’s Faculty of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Sciences. “At the same time, we are analysing changes in the microclimate, vegetation and soil to identify solutions that facilitate the effective combination of energy production with agricultural activities.” Volkswagen has chosen Poland as the location for a new €1.7bn plant producing materials for electric vehicle batteries. The investment has been welcomed by the Polish government, which is providing €350 million in grants for the project https://t.co/xh0LuzHOyq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2023 The study is expected to inform the wider practice of agrivoltaics, which aims to “create [solar] installations that coexist with their surroundings and bring additional benefits to the environment and local communities”, says Quanta Energy, the firm that constructed Volkswagen’s solar farm. “The photovoltaic farm now produces more than just green energy,” adds Marzena Pillich-Grońska, director of the Volkswagen plant. “It has also become a place where we support biodiversity, local agriculture, and the development of scientific knowledge.” In recent years, a number of Polish cities, including Kraków and Katowice, have also recruited sheep and goats as a greener alternative to mechanical cutting of grass on municipal land. Various firms operating in Poland have been investing in renewables to supply themselves with energy. In 2024, the largest chocolate maker in Poland, Mondelez Polska, said it would spend $1 million (3.8 million zloty) on solar installations at its production sites in the country. Successive Polish governments have also been seeking to bolster green energy. Last year, the country generated 29.4% of its electricity from renewables, up from 9.4% a decade earlier. Onshore wind led the way with 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. However, in 2023, a group of business associations and international companies, including Google, Amazon, Mercedes and Ikea, warned the government that there must be more rapid development of green energy in order to attract continued investment in Poland. However, since then, figures show a period of stagnation, despite the current government pledging to accelerate Poland’s green transition after taking power from its conservative predecessor in 2023.
