“Ordinary Filipinos should not suffer the effects of the crisis. It’s the government’s duty to protect the value of workers’ earnings and make sure that they take home a bigger part of their earnings for food, education, health, and other needs of the family,” Legarda said. /atm

World.title: Army recovers arms cache from terror group in Maguindanao Sur
World.content:
COTABATO CITY – Government forces running after an armed group accused of harassing civilian communities and government troops in Maguindanao del Sur recovered high-powered firearms, ammunition, and improvised explosive devices (IEDs) during a military operation on Tuesday, July 21, military officials said.

Lt. Col. Edgardo Batinay, commander of the 34th Infantry Battalion, led state forces in pursuing the armed group beginning at 7 a.m. in Barangay Tukanalipao, the same village where the 40 elite police personnel were killed during an operation against Zulkifli bin Hir, a Malaysian terror suspect, in 2015.

Article continues after this 

The military launched the intelligence-driven operation in response to a series of bombing incidents, harassment attacks, and ambushes allegedly perpetrated by the Paneneklan Group, a private armed group, in Maguindanao del Sur. This was the first time the military named the group.

READ: Army links fresh Maguindanao attacks to antiterror operations

Acting on information provided by a civilian regarding the group’s hideout, government forces located the encampment and recovered five high-powered firearms, assorted magazines, ammunition, and several improvised explosive devices.

However, nobody was found in the lair during the operation.

Military authorities identified the Paneneklan Group as “a lawless armed group with alleged links to the Dawlah Islamiyah-Hassan Group (DI-HG).”

Article continues after this 

The DI-HG has been associated with the possession of high-powered firearms, the use of IEDs, and other activities that pose security threats in the region.

Despite no terrorist being neutralized or arrested, Brig. Gen. Edgar Catu, commander of the 601st Infantry Brigade, credited the operation’s success to the cooperation of civilians in supporting peace and security efforts.

Article continues after this 

“The recovery of these firearms and explosive devices is a significant blow to the operational capability of the armed group to carry out violent activities and threaten communities, especially with the upcoming elections,” Catu said.

Elections are to take place in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao on September 14, including in Maguindanao del Sur where the lawless elements operate.

He added that military operations would continue until the remaining members of the armed group are arrested and brought to justice.

Maj. Gen. Jose Vladimir Cagara, commander of the 6th Infantry Division and Joint Task Force Central, commended the troops for the successful operation.

“This successful operation reflects the high level of readiness, professionalism, and dedication of our soldiers in fulfilling their mandate. Every firearm and IED recovered represents lives saved and communities protected,” Cagara said.

World.title: Bomb threat that disrupted classes in Bacolod City school a hoax
World.content:
BACOLOD CITY — The police cleared a public school in Barangay Pahanocoy here on Tuesday afternoon, July 21, following a bomb threat that turned out to be a hoax.

Police clearance came after a sweep of the Mariano G. Medalla Integrated School yielded negative results for explosives, the Bacolod City Police Office (BCPO) reported.

Article continues after this 

Responding personnel from BCPO Police Station 8 (PS8), led by Officer-in-Charge Maj. Rondyl Tapang, arrived on campus shortly after receiving the report at around 12:30 p.m. Tuesday.

READ: Pateros extends class suspension to Tuesday due to reported bomb threats

An Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Canine Unit using a trained bomb-detection K9 systematically inspected all four school buildings.

Following the clearance, OIC Principal Maria Cecelia G. Bergantin suspended classes for the day.

An investigation is ongoing to trace the origin of the threat, the BCPO said.

Article continues after this 

The alleged bomb threat at Mariano G. Medalla Integrated School was reported through a 911 call, Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya said.

“The City of Bacolod condemns this malicious attempt to incite fear and panic in our educational institutions. We maintain our position of non-tolerance for any act that threatens the safety of our students and educators,” the mayor said.

Article continues after this 

The city government remains in close coordination with the BCPO as they conduct a thorough investigation to identify the source of the false threat, he said.

To proactively improve security, the city government has prepared the installation of handheld and walk-through metal detectors in all elementary and secondary schools, he added.

Alongside the equipment, police personnel have also conducted security briefings and emergency protocol symposia for school officials, teachers, and students to ensure threat preparedness, Gasataya said.

World.title: NBI chief: Sara Duterte influenced individuals to threaten Marcos
World.content:
NBI Director Melvin Matibag. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines – National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag confirmed on Tuesday that Vice President Sara Duterte has influenced individuals to make threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

During the Senator-judges’ interjection period during the vice president’s impeachment trial, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked Matibag whether or not the NBI had spoken to anyone who had been influenced by Duterte’s previous threats to the president.

To this, Matibag answered: “We have already visited some of them and in fact, we have already filed cases against some of them. And those who made threats through social media, we have already spoken to, and the others are currently facing investigation.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Matibag: Duterte’s threat had ‘kinetic force,’ prompted other threats

Asked how the NBI knows that the threats were made out of Duterte’s influence, Matibag said the threats mirrored those the vice president made herself.

“According to those we spoke to, it’s clear that they’re always targeting the head of the president. We can correlate that with the statement of the mayor and the vice president themselves,” Matibag noted.

Earlier in the trial, Matibag made a comparison between the statements of the vice president and her brother Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, after both expressed, in separate instances, threatening to take Marcos’ head.

In a press conference on October 18, 2024, the vice president expressed that she “want[s] to remove his head,” and she “imagined cutting off [the president’s] head.”

In a more recent speech on April 12, 2026, Baste Duterte said: “We only need one head, the head of Bongbong Marcos!” /mr

World.title: Group hails subpoena for Sara Duterte’s bank, tax records
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte (INQUIRER file photo / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE)

ILIGAN CITY – Advocates for good governance welcomed the decision of the Senate impeachment court to subpoena the bank and tax records of Vice President Sara Duterte as “a victory for transparency.”

In a statement, the non-government group Pinoy Aksyon said the requested documents are significant references to ferreting out the truth on allegations she had amassed unexplained wealth during her tenure as an elected public official which were not reflected on her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

“It was rather a choice of siding with evidence over speculation, transparency over concealment, and full truth over incomplete picture to aid their consideration of the impeachment case against the Vice President,” Pinoy Aksyon chairperson BenCyrus Ellorin told the Inquirer.

Article continues after this 

The subpoena, Ellorin added, “is a vital key that opens the door for the full truth.”

The documents could either prove or disprove the allegations of unexplained wealth, hence, “a big service to the truth-seeking process.”

The bank and tax records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, are expected to be submitted to the impeachment court by 9 a.m. on July 30. /gsg

World.title: 140 hawksbill hatchlings released in Zamboanga Sibugay
World.content:
PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – Some 140 critically endangered Hawksbill sea turtle hatchlings (Eretmochelys imbricata) were released at Pandilusan Island, Payao, Zamboanga Sibugay on Sunday, July 19, marking another milestone in marine biodiversity conservation, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Region 9 (DENR-9) said.

Marie Angelique Go, DENR-9 regional executive director, said the operation was spearheaded by the Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) of Imelda, in partnership with local government officials and allied agencies.

Article continues after this 

Go said the conservation effort began when the mother sea turtle first arrived to lay her clutch at the beach nesting area. Prior to the hatchlings’ release, they were carefully translocated to a safer location after high tide threatened the original nesting site.

READ: 79 baby green sea turtles released in Panglao

The transfer was made to protect the developing hatchlings, ensure their safe emergence, and improve their chances of survival before they were released into their natural marine habitat, Go explained.

She stressed that the release highlights the importance of inter-agency collaboration and community stewardship in protecting Hawksbill turtles and conserving their nesting habitats.

Globally classified as critically endangered, Hawksbill turtles face severe threats from habitat loss, marine pollution, and poaching. As a keystone species, they play an irreplaceable role in maintaining the biological health of coral reefs. Conservationists emphasize that protecting these species is crucial to preserving ecological balance in coastal and marine ecosystems.

The DENR-9 encouraged communities to report wildlife encounters and support conservation initiatives, reinforcing the role of local vigilance in protecting endangered marine species. /mr

World.title: Sara Duterte spoke to a hitman 100% because she said so, says NBI chief
World.content:
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag takes his oath as he testifies before the impeachment court trying Vice President Sara Duterte. (PRIB/Senate of the Philippines)

MANILA, Philippines – National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag told the Senate impeachment court on Tuesday that Vice President Sara Duterte “100 percent” has spoken to a hitman “because Duterte herself said so.”

During the direct examination of Matibag, he told the court that the NBI has identified persons of interest who may point to Duterte’s supposed hitman.

He, however he refused to divulge more details, citing the ongoing investigation.

Article continues after this 

But later, during the senator-judges’ period of interjection, Senator-judge Bam Aquino asked what is the chance that Duterte did indeed speak to someone.

“Base po mismo sa pahayag ng bise presidente, nakasisiguro po na may nakausap. 100% po sapagkat siya na mismo ang nagsabi ng kanyang plano na siya ay may kinausap na papatay at pumayag yung papatay sa kanilang pag uusap,” said Matibag.

(Based on the vice president’s statement, it is certain that she’s spoken to someone. 100% because she herself stated her plan that she spoke to someone to kill and that person agreed.)

READ: NBI tags persons of interest in Duterte’s alleged kill plot vs Marcos

The NBI director was referring to Duterte’s declaration in an online press briefing on November 23, 2024, where she uttered: “‘Wag kang mag-alala sa security ko kasi may kinausap na ko na tao. Sinabi ko sa kaniya, “‘pag pinatay ako, patayin mo si BBM, si Liza Araneta, at si Martin Romualdez.” No joke. No joke.”

Article continues after this 

(Don’t worry about my security because I already talked to someone. I told him, “‘If I’m killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez.” No joke. No joke.)

Matibag is the last witness for impeachment Article IV, pertaining to Duterte’s alleged grave threats. /gsg

World.title: Kazakhstan, Austria Deepen Strategic Ties with New Connectivity Platform
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Austria officially launched the Austrian-Kazakh Connectivity Platform at the Austrian Parliament on July 15 to strengthen bilateral cooperation in transport, logistics, infrastructure, energy and investment, reported the Kazakh Embassy in Austria.

The platform aims to bring together government agencies, businesses and financial institutions from both countries to develop joint projects and improve transport connectivity between Europe and Central Asia.

The launch reflects the growing economic and political partnership between Kazakhstan and Austria, which have expanded cooperation in recent years through closer political dialogue and increasing trade and investment ties.

“Austria is home to highly competitive companies, advanced industrial expertise and a strong culture of innovation. Kazakhstan, in turn, offers considerable economic potential and is emerging as one of Central Asia’s key economic partners. Our role is to bring companies together and help turn business opportunities into lasting partnerships. The strong response to our inaugural event shows there is clear demand for a platform that can do exactly that,” said Karl Jurka, president of the Austrian-Kazakh Connectivity Platform.

President of the Austrian National Council Walter Rosenkranz welcomed the initiative, describing it as an effective mechanism for advancing cooperation in transport, logistics, sustainable infrastructure, digitalization and energy. He also highlighted the potential for further expanding bilateral relations.

The Kazakh Ambassador to Austria Mukhtar Tileuberdi said strengthening transport connectivity remains one of Kazakhstan’s strategic priorities. He presented the country’s efforts to further develop the Middle Corridor, a key trade route linking Europe and Asia.

Tileuberdi also briefed participants on Kazakhstan’s domestic reforms, noting that the country’s new Constitution entered into force on July 1 following its approval in a nationwide referendum. According to him, the updated Constitution expands Parliament’s powers, strengthens protections for citizens’ rights and freedoms, increases government accountability and further improves the investment climate.

He said the reforms initiated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev are aimed at building a Just Kazakhstan based on the rule of law, openness and sustainable development.

The launch marks a new step in Kazakh-Austrian relations, reinforcing both countries’ commitment to expanding strategic cooperation and promoting sustainable transport links between Europe and Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Produce Li Auto, Omoda, Jaecoo Vehicles, Autonomous Trucks by 2028
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to launch production of Li Auto, Omoda, and Jaecoo vehicles by 2028 as part of a broader effort to expand its automotive industry, strengthen domestic manufacturing, and introduce advanced technologies, Minister of Industry and Construction Yersayin Nagaspayev said at a July 21 government meeting.

The initiative follows agreements reached during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s recent state visit to China. In addition to passenger vehicle production, Kazakhstan will manufacture autonomous SITRAK semi-trailer tractors and cooperate with BYD to develop a nationwide network of high-speed charging stations for electric vehicles.

The country is also expanding commercial vehicle manufacturing. Hyundai Trans Auto is scheduled to begin producing 500 Volvo semi-trailer tractors annually starting in the fourth quarter of this year, while Barys Truck Manufactory, in partnership with China’s XCMG, will launch production of electric heavy-duty trucks, reported Kazinform.

Nagaspayev said automotive manufacturers are integrating artificial intelligence and digital technologies in line with the President’s instructions. An AI-powered situational center has already been commissioned to improve operational safety by analyzing data from surveillance cameras, sensors, and other information systems to detect risks and emergencies in real time.

Kazakhstan currently has 11 enterprises producing passenger cars, buses, trucks, and specialized vehicles. Last year, the country commissioned the KIA Qazaqstan and Astana Motors Manufacturing Kazakhstan plants, with combined investment exceeding 346 billion tenge (US$735 million).

World.title: UNESCO Committee Reviews Kazakhstan’s Bid to List Mangystau Rock Mosques as World Heritage
World.content:
ASTANA – The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has begun reviewing Kazakhstan’s nomination of the Rock Mosques of Mangystau and Associated Sacred Sites for inscription on the World Heritage List during its 48th session in Busan, South Korea.

The 48th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee opened on July 19 in Busan and will run through July 29, bringing together around 3,000 delegates from the 196 States Parties to the World Heritage Convention, along with representatives of international organizations and heritage experts, reported the Kazakh Foreign Ministry’s press service on July 20.

The committee will consider 30 new nominations for inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List and review 147 State of Conservation reports on properties already inscribed.

Kazakhstan is participating in the session as a member of the World Heritage Committee. Among the nominations under consideration is The Rock Mosques of Mangystau and Associated Sacred Sites.

According to State Counselor Erlan Karin, the nomination follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instruction at the 2024 National Kurultai in Atyrau to begin the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage status for Mangystau’s unique underground mosques.

Karin said extensive work has since been completed to prepare the nomination dossier, including scientific research and legal and institutional documentation. An evaluation mission visited Kazakhstan last year, and the country has recently received a technical assessment from the UNESCO World Heritage Center and the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS).

A decision on the nomination is expected during the current committee session and is regarded as a significant milestone for Kazakhstan’s cultural heritage preservation efforts.

World.title: China Eastern Plans Direct Astana-Shanghai Flights, FlyArystan Adds Chongqing Route
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is set to expand its air connectivity with China as China Eastern Airlines plans to launch direct flights between Astana and Shanghai this autumn, while FlyArystan will open a new route between Almaty and Chongqing in September.

Chair of the Civil Aviation Committee of Kazakhstan’s Transport Ministry Saltanat Tompiyeva met with China Eastern Airlines Senior Vice President for Marketing and Sales Jin Chenhua during a working visit to China, reported the ministry’s press service on July 20.

The officials discussed the launch of direct Astana-Shanghai flights. The airline confirmed strong commercial interest in the route and said it plans to begin operations this autumn after completing the necessary preparations.

The service will initially operate three times a week, with plans to increase frequency to daily flights.

The meeting also covered opportunities to expand air links between Kazakhstan and China. China Eastern expressed interest in increasing the number of flights to Kazakhstan and strengthening cooperation with Kazakh airlines.

China Eastern Airlines is one of China’s three largest state-owned carriers and the country’s second-largest airline. Based in Shanghai, it operates a fleet of 834 aircraft and carried around 150 million passengers in 2025.

FlyArystan launches Chongqing route

Also, low-cost carrier FlyArystan announced the launch of a new international route between Almaty and Chongqing.

The inaugural flight is scheduled for Sept. 23, with services operating twice a week. Flights will depart Almaty on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with return flights from Chongqing on Thursdays and Sundays.

The new service will become FlyArystan’s fifth destination in China, complementing its existing routes to Urumqi, Yining (Kulja) and Xi’an.

The flight time between Almaty and Chongqing will be approximately five hours.

World.title: Kazakhstan Holds Off Global Fertility Decline, For Now
World.content:
ASTANA – As fertility rates continue to fall across much of the world, Kazakhstan is among the countries where births are still above the population replacement level. New data, however, indicate that the country is beginning to mirror the broader global demographic slowdown.

According to the United Nations, the global fertility rate has dropped from around five children per woman half a century ago to roughly 2.2 today, reshaping population structures and creating long-term economic and social challenges for many countries. Much of Europe and East Asia has fallen well below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.

Kazakhstan, however, remains above that threshold at 2.57. A continuous belt of countries stretching from Pakistan to Mongolia still records fertility above the replacement level, and Kazakhstan is part of that group.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the country’s population has reached 20.58 million, an increase of more than 76,000 since the start of 2026.

Kazakhstan remains a regional demographic leader

Kazakhstan continues to rank among the region’s demographic leaders. According to available estimates, Uzbekistan records one of the region’s highest fertility rates at around 3.45 children per woman, while the Kyrgyz Republic stands at 2.75. Kazakhstan, at 2.57, remains well above Russia’s 1.46, Armenia’s 1.71, and Belarus’s roughly 1.2.

At the same time, birth numbers in Kazakhstan have started to decline from the unusually high levels recorded during and immediately after the COVID-19 period. According to an analysis by Finprom.kz, 74,100 children were born in Kazakhstan in the first quarter of 2026, down from 77,300 in the same period last year, a decline of 4.2%, or around 3,200 fewer births.

The decline affected both urban and rural areas, though it was sharper in the countryside. Urban births fell by 2.3%, from 46,700 to 45,600, while rural births dropped by 7.2%, from 30,700 to 28,500. No major gender imbalance was recorded. In the first quarter of 2026, 38,000 boys and 36,100 girls were born, compared with 39,600 boys and 37,700 girls a year earlier.

Regionally, the largest number of births was recorded in the Turkistan Region with 10,400 newborns, followed by Almaty city with 7,200, Shymkent city with 6,300, and the Almaty Region and Astana city with 6,200 each. The lowest totals were in the Ulytau Region with 738 births, the North Kazakhstan Region with 1,100, the East Kazakhstan Region with 1,600, and the Abai and Kostanai regions with 1,800 each.

Part of a broader global shift

Experts say Kazakhstan’s recent decline should not be viewed as a demographic crisis, but rather as part of the so-called second demographic transition seen in many countries as education levels rise, urbanization accelerates, women’s labor force participation expands, and the cost of raising children increases.

For years, Kazakhstan stood out from that global pattern by maintaining comparatively high fertility even as many countries saw sustained declines.

According to Aslan Temirkhanov, a medical doctor, specialist in molecular medicine and cell biology, and expert in youth reproductive health, the current decline is not critical and should be interpreted in context.

“We know that during the COVID-19 period, many countries saw a temporary spike in births because people were staying at home and their lifestyles changed. What we are seeing now is partly an adjustment after that peak,” Temirkhanov told The Astana Times.

In other words, Kazakhstan’s recent decline may say less about a sudden demographic breakdown than about normalization after an exceptional period. The more important measure, he suggests, is not the quarterly number of births alone but the country’s broader fertility trajectory over time.

“If we look not just at the absolute number of births but at broader demographic indicators, Kazakhstan still has a high fertility rate. In Russia, for example, the fertility rate is around 1.3. In the European Union it is roughly 1.5. In South Korea it is below 0.8,” he said.

Temirkhanov noted that economic uncertainty is one of the factors shaping reproductive decisions worldwide. In cities, especially Astana and Almaty, the cost of housing, childcare and everyday life can encourage couples to postpone having children or to have fewer children than earlier generations. Women’s educational attainment and labor force participation have also risen, which is generally associated with later family formation and smaller family size unless strong family support policies are in place.

However, that does not mean Kazakhstan is destined to follow the same path as East Asia or southern Europe. But it does suggest that the country’s demographic future will depend increasingly on how well it manages the social and economic conditions surrounding family life.

Education and healthcare as demographic investments

Temirkhanov said Kazakhstan’s relatively strong fertility rate reflects a combination of factors, including state support for families, cultural norms and the availability of reproductive health education and services. He also pointed to cultural expectations around family, but emphasized that one of the most important factors is comprehensive sexuality education.

“Education affects the quality of family planning, knowledge about contraception, understanding when to see a doctor and awareness of reproductive health services,” he said.

According to Temirkhanov, many young people in Kazakhstan are still unaware that the country has youth health centers offering free counseling and services related to reproductive and mental health.

Kazakhstan has more than 100 youth health centers that provide medical, preventive, psychosocial and legal services to adolescents ages 10 to 18 and young adults ages 18 to 29 on issues related to reproductive and mental health. He cited a 2025 UNFPA study on adolescents and youth ages 15-19 and 20-24, which found low levels of reproductive health knowledge. According to the report, only 11.7% of respondents demonstrated awareness of HIV, including 8.1% of adolescents ages 15-19 and 19.1% of young people ages 20-24.

“Awareness of sexually transmitted infections and their consequences, including infertility if left untreated, was also low. More than 60% of young people do not know enough about these infections, why they need to be diagnosed and treated, or what the consequences can be if they are ignored,” Temirkhanov said.

That matters because untreated infections, misinformation and delayed access to specialist care can all affect fertility outcomes later in life.

Temirkhanov highlighted that Kazakhstan has made notable progress in reproductive healthcare and infertility treatment, particularly through the presidential Ansagan Sabi (long-awaited child) program launched in 2021. The program allocates 7,000 In vitro fertilization (IVF) quotas annually for married couples, with services provided by around 20 clinics nationwide. Over five years, specialists have conducted 28,000 IVF programs, resulting in the birth of 12,000 children, while another 10,000 women are currently pregnant, according to available data. The program’s success rate stands at around 30%, which experts consider high by international standards.

Temirkhanov noted that reproductive health challenges vary significantly between urban and rural areas. In cities, infertility is more often linked to endocrine disorders, stress and physical inactivity. In rural areas, doctors more frequently see advanced inflammatory conditions and untreated pelvic diseases, often due to weaker access to specialized care.

“There is a serious shortage of primary healthcare personnel in villages. Access to specialized care and laboratory testing is generally better in cities,” he said.

Reproductive health myths

Temirkhanov noted that one of the most persistent myths in Kazakhstan is that comprehensive sex education encourages teenagers to become sexually active earlier.

“That is absolutely false. International research consistently shows the opposite: the more informed young people are about reproductive health, infections and consequences, the later their sexual debut tends to be,” he said.

He said Kazakhstan’s average age of sexual debut is currently around 16.8 years, underscoring the need for better education rather than less. Temirkhanov also pointed to misconceptions around HPV vaccination, calling it one of the most important issues in reproductive health.

“The human papillomavirus is a leading cause of cervical cancer, one of the deadliest cancers affecting women. Countries that introduced human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programs more than a decade ago, including Australia and Denmark, have dramatically reduced cervical cancer rates,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s demographic advantage remains intact, but it can no longer be taken for granted. Sustaining it will require a more deliberate strategy that treats reproductive health, family well-being, education and regional healthcare disparities as part of the same policy challenge.

World.title: What Drives Kazakhstan’s Economic Lead in Central Asia?
World.content:
ASTANA — Chinese business publication All China Review on July 16 placed Kazakhstan at the center of Central Asia’s economic growth, citing its output, investment stock, banking system and transit role. Kazakh economists said the country’s position rests on the combined weight of these factors.

Published on the day President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai, the article compares the five Central Asian economies through their scale, structure, financial capacity and links with China.

The structure behind the scale

According to All China Review, Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) reached $306 billion in 2025, accounting for 53.7% of Central Asia’s combined output.

Uzbekistan recorded $147.1 billion, followed by Turkmenistan at $77.4 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic at $21.6 billion and Tajikistan at $17.5 billion.

The gap was also reflected in GDP per capita, which stood at approximately $15,000 in Kazakhstan, compared with $11,600 in Turkmenistan, $3,800 in Uzbekistan, $3,000 in the Kyrgyz Republic and $1,700 in Tajikistan.

The publication links Kazakhstan’s regional position to the structure of its economy, highlighting the contributions of trade, manufacturing and mining, as well as the overall scale of its economy. Trade accounts for close to 20% of gross value added, while manufacturing contributes 13% and mining 11.9%.

It also points to the expansion of manufacturing, digital industries, logistics, financial services and innovation-driven sectors as part of efforts to reduce reliance on commodity exports.

Financial analyst Andrey Chebotarev offered a brief reflection on the article in a post on his Finance.kz Telegram channel.

“Sometimes it is useful to see ourselves through someone else’s eyes,” he wrote.

Capital and financial capacity

Foreign direct investment (FDI) provides one of the widest gaps in the comparison.

Citing United Nations Trade and Development data, All China Review reported that Central Asia’s accumulated inward FDI reached $220.5 billion in 2024. Kazakhstan accounted for $151.3 billion, or 68.6% of the total. Turkmenistan held $44.6 billion, Uzbekistan $16.7 billion, while the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan each accounted for approximately $4 billion.

The figures cover investment accumulated over time, reflecting Kazakhstan’s longer history of attracting projects in energy, mining, infrastructure and other sectors. The publication links this concentration to the size of its market, its location between Europe and Asia, and its financial infrastructure and investment framework.

Kazakhstan also has the region’s largest banking system. Banking-sector assets reached $140 billion as of January 2026, while deposits totaled $96.4 billion.

According to the All China Review, the larger deposit base provides more stable funding for private-sector lending and long-term investment. The figures establish Kazakhstan’s lead in financial scale, though they do not address lending costs, access to credit or competition within the sector.

China ties extend beyond trade

Kazakhstan’s economic relationship with China forms a central part of the article. Bilateral trade reached a record $48 billion in 2025, according to Kazakh government data cited by the publication. The two countries aim to increase that figure to $100 billion by 2030.

Accumulated Chinese direct investment in Kazakhstan stood at approximately $11.4 billion by mid-2025, according to Eurasian Development Bank figures included in the article. All China Review described it as the largest amount among the five Central Asian states and close to one-third of Chinese capital invested in the region.

Transport adds another dimension to the relationship. More than 85% of overland cargo between China and Europe passes through Kazakhstan, while bilateral rail freight reached 35.6 million tons in 2025, up 11% from the previous year.

Kazakhstan has invested more than $35 billion in transport and transit infrastructure over the past seven years, according to the publication. Projects include the Aktau container hub, Kazakhstan’s dry port in Xi’an and the second track on the Dostyk-Moyynty railway.

They support routes connecting China with the Caspian Sea and Europe, including the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

Industrial cooperation is developing alongside trade and transit. Kazakhstan and China have completed 62 joint projects worth $8.7 billion, creating approximately 11,000 jobs.

Another 55 projects valued at $13.5 billion are under development, while a wider portfolio includes 222 proposed projects worth more than $60.5 billion. The sectors range from agricultural processing and metallurgy to unmanned aerial vehicle manufacturing.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov wrote on his Tengenomika Telegram channel that Kazakhstan’s position cannot be attributed solely to territory or natural resources.

“Kazakhstan’s competitive advantage is based not only on its large territory or rich natural resources. It is based on a combination of economic scale, a developed banking system, the region’s largest volume of foreign investment, modern transport corridors and close economic ties with China,” he wrote.

World.title: Kazakhstan Monitors CPC Exports After New Drone Attack on Oil Tanker
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh Energy Ministry is closely monitoring operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) after another drone strike targeted an oil tanker loading Kazakh crude at the consortium’s Black Sea marine terminal overnight on July 20, reported the Kazinform news agency.

The attack came after CPC resumed loading operations following an earlier drone strike on two civilian tankers at the terminal on July 19. According to CPC, the tanker NELSA was loading oil at Single Point Mooring (SPM)-1 when it was struck by an unmanned aerial vehicle. The drone hit the vessel’s starboard stern, triggering a fire on deck and in several compartments.

The fire was extinguished within several hours by the vessel’s loading crew and CPC emergency response teams. CPC tugboats evacuated the ship’s 22-member multinational crew, while the captain and chief officer remained on board. The tanker remained afloat.

Oil loading operations have been suspended while authorities assess the vessel’s condition. No oil spill or ignition of crude in the cargo tanks was reported.

In a statement, the Kazakh Energy Ministry said it remains in constant contact with the CPC regarding the incident.

“According to available information, a UAV attacked the tanker NELSA while it was loading at the CPC marine terminal. The resulting fire was promptly extinguished. There were no casualties, and no oil spill occurred. An assessment of the vessel’s technical condition and the consequences of the incident is currently underway,” reads the ministry’s statement.

The consortium urged its shareholder countries to condemn the repeated attacks and work together to prevent further strikes on critical export infrastructure.

“We expect the CPC participating states to condemn these attacks and, in strict accordance with international law, develop practical measures to stop attacks against infrastructure used to export hydrocarbons produced by international consortia in Kazakhstan,” reads the consortium’s statement.

The latest incident follows Kazakhstan’s earlier condemnation of drone attacks on July 17 and 19 targeting civilian vessels transporting oil through CPC infrastructure in the Black Sea. Both the Foreign Ministry and Energy Ministry described attacks on civilian energy infrastructure as unacceptable and warned that they threaten international energy trade and Kazakhstan’s economic interests.

World.title: Four Parties Complete Candidate Registration for Kurultai Elections as Kazakhstan Advances Preparations
World.content:
ALMATY – Four of the seven political parties approved to contest Kazakhstan’s Aug. 23 Kurultai elections have officially registered their candidate lists with the Central Election Commission (CEC), while the remaining parties continue submitting documents for registration. The CEC also announced that 76 international observers have been accredited to monitor the vote.

The parties that have completed registration are the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Ak Zhol (White Way) Democratic Party, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) and the Respublica Party, while the Adilet (Justice) Party, the Auyl (Village) Party and the Baytaq (Vast) Green Party of Kazakhstan are still in the process of registering their candidate lists.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan registered a list of 72 candidates. Having secured more than 5% of the vote in the previous parliamentary elections, it was exempt from paying the election deposit.

The Ak Zhol Democratic Party registered 63 candidates, including 22 women, youth and persons with disabilities, representing 34.9% of the list and exceeding the legally required 30% quota. The party was also exempt from the election deposit after winning 8.41% of the vote in the 2023 Mazhilis elections.

The OSDP submitted a list of 33 candidates, of whom 14 belong to the quota categories of women, youth and persons with disabilities.

The Respublica Party registered the largest list among the four parties, nominating 75 candidates. Women, youth and persons with disabilities account for 38 candidates, or 50.7% of the list, well above the statutory quota.

International observation mission expands

The CEC also accredited 76 international observers representing four foreign countries and three international organizations.

According to Deputy CEC Chair Mukhtar Yerman, the observers include representatives of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights election observation mission.

CEC Chair Nurlan Abdirov said the accreditation of international observers remains open upon nominations submitted through Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and will continue until 6 p.m. on Aug. 17, in accordance with the election calendar.

Earlier, experts gathered to discuss expectations, party roles and participation on July 17 ahead of Aug. 23 Kurultai elections under the new Constitution.

World.title: Armenia sets new tourism record as visitor numbers hit all-time high
World.content:
Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

Armenia‘s tourism sector has reported a new record. The country welcomed 1.042 million tourists in the first half of 2026. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, the number of tourists who visited Armenia between January and June was 14.8% higher than during the same period last year.

Although this is the highest figure on record, the Tourism Committee expects to break the record again by the end of the year. Officials expect the number of tourists to surpass last year’s total of 2.2 million visitors.

Main sources of tourist arrivals

According to the Tourism Committee, visitors from Russia, Georgia and Iran have made up the largest share of tourists travelling to Armenia for many years. As of June this year, that pattern had not changed. The figures are as follows:

Around 40% of all visitors came from Russia,

15% from Georgia,

8% from Iran.

Compared with the three leading source markets, visitor numbers from other countries remain relatively low. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, several factors explain why tourists from these countries account for the largest share of arrivals:

“Iran and Georgia are Armenia’s closest neighbours, while Armenia has historical ties with Russia. It is also important that people can travel to Armenia from these countries relatively quickly. The presence of Armenian diaspora communities in these countries also plays a role.”

Hovhannisyan said countries with direct flights to Armenia, as well as those whose citizens benefit from simplified visa rules, have seen growing numbers of visitors. She cited China as an example, saying the sharp increase in Chinese tourists followed the launch of direct flights between Urumqi and Yerevan, along with the introduction of a visa-free regime.

Hovhannisyan also explained what has driven growth from other countries:

“The significant increase in the number of tourists from Italy is due to the expansion of flights between our countries. The same factor has influenced arrivals from Germany, where visitor numbers had previously declined. The launch of a direct flight from Kazakhstan has also boosted tourist flows.”

Armenia has also recently become a more popular destination for tourists from Spain, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.

Hovhannisyan said visitor numbers from those countries remain well below the figures for Russia. However, she added that the recent launch of direct flights between London and Yerevan gives reason for optimism.

“The peak tourism season is gradually getting longer”

Armenia usually sees the highest number of tourist arrivals during the summer and in September and October. Activity typically begins to slow towards the end of November. According to Hovhannisyan, however, the peak season is gradually becoming longer. She said more tourists are now choosing to visit the country during the winter months.

“It is encouraging to see growing activity during the winter as well. The government is taking steps to support this trend. If this January’s record figures are sustained and become the norm, we can expect strong tourism for almost the entire year.”

Trade fairs and other PR efforts to attract tourists

The Tourism Committee is running a number of programmes to make Armenia a more attractive destination on the international tourism market.

According to Diana Karapetyan, head of the Marketing Department, Armenia showcased national pavilions at major tourism fairs in Spain, Germany, Romania and Russia this year.

“By the end of the year, we plan to take part in several more international events. Armenian tourism companies attending these exhibitions present highly attractive offers. They promote our country’s cultural events, cuisine and tourist attractions. They also offer tastings, distribute brochures and show promotional videos.”

The committee also works with international media outlets, PR agencies, well-known bloggers and influencers. It organises familiarisation trips to Armenia and runs promotional campaigns. Karapetyan said these efforts have led to more frequent coverage of Armenia in the international media, with growing attention to its tourism appeal and potential.

“Armenia has established itself on the global tourism market as a safe and reliable destination,” she said.

Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

World.title: Aleksandre Kartozia to receive accreditation as Georgia’s ambassador to Germany
World.content:
Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

Aleksandre Kartozia, who was appointed Georgia‘s ambassador to Germany in September last year, is set to present his credentials to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on 23 July.

The information was published on the official website of the German president.

The website lists the ambassadorial accreditation ceremonies scheduled for 23 July. Seven ambassadors are due to present their credentials, with Kartozia first on the programme. According to the schedule, his accreditation ceremony is set to begin at 10:30.

Ambassadors from Chile, Honduras, Nigeria, Mauritania, Madagascar and the Vatican’s Apostolic Nuncio are also scheduled to be accredited on the same day.

Why is the accreditation important?

Aleksandre Kartozia was appointed Georgia’s ambassador to Germany in September last year, succeeding Levan Izoria, who had served in the post since 2020.

Before an ambassador can officially take up their duties in Germany, they must present their credentials to the country’s president. Only after this ceremony are they formally accredited and able to carry out the full responsibilities of the role. Until now, Kartozia had been awaiting an invitation to present his credentials.

Letters of credence are official documents by which one head of state appoints a diplomat as their representative to another country.

The documents identify the appointed diplomat and their diplomatic rank. They also contain a formal request from the sending head of state to the receiving head of state to “give credence” to everything the diplomat says or does on behalf of their country.

The accreditation also carries added political significance given the strained relationship between Georgia and Germany.

Relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have been tense over the past two years. Senior Georgian officials have repeatedly criticised Germany’s ambassador to Georgia, Peter Fischer, while Germany has voiced concern over developments in Georgia.

There have also been several occasions when the German ambassador was summoned by the Georgian authorities.

On 31 December 2024, Germany imposed entry bans on nine people it said were responsible for violence against protesters and opposition figures in Georgia.

Who is Aleksandre Kartozia?

Aleksandre Kartozia served as Georgia’s education minister from 1998 to 2004 under President Eduard Shevardnadze.

He has worked as a researcher and taught courses and seminars at leading universities in Berlin, Frankfurt and Bremen. In 2022, he was awarded the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

During his tenure as education minister, Kartozia faced corruption allegations. In 2002, Givi Targamadze, a member of Georgia’s Anti-Corruption Council, publicly accused him of corruption. In 2004, prosecutors charged Kartozia and his deputy, Vladimir Sanadze, with abuse of office and the embezzlement of public funds.

Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

World.title: President Aliyev’s visit to Germany: Pragmatism, energy and changing South Caucasus
World.content:
President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan arrived in Berlin on Sunday evening for an official visit. An official welcoming ceremony was held at Berlin Brandenburg Airport, where the Azerbaijani leader also met Michael Harms, chairman of the German Eastern Business Association.

As the visit has only just begun, few details have emerged about its outcomes. However, information released so far, together with the broader context, suggests the trip could mark a new phase in relations between Baku and Berlin, driven by pragmatism, closer economic cooperation and a shared interest in regional stability.

What is known so far?

According to official information, Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms highlighted growing interest among Azerbaijani and German businesses in expanding cooperation. The two sides also discussed ways to institutionalise that cooperation. They exchanged views on opportunities in both conventional and renewable energy, as well as on developing transport, logistics and communications links, including the Middle Corridor.

Officials also noted that Azerbaijan has adopted a new state programme for agriculture. The two sides discussed the potential for introducing German technologies, particularly in the field of smart farming. Tourism development and other issues of mutual interest were also on the agenda.

The groundwork for the visit had been laid well before Aliyev arrived in Berlin. On 4 December 2025, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called President Aliyev to congratulate him on progress in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. He reaffirmed Germany’s support for regional stability and invited the Azerbaijani leader to visit Germany. Aliyev accepted the invitation and, in turn, invited the chancellor to visit Azerbaijan.

On 15 June 2026, Germany’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ralf Horlemann, said during a farewell meeting that the visit was expected to take place later in the year.

Bilateral trade reached around €1.7 billion in 2025, while more than 250 German companies operate in Azerbaijan. Since the beginning of 2026, Azerbaijan has also started direct gas exports to Germany and Austria. These figures, together with recent economic initiatives, underline the visit’s strong commercial focus.

The broader trajectory of bilateral relations is also noteworthy. In April 2025, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier paid an official visit to Azerbaijan—the first official visit by a German head of state to the country. Aliyev, for his part, has travelled to Germany on several occasions to attend the Munich Security Conference and other international events.

Why is this visit taking place?

The visit reinforces the pragmatic nature of relations between Azerbaijan and Germany, which are increasingly centred on expanding economic cooperation. As Europe continues to diversify its energy supplies and reduce its dependence on Russian gas, Azerbaijan has strengthened its position as a reliable and predictable energy supplier.

The start of direct gas exports to Germany and Austria in 2026 marked a significant step in that process. But the visit’s agenda extends beyond energy. Discussions are expected to focus on a broader “energy-plus” framework, encompassing cooperation in logistics, the Middle Corridor, industry, agricultural technology and tourism. German businesses, supported by the German Eastern Business Association, have shown growing interest in these sectors.

Germany also attaches considerable importance to stability in the South Caucasus, particularly the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. This was reflected in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s phone call with President Aliyev in December 2025, during which he highlighted the importance of the peace agenda. From Berlin’s perspective, Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy has therefore taken on additional significance, with Baku seen both as an energy supplier and as a participant in efforts to strengthen regional stability.

The Berlin visit also comes against the backdrop of growing tensions between Azerbaijan and the Council of Europe, following President Aliyev’s remarks at the Shusha Global Media Forum that the country could fully withdraw from the organisation. In that sense, the trip highlights the tension between Europe’s values-based agenda and its pragmatic interests. At the same time, current developments suggest that relations between Germany and Azerbaijan continue to be shaped primarily by economic interests and a shared commitment to regional stability.

Europe’s approach to Azerbaijan remains far from uniform. While some European institutions have taken a critical stance towards Baku, bilateral relations with individual partners continue to be driven largely by pragmatic considerations. This reflects Azerbaijan’s continued pursuit of a selective and multi-vector foreign policy.

What outcomes can be expected?

As the visit has only just begun, few official details have been released. Even so, the main areas of cooperation are already becoming clear. One of the central themes of Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms was the institutionalisation of business ties, including the creation of new mechanisms for cooperation, business councils and joint working groups.

Among the most likely outcomes are progress in talks on increasing energy exports, broader involvement of German companies in Middle Corridor projects, greater technology transfer and investment in agriculture, as well as new joint initiatives in tourism.

Meetings with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, other senior government officials and representatives of the German business community are also expected to take place during the visit. The agenda may include the signing of cooperation agreements and the adoption of roadmaps for future collaboration.

The longer-term outlook extends well beyond the immediate visit. Both sides are seeking to diversify Azerbaijan’s ties with Europe, expand investment, strengthen the Middle Corridor’s role in Eurasian logistics and increase bilateral trade, which currently stands at €1.7 billion. At the same time, risks remain. Future cooperation could be affected by fluctuations in energy prices, differing approaches among European governments towards Azerbaijan and the overall stability of the South Caucasus.

The visit therefore reflects the pragmatic and multi-vector nature of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. Baku is seeking to move beyond its role as an energy supplier and position itself as a broader economic and logistics partner. Berlin, for its part, has an interest in strengthening cooperation with a reliable partner while supporting stability in the South Caucasus. The full results of the visit will become clearer in the coming days, but it is already evident that relations are evolving towards an “energy-plus” partnership from which both sides expect tangible economic benefits.

President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

World.title: ‘Police violence in Georgia has become part of everyday life,’ says Social Justice Center
World.content:
Police violence in Georgia

According to the Social Justice Center, physical violence, ill-treatment and abuse of power by law enforcement officers in Georgia have gone beyond isolated cases of police misconduct and become a routine feature of the system.

The organisation says recent information points to the normalisation of inhuman treatment of detainees, describing the trend as deeply alarming.

The organisation says police violence is driven by several factors, including a lack of political will, weak institutional oversight, a culture of impunity and political influence over the police.

It argues that the cases reported by the media represent only a fraction of the true scale of the violence.

According to the organisation, most victims choose not to speak out against law enforcement for fear of retaliation, fabricated evidence, new criminal charges or being falsely accused of drug offences.

High-profile cases: Torture, coma and death

The Social Justice Center highlights several serious cases that have recently received widespread media attention.

The case of Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili

Friends Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili were arrested at a police station in Tbilisi last year following a fight at a restaurant in the city of Gori.

Kakitashvili says that he and Tatunashvili were severely beaten inside the police station. After being questioned at the Gldani-Nadzaladevi police station, Tatunashvili was taken to hospital in a coma. He died on 9 June 2025.

Alan Kakitashvili himself spent nine months in prison before being fully acquitted by two courts.

Although an investigation into the alleged police violence has been launched, Tatunashvili has yet to be granted victim status and has not been questioned by investigators.

Violence at Dusheti police station

The Georgian broadcaster Pirveli recently aired a report in which Aleksandre Gogochuri said he had been beaten by around 15 employees of the Dusheti municipal administration.

According to the Social Justice Center, prosecutors dropped the criminal investigation against the alleged perpetrator but instead charged Gogochuri with giving false testimony, avoiding the question of possible police accountability.

Gori: Dozens of police officers accused of assaulting two men

On 27 May 2026, the news outlet Kartlis Ambebi published video footage appearing to show more than 10 police officers beating two men.

These are only a small number of the high-profile cases reported in recent months.

The Social Justice Center says it has documented hundreds of cases of violence during the dispersal of protests and the arrest of demonstrators over the past two years.

The organisation also cites findings by the Public Defender, which indicate that the number of people reporting ill-treatment after arrest has continued to rise.

According to the report, 30.2% of those detained during the 20–21 June 2019 protests said they had been subjected to ill-treatment. That figure rose to 79.5% among those detained between 29 November and 2 December 2024, and to 88% for arrests made between 2 and 3 February 2025.

Despite the scale of the violence, the organisation says no adequate legal response has been taken to date.

What needs to change?

The Social Justice Center says preventing police violence requires:

Independent and impartial investigations into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased;

into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased; Appropriate legal classification of ill-treatment under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, rather than general offences related to abuse of office;

of ill-treatment under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, rather than general offences related to abuse of office; Investigations extending beyond direct perpetrators to include senior officials who may bear responsibility;

to include senior officials who may bear responsibility; Stronger protections for victims , shielding them from retaliation, renewed prosecution, new criminal charges or fabricated evidence;

, shielding them from retaliation, renewed prosecution, new criminal charges or fabricated evidence; Mandatory video and audio recording for all law enforcement officers, not only patrol police;

for all law enforcement officers, not only patrol police; Institutional reform, including depoliticising the police and strengthening public and legal oversight of the force.

Police violence in Georgia

World.title: Courtrooms without cameras: How Georgia’s courts closed their doors to media
World.content:
How the media lost access to Georgia’s courts

For more than a year, video recording has been completely banned during court hearings in Georgia.

Since July 2025, photography, video recording and audio recording have been prohibited not only inside courtrooms, but also in the corridors and courtyards of court buildings. The ban was introduced while the courts were hearing cases against pro-European protesters and opposition politicians—cases of significant public interest.

For the past year, journalists have been forced to work outside court buildings. They spend hours waiting for hearings to end, standing outside in the sun, rain, snow and wind.

Georgia’s courts have been closed to the media before. The first ban was introduced in 2007, during the rule of the United National Movement. In 2013, the Georgian Dream party, which had come to power promising to restore justice and reform the judiciary, reopened the courts, presenting the move as a major achievement.

How have the rules for journalists covering Georgia’s courts changed? What led to the latest restrictions? And how did the country return to a practice that the government once proudly abolished?

The latest changes: a ban on video recording in court

Last summer, the Georgian Dream party fast-tracked amendments to the Organic Law on Common Courts. The changes came into force just days later.

On 26 June 2025, parliament—made up solely of Georgian Dream and its satellite parties—approved the amendments in their third reading. Eighty MPs voted in favour of the bill, with no votes against.

Outside Tbilisi City Court, journalists and camera crews wait for the hearing to end.



Following the changes:

Photography, filming, video recording, live broadcasting and audio recording were banned inside court buildings and in their courtyards.

From then on, only the court or a person authorised by the court would have the right to make such recordings.

Under the amendments:

Courts may themselves release photographs, film, video and audio recordings of court hearings, provided this does not violate the law.

Media outlets must apply in advance to Georgia’s High Council of Justice for permission to record video footage.

On the day the amendments came into force (30 June), journalists applied to the High Council of Justice for permission to film specific court hearings. They never received a response.

Later that evening, journalists gathered outside the High Council of Justice in protest. They sought to attend a council meeting, but court administration officials refused to let them in.

Journalists submitted several more requests in the months that followed, again without success.

The online outlet Publica covers all of Georgia’s high-profile court cases. Its journalists have submitted around 20 applications to the High Council of Justice.

Natia Amiranashvili, who regularly reports from the courts, says none of them has ever received a substantive reply.

“We received neither permission nor a refusal. <…> In response to every application, we were told by email that requests had to be submitted on paper rather than electronically. It gives the impression that they are trying to make the application process less accessible for the media.”

The High Council of Justice has granted permission to cover court proceedings only once—and only selectively. The pro-government TV channel Imedi and the Georgian Public Broadcaster were allowed to film the trial of Giorgi Bachiashvili, the businessman whom Bidzina Ivanishvili had described as his “personal prisoner”.

What led to the changes?

The closure of the courts to the media coincided with a period when judges were hearing cases involving opposition politicians and people arrested during the pro-European protests. Reports by human rights organisations say many of these proceedings failed to meet the standards of a fair trial.

Video footage and photo reports from court hearings vividly illustrated what was happening. Every day, dozens of hearings were held at Tbilisi City Court, with journalists reporting directly from inside the courtrooms.

Reporters attended hearings with their laptops, posting live updates on social media as proceedings unfolded. During breaks, they published videos and photo reports from the court corridors.

Many in Georgia believe this coverage helped undermine Georgian Dream’s disinformation campaign, which sought to portray those detained as criminals.

“The media’s consistent and highly important work allowed the public to clearly see the scale of the legal and moral contradictions in these trials. It exposed the extent to which the court, the prosecution and their witnesses flagrantly violated the law, and how little compassion the court showed towards the defendants and their families,” the Social Justice Center said in its assessment.

According to the organisation, this strengthened public solidarity with the defendants and highlighted the systemic problems facing Georgia’s judiciary.

“That was, of course, unacceptable and dangerous for Georgian Dream and the judicial clan.”

Journalists covering the trials say they sensed long before the amendments were adopted that the courts would eventually be closed to the media.

Minda Gabadze, a photojournalist at Publica, attended virtually every trial involving prisoners of conscience. She became one of the leading chroniclers of these proceedings, creating a unique visual archive.

In her column, The Photojournalist’s Final Word, Gabadze describes how court officials repeatedly tried to prevent journalists from taking photographs.

“My camera contains several photographs showing the hand of a court press officer or a court bailiff reaching into the frame. <…> Their goal was to prevent us from capturing emotional images. That is why members of the court’s press office spent hours attending the hearings,” she writes.

Georgia’s courts have been closed before: the 2007–2013 timeline

Open justice was one of the core principles enshrined in Georgia’s Organic Law on Common Courts. Court proceedings were to be held in public, and photography and video recording during hearings were permitted.

But at one point, open court proceedings became a problem for the authorities. This happened during the rule of the previous government, the United National Movement.

In 2007, a Georgian court was hearing the case of the murder of Sandro Girgvliani, a 28-year-old banker. He was found dead near Okrokana Cemetery in Tbilisi in 2006, and investigators later confirmed that he had been murdered.

The case implicated senior officials from the government of the time, including law enforcement officers. It sparked widespread public outrage and fuelled suspicions that the investigation was protecting those responsible.

On 11 July 2007, amendments to Georgia’s Organic Law on Common Courts banned photography and video recording inside courtrooms. The government argued that cameras could influence witnesses, trial participants and the administration of justice.

The then Public Defender, Sozar Subari, strongly criticised the amendments, arguing that they undermined the right to a fair trial.

Today, Subari is a member of parliament and a supporter of the very restrictions he once opposed. He entered parliament in 2012 on the Georgian Dream ticket and, following the most recent elections, represents the People’s Power party, a satellite party aligned with Georgian Dream.

In 2012, Georgia underwent a change of government. The new Georgian Dream administration presented greater transparency in the courts as one of its key political promises. One of its first judicial reforms was to reopen the courts to the media.

In the spring of 2013, journalists regained access to the courts, although only partially. The Georgian Public Broadcaster was granted exclusive rights to record court hearings and was required to share its footage with other media outlets.

If the broadcaster chose not to cover a particular hearing, another television company could do so instead by obtaining permission from the presiding judge before the hearing began.

All forms of media coverage were also permitted inside court buildings and in their courtyards. Even photography inside courtrooms required only the approval of the judge hearing the case. One media outlet would be authorised to take photographs and then distribute them to other news organisations.

The Georgian Dream government highlighted these legislative changes as one of its signature judicial reforms and a major achievement.

What have been the consequences of the amendments?

For the past two years, Nina Baidauri, a journalist at Netgazeti, has spent much of her working time covering court hearings. Before the amendments, Netgazeti was also able to publish photographs and video footage from inside the courts.

Now, Baidauri says she has to rely almost entirely on text to help readers imagine the defendants’ emotions, body language and behaviour.

“No matter how well you write, in today’s world—and particularly in the context of information warfare—text alone does not have the same impact as video. That is especially true in politically motivated cases,” she says. “We could no longer film the defendants. We could no longer present them to the public. We could no longer show their emotions or capture their testimony. We could no longer let people hear their voices. What cannot be seen simply does not resonate in the same way.”

Why are the amendments controversial?

Civil society organisations argue that the amendments go far beyond restricting journalists’ work. In their view, they are part of an effort to turn the judiciary into a political instrument of Georgian Dream.

They say the changes undermine the fundamental principles of openness and transparency in the justice system.

In a joint statement, several organisations said the amendments “return us to the practices of 2007–2013”, when photography and video recording during court hearings were subject to strict restrictions.

“These amendments are yet another significant and alarming step in Georgian Dream’s accelerated process of consolidating and entrenching authoritarian rule,” the Social Justice Center said in its assessment.

Mamuka Andguladze, head of the Media Advocacy Coalition, argues that an open judiciary should primarily be in the interests of the courts themselves.

“Openness is the way for courts to demonstrate to the public that the rule of law is being upheld. But captured state institutions are not interested in transparency—quite the opposite,” he says.

How the media lost access to Georgia’s courts

World.title: Opinion: Can Abkhazia agree on its relationship with Russia?
World.content:
Can Abkhazia have a unified approach to foreign policy? Abkhaz blogger Akhra Bzhania raised the question following a meeting between leaders of political organisations represented on the president’s Consultative Council and Russia’s new ambassador, Vyacheslav Gladkov.

Commenting on the meeting, Timur Gulia, leader of the opposition veterans’ organisation Aruaa, said it demonstrated that the people of Abkhazia were united on foreign policy.

“Above all, we are united in our attitude towards our strategic partner and ally, the Russian Federation, and in our commitment to further developing our relations,” Gulia said.

Bzhania, however, argues that it is inaccurate to claim that all Abkhazians share a single vision of the territory’s foreign policy.

Akhra Bzhania wrote:

“Different sections of Abkhaz society undoubtedly have different views on foreign policy, which in our case is 90% focused on Abkhaz-Russian relations.

People differ, for example, in their views on the politically motivated criminal cases brought by the Russian side against our citizens, or on interference in our elections.

The current president of Abkhazia, when he was still vice-president, publicly supported controversial initiatives backed by Russia, arguing that they were in our interests and would strengthen our foreign policy standing.

Neither he nor the foreign ministry objected when Russia’s former ambassador described the opposition as ‘marginal’, or when Russia’s main state television channels claimed to have uncovered a pro-Western network and Turkish agents in Abkhazia… And none of the current Abkhaz leadership has since renounced those views.

So how can we possibly speak of a unified approach to foreign policy?”

“It is understandable that the president wants to present the whole of Abkhaz society to Russia as friendly and, in doing so, ease the tensions that have emerged in bilateral relations.

But the fact is that Abkhaz society is already friendly towards the Russian Federation. It simply opposes some of Moscow’s specific initiatives.

So, to avoid misunderstandings, it might be better not to try to reconcile the opposition with the ambassador, but for the authorities themselves to be the first to speak out against projects that are not in Abkhazia’s interests.

Following the Consultative Council meeting, both the authorities and the opposition made positive statements. But how long will that last, and will it benefit the public? I don’t think so. In a society where people are prepared to take to the streets to defend their legitimate rights, no opposition can engage in dialogue with the authorities without damaging its own credibility.”

“As for the value of these consultations, I deeply regret that the main role of the broader opposition in our country today is to keep a stick over the authorities’ heads. And to hold it high enough that it can be seen beyond Abkhazia’s borders.

That is the best way to discourage ‘indecent proposals’. Any draft law or other initiative would then be weighed a hundred times to determine whether it truly serves Abkhazia’s interests, because people would know there is a strong and fierce watchdog in our yard that is better not to provoke.”
