World.title: Man arrested in Georgia over attack on Russian-speaking tourist. What we know
World.content:
Russian tourist assaulted in Georgia

A young Georgian man has been arrested on charges of attacking a Russian-speaking tourist in Georgia. If convicted, he faces up to three years in prison.

Video of the incident quickly spread across social media, including Russian-language Telegram channels and Instagram accounts.

Russian-speaking social media users have described the incident as an attack motivated by ethnic or linguistic hatred.

Relatives of the accused, who say they witnessed the incident, have given a very different account. According to them, the confrontation was preceded by insults from the Russian-speaking tourists.

Here’s what is known about the incident so far.

What does the viral video show?

Footage of the incident was posted on Instagram on 18 July by Polina Kurta.

She shared the video with the following caption:

“Our holiday at @agaraniestate turned into a nightmare when a man, after hearing us speaking Russian at a hotel in Kakheti near Tbilisi, broke into our room (the reception staff told him our room number) and assaulted my friend @julimurr simply because she speaks Russian.

I’m sitting in an ambulance in Tbilisi, and I’m terrified for my life and for my friend’s.”

In a series of Instagram Stories, the author also appealed to Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze to pay attention to the incident and help address the situation.

The video is 30 seconds long. It shows a young man entering a hotel room and speaking aggressively to a young woman in English. The woman tries to push him out of the room and grabs his arm. In response, the man swears at her and punches her in the face, knocking her to the floor.

The footage then shows paramedics inside the room. The young woman is lying on a bed with blood visible on her face.

On Instagram, Polina Kurta describes herself as a brow artist. Her social media profile suggests she is based in Moscow.

Following the incident, Kurta wrote on Instagram Stories that she is of Ukrainian origin and lives in Russia. She said her friends are Ukrainians and that they had travelled to Georgia to celebrate a birthday.

Polina Kurta’s Instagram Stories after the incident

Background to the incident

The incident took place on 18 July at the Agrani Estate hotel in the eastern Georgian town of Telavi.

At the time, the hotel was hosting the wedding celebration of a Georgian couple. The Russian-speaking women were staying at the same hotel.

The young man accused of assaulting one of the women is the groom’s brother.

After the video was published, many people who had attended the wedding shared their own accounts of the incident on social media. Among them was Tamuna Tskitishvili, a relative of the detained man.

She claimed that the hotel guests had been annoyed by the wedding celebration. According to her, they poured water and wine from a balcony onto wedding guests, spat at them, and later even poured urine on them.

“They dispersed for a while but kept provoking us. When they saw there were lots of drunk young people, they started getting on everyone’s nerves, shouting things like ‘Papuans’ and ‘Georgian pigs’. While the bride was dancing, they spat at her. We asked the hotel administration a thousand times to deal with the situation, but unfortunately they couldn’t. We don’t know exactly when or how it happened, but the groom’s brother went over to speak to [the tourist], and she grabbed him by the throat. He was drunk, and I’m not trying to justify what he did. But that’s what happened beforehand,” she wrote.

Several short videos later circulated on social media showing young women standing on a balcony arguing with guests attending the wedding.

In another video, a wedding guest can be heard shouting at the women on the balcony: “You’re not in your own country!”

The author of the video, Polina Kurta, has repeatedly said in her Instagram Stories that her friend was assaulted for speaking Russian. She also claims that reports alleging the women had insulted wedding guests are false.

What the defendant’s lawyer says

After the incident attracted widespread attention, photos began circulating online showing apparent injuries to the neck of the accused, Giorgi Chigladze.

Giorgi Chigladze, who is currently in custody. Photo: social media.

The defendant’s lawyer, Lasha Kapanadze, says Chigladze sustained neck injuries inside the hotel room before he struck the woman.

He argues that Chigladze “was the victim of a provocation.”

Kapanadze, who also attended the wedding, said the celebration was taking place on a first-floor terrace, while the women were staying on the third floor.

“From the third floor, the young women began shouting ‘Kiss! Kiss!’ at the bride and groom. People noticed them. In response, [the tourists] became angry and started throwing liquid and spitting at the guests. The liquid got onto the sound equipment, and the music stopped,” he said.

According to Kapanadze, the incident escalated into a heated verbal confrontation. As tensions grew, the musician hired to perform at the wedding, Aleksandre Mrelashvili, eventually left the celebration.

Chigladze then went up to the third floor.

According to his lawyer, he was trying to explain to the women that they had disrupted his brother’s wedding. The woman insisted that he speak Russian, while Chigladze asked her to speak Georgian or English instead, “because she was in his country.”

“She then became even more aggressive, grabbed Chigladze by the throat and injured him. Chigladze grabbed her by the arm and shouted, ‘You fucking whore!’

“The verbal confrontation then turned physical, and the woman struck the defendant several times. Other women in the room began recording the incident.

“She hit Chigladze in the chest with both hands. He felt pain. Acting in self-defence, he swung his right arm and struck her in the face with his elbow, causing her to fall.”

The hotel’s response

Following the incident, the Agrani Estate hotel complex published a lengthy statement on social media.

The hotel sought to distance itself from the incident, saying it called the police immediately after the situation escalated and has been cooperating fully with the investigation.

“There is no place for violence at Agrani Estate. We deeply regret that such an incident occurred on our premises and sincerely wish everyone affected a full recovery and well-being,” the statement said.

The hotel’s post has since attracted thousands of critical comments. Users questioned what staff had done to stop the confrontation, why appropriate safety measures had not been in place, and why the hotel had not been closed to other guests while such a large wedding celebration was taking place.

“Agrani Estate is proud to welcome guests from all over the world, regardless of their cultural or national background,” the hotel administration said.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry account

According to Georgia’s Interior Ministry, the case is being investigated under Article 120 of the Criminal Code, which covers the intentional infliction of minor bodily harm. The offence carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison.

“According to witness testimony, during a wedding ceremony at a hotel in Telavi, foreign nationals staying at the hotel insulted wedding guests from a balcony and poured water over the sound equipment. The defendant then inflicted physical injuries on one of the foreign nationals.

“As a result of operational measures and investigative actions, the person responsible for the offence has been arrested,” the ministry said in a statement.

Social media reaction

The incident at the hotel in Georgia’s Kakheti region has become one of the most widely discussed topics across Georgian social media.

While Georgian users have largely condemned violence against women, many also argue that provocations involving Russian tourists have become more frequent in recent years.

Some expressed concern that the defendant could face an especially harsh punishment in order for the ruling Georgian Dream party to avoid tensions with Russia.

Lawyer Saba Brachveli has pointed out that Giorgi Chigladze also sustained injuries, arguing that this may indicate provocation and should be taken into account by investigators.

“Our criminal law recognises the concept of provocation. That is, when a person deliberately creates or provokes the threat of an attack in order to later use force (or other means) against the attacker and justify that use of force by citing an attack that they themselves instigated,” he wrote.

According to Brachveli, the criminal justice system must be flexible and proportionate to the context in which it operates.

“Whether this is a case of provocation, legitimate self-defence or another legal mechanism, the state cannot tell society that a person who was subjected to verbal and physical abuse, whose brother’s wedding was disrupted, whose equipment was damaged, whose musician was forced to leave, and who was asked to speak the language of the occupying power in his own country is the one at fault,” he wrote.

Russian tourist assaulted in Georgia

World.title: Former bodyguard runs for president in South Ossetia
World.content:
Candidates are beginning to emerge to challenge front-runner and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov in the presidential election in South Ossetia.

The opposition party Iry Farn (Grace of Ossetia) has nominated its leader, Khokh Chochiev, as its presidential candidate. He has also secured the backing of Irystony Nog Faltar (New Generation of Ossetia). His nomination documents are due to be submitted to the Central Election Commission in the coming days.

“I am convinced this is the right step. We made this decision after careful consideration. I promise to see it through to the end, without backing down. The rule of law is the main principle. If we live by the law, every other issue can be resolved. I will present the details of my programme at meetings with voters,” Chochiev said.

Little is currently known about Chochiev. His official biography has not yet been published. People in Tskhinvali describe him as “a good guy”, while sources told JAMnews that he had worked for several years as a bodyguard to Leonid Tibilov, the third president of South Ossetia.

The sources said they were unable to confirm whether Chochiev still has ties to Tibilov’s family or is backed by people from the former president’s circle, adding only that he “appears to be running independently”.

Chochiev has little political experience. He entered politics only recently, ahead of the 2024 parliamentary election. His party, Iry Sombon, was established specifically for that election, but its young activists failed to win any seats.

The current presidential campaign appears to be another attempt to raise his political profile and gain experience. He is widely seen as having little chance of defeating Marat Kambolov. His support is expected to come mainly from relatives, friends and voters who favour a locally based politician over Kambolov, who arrived from Russia only a few months ago.

However, Chochiev is not the only local politician seeking the presidency. Two other politicians from Tskhinvali have also announced their intention to run: Giorgi Kabisov, leader of the Iron (Ossetian) party, and independent MP Oleg Kozayev. Neither has yet been officially registered as a candidate.

The snap presidential election is due to take place in September 2026.

World.title: AI companies 'stole' Australian culture, news bosses say as they call for licensing deals
World.content:
The heads of Australia's biggest media companies have demanded that AI companies pay for the "public good" of Australian news and culture used without permission to train their technology.

Australian news agencies are already in talks for licensing deals, with the ABC's chief revealing that AI developer Anthropic had approached it about audio and video that capture how Australians speak.

The comments came during a panel featuring the heads of the ABC, SBS, Nine and News Corp Australasia at the annual Andrew Olle lecture on Tuesday night.

The wide-ranging discussion covered everything from the role of AI in journalism to new detail about the departure of former Today show host Karl Stefanovic.

ABC chief reveals AI firm Anthropic approached the broadcaster seeking audio and video of Australians speaking. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

ABC managing director Hugh Marks told the audience that journalism was a public good that needed to be protected.

"If we lose sight of the work that's being done … then I think we'll have a worse nation," he said.

Mr Marks argued that AI companies should strike deals with Australian news companies to license works, but also acknowledged a "delicate balance" with also providing high-quality information to Australians who are using AI.

This obligation to inform shouldn't mean that news organisations should be expected to let AI companies train on news free of charge, SBS managing director Jane Palfreyman said: "Our collective view on that would be no."

Hugh Marks says AI developers should pay Australian news organisations to license their content. (ABC News: John Gunn)

News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller said that AI companies knew that the "theft" of Australian works was a "risk to their business in Australia".

Nine chief executive and managing director Matt Stanton said his company's recent licensing deal, under which its journalism will be cited in answers from Microsoft's AI tool Copilot, was a "good deal for both sides".

Mr Stanton said that Nine's decision to cut 30 job was not "directly" as a result of AI, when pressed by panel moderator ABC Radio Sydney Mornings host Hamish Macdonald.

He also said Karl Stefanovic's "different directions" of his podcast had prompted Nine's decision to part ways with the former Today host, even before his controversial podcast with Tommy Robinson.

Paying for journalism

The panel discussion followed a lecture by global news agency Reuters' editor-in-chief Alessandra Galloni, who urged news organisations to set firm terms for artificial intelligence companies using their work and to share what they learn when AI tools go wrong.

How journalism can stay relevant in the AI age What will a trusted, sustainable, global news organisation look like in an era of agentic AI?

Ms Galloni said journalism remains the source of reliable, first-hand reporting on which people and increasingly AI systems depend.

She cited recent research showing that 10 per cent of people access chatbots for news each week, including 16 per cent of people under 35.

Ms Galloni argued publishers had no reason to give up on reaching those audience but should strike deals to have their journalism correctly attributed, accurately represented and paid for by the AI companies.

"Our journalism should be licensed, not taken," she said.

She cited a speech delivered by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week where he promised that Australian writers, musicians, artists and journalists would retain control over work used to build and train AI.

Using AI in the newsroom

Ms Galloni argued that it is the responsibility of news organisations to help society understand the "pitfalls and possibilities of AI."

She said that Reuters using AI to help reporters search large collections of documents, find patterns and turn official material into fast news updates, summaries and translations.

She cited investigations that used AI to document thousands of social media posts and speeches by US President Donald Trump, and to convert 20,000 pages of Syrian government documents into searchable text that was used in an investigation that uncovered a mass grave.

Experts, union warn about ABC's AI use Experts and the journalists’ union have welcomed the ABC’s plans to use artificial intelligence responsibly, but warned misuse could damage trust in the public broadcaster.

Reuters is also using AI to produce headlines from press releases, draft first paragraphs in urgent stories, generate bullet-point summaries and translate stories, Ms Galloni said.

But Reuters only published journalism produced with AI once it had been reviewed by a journalist and its use was disclosed when it played a significant role in what was published, she said.

She said on top of the AI's struggles with providing nuance and context, it is also vulnerable to hallucinations and other mistakes. One third-party tool tested by Reuters had once mistaken a SpaceX spacecraft for a missile, she said.

"Thankfully we caught it," she said.

Ms Galloni said even advances in AI could not replace the reporting that made news valuable in the first place.

Reuters has 2,600 journalists in 165 countries, she said, including 70 staff covering the war in Ukraine and Russia.

"In my conversations with tech companies, I have often been struck by how little they understand about what original, first-hand, on-the-ground journalism is and looks like," she said

Sharing what works

Ms Galloni called on rival news organisations to share the lessons emerging from those experiments, drawing a comparison to the way that competing journalists will exchange safety information when in war zones.

"I would venture that it is our collective responsibility — to the public, to society — to enhance our and their understanding about the pitfalls and possibilities of AI," she said.

The Andrew Olle media lecture was first held in 1996 to honour the ABC radio and television broadcaster who died from an undiagnosed brain tumour in 1995.

Each year's lecture features a speech on the future of journalism in Australia and raises funds for charity Brain Cancer Australia.

Previous lecturers have included New York Times executive editor Joseph Kahn, Ray Martin and former News Corp co-chairman Lachlan Murdoch as well as ABC journalists Leigh Sales and Fran Kelly.

World.title: Inquest to determine whether man killed his mother and staged her death
World.content:
Warning: This article contains references to mental health and suicide. It also contains details readers may find distressing.

An inquest is being held to determine whether a man killed his mother before placing her in the driver's seat of her car to stage that she was behind the wheel during a crash.

Tracee Ann Grosvenor, 58, and her son Ethan Grosvenor, 27, crashed into a tree on Langhorne Creek Road, about 60 kilometres south-east of Adelaide, on December 3, 2022.

Opening the inquest in South Australia's Coroners Court today, counsel assisting the coroner Darren Evans said the court would ask Deputy State Coroner Naomi Kereru to determine if Mr Grosvenor killed his mother.

Mr Evans said the court would also seek to determine whether "safety issues" had been identified and addressed after Mr Grosvenor took his own life 11 days later.

He told the court Mrs Grosvenor was in the driver's seat when police arrived at the crash scene early on December 4, but that DNA evidence later showed her body had been moved.

"Her lower legs and body were in the driver's side, with her upper body lying across the centre console into the passenger side," Mr Evans said.

"Members of SAPOL's Major Crash Section formed the view that the injuries Mrs Grovsenor had sustained were inconsistent with the dynamics of the collision if she was seated in the driver's seat.

"DNA evidence subsequently effectively confirmed that Mr Grosvenor was driving the car at the time [of the collision] and that after [it] he had picked Mrs Grovsenor up over his shoulder and put her into the driver's seat."

Tracee Ann Grosvenor died in December 2022. (Supplied)

Mr Evans also said that, after the crash, an "independent witness" came forward and said she had seen the same car pulled over by the side of the road about 10:30pm on December 3 and that "Mrs Grosvenor was in the passenger seat, appearing distressed".

Mr Grosvenor sustained minor injuries in the accident and was detained under the Mental Health Act.

The act gives South Australian doctors the power to lawfully treat and, in certain cases, detain people affected by mental illness.

Son died days after crash

Mr Evans told the court that Mr Grosvenor took his own life on December 14, 2022, after leaving the waiting room of the Adelaide Dental Hospital on North Terrace in the CBD.

The inquest heard that Mr Grosvenor was supervised by his occupational therapist, Rachael Rolla, at the appointment because he was at "risk of absconding".

Naomi Kereru will hand down her findings later. (ABC News)

Ms Rolla told the court the 27-year-old "asked to go to the toilet" and never returned.

"There was no policy at the time to indicate what to do if someone had asked to go to the toilet," she said.

Ms Rolla said she was aware Mr Grosvenor had gone missing from the Adelaide Dental Hospital days earlier on December 9, 2022, while being supervised by registered nurse Jennifer Williams.

"At that point, did you consider: 'Well, I know that he went missing before in this building, I really should pay particularly close attention to where he is about to go?'" Mr Evans asked.

Ms Rolla responded: "I didn't think it was appropriate to follow a male to the toilet."

The inquest heard that, since Mr Grosvenor's death, changes had been made to the "protocols and procedures" that "governed" mental health patient trips into the community.

Julie Chapman hopes the inquest provides answers. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

Outside the Coroners Court today, Mrs Grosvenor's sister, Julie Chapman, said she hopes the inquest can help achieve justice.

"The system has failed us. We feel like we've just fallen through the cracks," she said.

Ms Chapman said Mr Grosvenor had a history of mental health challenges and had displayed violent behaviour towards his mother, but said mental health services had failed to intervene.

"We need mental health to be taken seriously; we need families to be listened to," she said.

Ms Kereru will deliver her findings at a later date.

World.title: Officer handcuffed teen in lead-up to police station rape, court told
World.content:
A former NSW Police officer accused of raping a 17-year-old girl at the station where he worked "locked up" and "handcuffed" her on two separate occasions months before to the alleged assault, a court has heard.

David Robert Blackbourne was serving as a police officer when he allegedly raped the teenage girl in a NSW-Victoria border town in October, 1998.

He has been charged with two counts of assault with act of indecency, two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, and one count of holder of public office misconduct him or himself.

Mr Blackbourne, 56, was arrested in 2023 and has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His trial began this week in Sydney's Downing Centre District Court, where the complainant took the witness stand on Tuesday.

She told the court that the accused locked her in a cell months before the alleged rape.

She said she and a friend were picked up by Mr Blackbourne and another officer in a NSW Police vehicle late at night and driven to the station.

"We were told they kept drinks that were confiscated from when they were working and they were kept in a fridge in the police station," the complainant said.

The woman told the court she was offered an alcoholic beverage and that shortly after Mr Blackbourne asked her whether she wanted to see inside one of the cells.

She said yes and walked down the corridor to the cells, the court heard.

"It was a big brick cell and it was very cold and dark and damp," the woman said.

" I went inside and that is when Dave locked me in the cell. "

She said told the court she was in the cell for approximately 10 minutes before Mr Blackbourne unlocked the door.

"I became quite panicked. It was cold and dark," she said.

'Put handcuffs on me'

The complainant told the court that about five weeks later Mr Blackbourne picked her up with a friend and drove them into bushland.

"He stopped the police car and then another police car entered into bushland," she said.

The complainant told the court that David Blackbourne handcuffed her in a police vehicle. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The woman said a second police officer entered the vehicle and sat in the back seat next to her friend.

"I was in the front seat with Dave and that is when Dave put handcuffs on me," she said.

"He then kissed me."

The Crown prosecutor asked the victim whether she gave Mr Blackbourne permission.

"No I did not," she said.

'He wasn't in a good mood'

The woman told the court that in October 1998 she attended a police station and Mr Blackbourne gave her a police hat that was to be worn at a year 12 muck-up day.

"I walked into the police station and I remember we had a very brief conversation … he wasn't in a good mood," she said.

The woman said Mr Blacbourne gave her the hat near the front counter, but "things changed very quickly".

"He said, 'You are not leaving yet,'" the complainant told the court.

"He then kissed me."

She told the jury she was taken behind the counter and that Mr Blackbourne pulled her pants down and raped her.

She said he then took her to another room and sexually assaulted her again.

"I felt like I was trapped in there," the woman told the court.

She said she left the police station after the alleged assaults and walked home.

She said she was very upset and overwhelmed and stopped on a bridge on the way to her house.

"I was contemplating jumping off [the bridge]," the woman said.

She told the court that the first person she told about the alleged incident was her now-husband in 2002.

The woman contacted Victoria Police in 2016 and the investigation was handed to NSW Police in 2021.

The trial, presided over by Judge Huw Baker SC, continues.

World.title: Five teens plead guilty over deadly train station ambush
World.content:
Five teenagers have admitted to their roles in luring and violently ambushing a man with an acquired brain injury to a New South Wales train station under the pretence he would have sex with a 13-year-old girl.

The four boys and one girl, who were aged between 13 and 15 when Jack Westren was fatally stabbed, pleaded guilty to manslaughter at Port Kembla Children's Court on Tuesday.

Mr Westren, who suffered a brain injury in a motor vehicle accident in 2008, died near Shellharbour Junction train station after being assaulted on January 28 last year.

Court documents state Mr Westren's medical issues manifested in various ways, including messaging girls on social media and asking them inappropriate questions.

His intellectual functioning was assessed to be in the "extremely low" range.

The five teenagers admitted to their involvement in Jack Westren's death. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

According to court documents, Mr Westren asked someone on Snapchat to give him a girl's phone number on the day of the attack.

That person gave him the number of a 13-year-old boy but said it belonged to "Amy".

Mr Westren began messaging that number, saying, "Do you have a boyfriend yes or no?"

The pair exchanged messages that discussed meeting up to have sex. The boy told Mr Westren him throughout the night "I want you" and "I like older boys".

Flowers were left at the station after Jack Westren's death. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

Girl used as 'bait'

Court documents show the boy then shared screenshots of the messages exchanged between Mr Westren and "Amy" with his friends.

"There's a paedophile that we're trying to get to come to Shelly tomorrow youse want to bash him?" one message in the group chat said.

Video taken that night showed some of the boys in a front yard, wearing balaclavas and "simulating assaults, kidnapping and robberies with weapons", according to the documents.

The next day Mr Westren asked "Amy" what train she was going to catch to Shellharbour.

The boy and three friends, including a 13-year-old girl who would act as "bait", boarded a train to meet him while the boy continued to exchange messages with Mr Westren.

Jack Westren was fatally attacked after being lured to the station. (Supplied: Simone Westren)

"You are with three boys. I saw you but you just didn't see me," Mr Westren said in a message while he was on the train.

" Have you got people waiting to bash me? "

Another group was waiting in Shellharbour, with some discussing in a group chat that they "were going to bring machetes".

Tamara Doust, 39, allegedly received a message from one of the boys that said, "Wanna come up Shelly? The boys are having a fight".

"Yeah G, what time?" she allegedly replied.

Ms Doust allegedly drove some of the boys to the mall, where they met up with the rest of the group and played games at Timezone before going to Shellharbour Junction.

She allegedly took 11 teenagers to the station, six of whom travelled in the boot.

In a video recording taken by the girl in the boot, one of the boys could be seen wearing a knuckleduster and saying "imagine this hitting him".

Jack Westren believed he was going to meet a girl he met online before he was fatally stabbed. (Supplied: Simone Westren)

'What we did was good'

Court documents state that the ambush that followed was recorded by the girl on her mobile phone.

Ms Doust allegedly ran towards Mr Westren, hit him in the head and called him a "paedo".

He fell to the ground before the teenagers repeatedly kicked and punched him. One allegedly stabbed him in the heart and liver before they all fled back to the car.

People nearby ran to Mr Westren's aid and administered CPR until an ambulance arrived, but he died at the scene.

Some of the teenagers subsequently discussed the incident on social media before their arrest.

"What we did was good," one of the boys said on Snapchat.

The teenagers who faced court today had a charge of murder withdrawn due to their guilty plea to manslaughter.

Court documents stated all were liable for manslaughter on the basis that they agreed to attack Mr Westren as a group in a situation involving dangerous weapons and would have foreseen "an appreciable risk of serious injury".

Ms Doust, who is yet to enter pleas to a charge of murder, will face Wollongong Local Court on Wednesday.

A sixth teenager, a 15-year-old boy, will face the children's court next week.

He is yet to enter a plea to the charge of murder.

World.title: Who paid for Pauline Hanson's trip to Europe? Not taxpayers, she says
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says her trip to Europe did not cost taxpayers "one cent" but has not revealed how it was funded.

In her first public remarks since returning to Australia, Senator Hanson spoke in Western Australia on Tuesday to defend her travel and hit back at criticism of several inflammatory anti-immigration comments she made while away.

She spent more than a week abroad, including speaking at two conservative conferences in the UK and attending a fashion show in Italy with her billionaire donor Gina Rinehart, with whom she was also spotted poolside at a luxury hotel in Sicily.

Asked about Ms Rinehart's influence, Senator Hanson said the mining magnate was a "very proud, patriotic Australian" and "backs" One Nation because she sees the same thing in the party.

Speaking at the Perth leadership breakfast hosted by The West Australian newspaper, Senator Hanson insisted she would "not apologise" for the trip, which also included an appearance on the Tommy Robinson Show, a podcast hosted by far-right, anti-Islamic activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who has an extensive criminal record.

Pauline Hanson fires up in Q&A over White Australia policy Pauline Hanson angrily denies suggestions her strident opposition to migration by anyone from "radical Islamic countries" amounts to a version of the White Australia policy.

During her appearance on Robinson's podcast, published last week, Senator Hanson pinpointed the dismantling of the White Australia Policy as the moment problems started with Australia's immigration system.

But she later argued she was not advocating for its return, despite claiming immigration should end from "certain countries that wear the burqa" and from "radical Islamic countries."

Senator Hanson pushed back on a suggestion from a journalist at the media event on Tuesday that her policies, which include banning migrants from "nations known to foster extremist ideologies," were a version of the White Australia Policy.

"No, it's got nothing to do with that. Don't go there with me," she said.

One Nation's policy statement nominates Gaza as a region from where migrants would be barred from entering Australia, but does not mention other areas specifically.

Senator Hanson has previously suggested she would rely on advice from security agencies about which areas to block immigration from.

Hanson admires Trump's deportation plan

During a segment on Seven's Spotlight program, which was filmed during her time overseas, Senator Hanson was asked about her views on the "concept of mass deportation."

"Oh, I love it," she told the network.

She later clarified that she wanted to target "the ones who are here illegally in this country."

Figures released by the Department of Home Affairs in June show a third of overstayers are from China, Malaysia and the United States.

Senator Hanson said she admired US President Donald Trump's approach to mass deportation as a "great way of doing it." (Reuters: Saul Loeb/Pool)

On Tuesday, Senator Hanson said she admired US President Donald Trump's approach to mass deportation as a "great way of doing it."

"Trump said 'OK, all those that are in the country illegally, I'll actually give you a one-way ticket out of the country,'" she said.

"And he said, 'then you can apply to come back in some time later.'

"'But if you don't go, and we find you, you will never get back in the country again.'"

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce also fielded questions about how deportations would work during an interview on 7.30 on Monday night, after he suggested illegal immigrants might be caught when they go to see a doctor or nurse.

Asked whether One Nation would require medical professionals to report people who had overstayed their visa to authorities, Mr Joyce attempted to clarify his position.

"No Sarah, that's ridiculous … If they're illegal, they're not supposed to be in Australia, that's why they're termed illegal immigrants. People who are illegal immigrants should be sent home," he said.

Loading...

Asked if the medical system would be used to identify illegal immigrants, Mr Joyce instead said that borders needed to be reinforced.

"From time to time, [illegal immigrants] are going to come up against a whole range of issues, whether that is health issues, parking fines, whatever it is, it's going to pop up.

"And they've got to be sent off, otherwise the whole thing is a farce."

Joyce doesn't know who paid for Europe trip

In 2017 Mr Joyce returned $40,000 to Ms Rinehart, which the billionaire had presented to him personally as an award for his efforts in agriculture.

Although initially accepting the cheque, Mr Joyce later handed it back after criticism from Labor politicians and the National Farmers' Federation.

Mr Joyce was asked on Monday if he thought it was appropriate for Ms Rinehart to gift Senator Hanson a trip to Europe, given that he had previously found it appropriate to return his own gift.

Mr Joyce said he had not asked his leader who paid for her trip, but that it would be highlighted in her declarations.

"I haven't confirmed it and I don't know … I don't occupy my day worrying about what Pauline has paid for or has not paid for," he said.

"If she hasn't paid for it, you'll be able to see it … it will be on the declaration of interest, just like everything else is."

Barnaby Joyce says he has not discussed the funding of the trip with Senator Hanson. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He said Ms Rinehart had "never asked for anything" and he had "never offered."

Senator Hanson will have 28 days to declare her trip to Europe if Ms Rinehart, or any other person, paid for it.

In an initial pitch email from a producer of the Spotlight program that Senator Hanson posted to social media, the network offered to pay for her flights.

In a statement, the network said the email was one of many sent over a period of six months, and said the only part of the trip they paid for was a hotel room where they filmed an interview.

Ms Hanson also questioned whether the pitch reflected what was aired, with the email stating the focus would be on "uncontrolled immigration".

The show's producer said this would be "the backbone of our story", after claiming the segment aimed to "enlighten viewers" about the scale of the issue.

Taylor rubbishes rumours of One Nation, Liberal coalition in SA

While Senator Hanson was courting conservatives in Europe, rebel Liberal Senator Alex Antic said his party should be more "realistic" about its election prospects and doubled down on the idea of an expanded Coalition that could include One Nation.

On Friday, Mr Antic took to social media calling One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts, known for his antisemitic views, a "clear thinker" and "decent bloke."

Senator Roberts has been criticised for past comments including that American conspiracy theorist Alex Jones was a "beacon of hope around the world", declaring Russian President Vladimir Putin had "earned his respect" for invading Ukraine, and falsely claiming COVID-19 vaccines caused miscarriages.

On Monday, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said he did "not agree with those views" and dismissed the idea of a Coalition with the minor party.

"That will not be happening," Mr Taylor said.

"I'll continue to make the point that One Nation is not fit to govern."

Meanwhile, questions over the future of Senator Antic have been hosed down by insiders, who believe no-one in the party will move to intervene despite his comments in support of One Nation.

A senior Liberal has told the ABC that while there was an appetite among some in the party, including a growing number of conservatives, to respond more forcefully to Senator Antic's dissent, there was "not an option" currently under any serious consideration.

They said Senator Antic could only be kicked out of the party from within South Australia, and there was little chance of that happening given his "total control" of the state's executive through factional allies.

Alex Antic's opinion of Malcolm Roberts is a departure from the rest of his Liberal Party colleagues. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Another said they could "not see" federal Liberal Party president Tony Abbott instigating any intervention to deal with the South Australian.

But they acknowledged Senator Antic had significant political power in the state, meaning talk of a "merger" or pact with One Nation — first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald — could not be "entirely dismissed".

In terms of potentially ousting Senator Antic from the parliamentary party room, a Liberal MP said they did not believe Mr Taylor would do it.

Separately, a Liberal described Senator Antic as the "master of trolling" and speculated his public support of One Nation and backing of Senator Roberts in defiance of Mr Taylor was aimed at "winding people [in the party] up more than anything else".

World.title: Can journalism reinvent itself before AI completely upends it?
World.content:
This is an edited version of the 2026 Andrew Olle Media Lecture delivered by the editor-in-chief of Reuters, Alessandra Galloni, in Sydney on Tuesday, July 21.

I am the first representative of a news agency to give this lecture. I note this, because it provides some context and — I hope — credibility to what I'd like to explore today: how journalism can stay relevant in the era of artificial intelligence.

AI is reshaping how we seek, consume and monetise information. Today, 10 per cent of news consumers globally use AI chatbots to get their news. That is nearly 50 per cent more than a year ago, according to the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026. Among people under 35, that figure is 16 per cent — and these numbers are almost certainly under-counts, as they do not include AI-generated summaries in Google, embedded AI in news apps, or the AI your phone surfaces before you even open a browser.

There is growing anxiety over how AI will undermine journalism and journalists. The fear is AI companies will continue to expropriate the content we have worked hard to gather and use it to train their models, stripping us of our intellectual property largely without consent or compensation. And, as a result, the revenue that should accrue to newsrooms and the audiences we have built are instead going to tech giants — a plunder that will undermine original reporting into the future.

AG Sulzberger, publisher of the New York Times, lent a very eloquent voice to these fears in a recent speech in Marseille. He warned that tech companies are "hijacking the public square" leading to "a future where a crucial wellspring of a healthy society and a stable democracy — the truth, understanding and accountability provided by original journalism — continues to dry up."

Anthony Albanese last week said Australia would legislate standards that would preserve the creativity of artists and "the journalism that is essential to our democratic society". (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

The NYT is leading a pack of news publishers that is taking legal action against the tech companies, pushing the courts to clarify whether large-scale AI training on journalistic content is fair use or infringement of copyright. The outcome of these types of cases will be relevant for all of us.

Some of these same publishers, in addition to news organisations such as my own, have signed licensing deals with AI companies for the use of our content. In parallel, countries are legislating how to protect intellectual property in the era of AI.

Your prime minister, Anthony Albanese, just last week said Australia would legislate standards that would preserve the creativity of this country's artists and "the journalism that is essential to our democratic society".

Clearly, the battle to define the relationship between AI companies and the media world is well underway. But there is still much to be settled.

And so, after two decades of battling the advertising drain of social media platforms and algorithms, the scourge of misinformation, and the slow creep of news avoidance, we now face a new, potentially existential challenge.

Let's go back 175 years

First, we have decades of know-how in licensing our news to other media organisations and businesses and protecting our intellectual property in the process.

Second, we are a font of factual, primary-source, first-hand reporting that powers a large part of the news industry.

Third, as a key foundation of the world's news, dispatchers of millions of items of information every day, we must be involved in setting the gold standard for how to use AI responsibly in newsgathering.

Before we try to peer into the future, let me take you back 175 years. The creation of Reuters coincided with the advent of the electric telegraph. Our founder, Paul Julius Reuter, was born Israel Beer Josaphat in Kassel, Germany. He reinvented himself, moving countries, changing his name and his religion before he reinvented the way news was disseminated, setting up Reuters news agency in London in 1851 with a desire to be first.

Some of you will have heard the story of the Reuters pigeons: 45 of them carrying stock market prices between Aachen and Brussels, across a gap in Europe's fledgling telegraph line, beating the mail train by hours.

The less famous story, and the one I love, dates to April 1865. President Abraham Lincoln had been shot at Ford's Theatre in Washington DC. In those days, news took roughly 12 days to reach Europe by sea from the United States. James Heckscher, Reuters' correspondent in New York, or agent as our journalists were called in those days, arrived at the harbour with the news about Lincoln, but found that the last British mail steamer had already sailed. Undeterred, he hired a tugboat, chased the ship down, and threw his dispatch on board.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Paul Reuter had already worked to shave hours off the arrival of American news into London and the rest of Europe. From the existing London-Cork telegraph line, he had built a privately-funded extension to a village called Crookhaven, at the south-western tip of Ireland.

As the steamer with the news about Lincoln came within sight of Crookhaven, a small boat of Reuters' operators rowed out, grabbed the dispatch off the ship and wired it from Crookhaven to Cork and onto London. Papers in the UK capital had the news before the steamer had even docked.

The value of trusted news

A century-and-a-half ago, Reuters had already understood the value of trusted news, of being first with that news and of assembling an infrastructure to get that news to people.

Today, our clients include broadcasters, newspapers and financial institutions around the world. We also have a direct-to-consumer business, in the form of our fast-growing, subscription-based website. But it is largely through our thousands of media clients that Reuters journalism reaches billions of people a day.

We invest in the hardest, most expensive part of the work — the origination — and we license it to the organisations that have the audience. Our north star is to offer access to fact-based, verified, independent reporting about the world, whether on our platforms or those of our partners.

Experts and union warn about ABC's AI use Experts and the journalists’ union have welcomed the ABC’s plans to use artificial intelligence responsibly, but warned misuse could damage trust in the public broadcaster.

Our trusted journalism has thrived for 175 years — editorially and commercially — as we have sold it, on our terms, to the people who need it, under conditions we set. We have done this with newspapers. We have done this with broadcasters. We have done this with terminals on trading floors. And we are doing this with Reuters.com.

So if a growing share of the world will now get their news via an AI system — a chatbot, an agent, an LLM-powered interface curated for individual use — then there is no principled reason we cannot sell our verified reporting to AI companies, provided it is:

properly represented

properly attributed

properly compensated.

What does that mean? In licensing deals with AI companies, as with other clients, we need to guarantee that certain principles are respected.

This includes ensuring that our clients do not alter the editorial meaning of our reporting — and demanding corrective action if it is. It includes demanding attribution. And it includes fair payment: our journalism should be licensed, not taken.

Our experience licensing to thousands of companies means we have a good understanding of the market value of our work and the contractual terms needed to protect it.

We have already applied this experience to all of our AI-related deals.

Our approach is rooted in a set of principles that was enshrined almost a hundred years ago. In 1941, in the middle of the Second World War, the British government applied pressure on Reuters to serve the national interest with what was essentially propaganda. Reuters' owners refused to bow to that pressure.

Instead, they restructured the company — selling it to a broader group of newspaper proprietors — and created principles that were to govern the agency from that point forward. Integrity. Independence. Freedom from bias.

The Trust Principles were not actually a mission statement. They were a defensive move designed to make sure that this particular news agency could never again be leaned on in the way it was in 1941. And to make sure these principles were upheld, a unique ownership mechanism was created: a single "Founders Share", held today by an independent Thomson Reuters Founders Share Company, with the power to outvote every other shareholder combined.

Commercial arrangements Reuters has entered into since then — client contracts, partnerships, other deals — have been in line with these principles. And these principles are what guide my news organisation in all our interactions with a government, a broadcaster, a financial institution — or an AI company.

Australia's role in building trust

Now, Australia has played a big role in our trusted reputation.

From 1947 until 2020 — 73 years — the Australian Associated Press was a co-owner of Reuters. AAP and its New Zealand equivalent were brought in as owners alongside the British newspaper associations six years after the Trust Principles were written. That means Australian journalism was, quite literally, part of what protected the independence of Reuters for the whole second half of the 20th century and the early decades of this one.

Three illustrious Australians are part of this history too.

The chairman of the Thomson Reuters Founders Share Company for the past eight years, up until last December, was your very own chairman, Kim Williams. And I think you know Kim well enough to know how firmly he held my feet to the fire!

The CEO of Thomson Reuters, Steve Hasker, has firmly defended our adherence to the Trust Principles. In my time as editor-in-chief, he has never sought to influence or dissuade us from any area of coverage, even when Thomson Reuters' own business has suffered from its association with our hard-hitting, independent stories.

The third Australian is Simon Robinson, my deputy and the executive editor of Reuters for the past few years, who will soon be the ABC's head of news. I know that, along with his sharp journalistic sensibility and deep experience in managing the Reuters newsroom, he will bring to the ABC the spirit of the Trust Principles.

ABC appoints Reuters exec Simon Robinson as news director Senior Reuters executive Simon Robinson takes over from former director Justin Stevens who announced his resignation on Wednesday after four years in the job.

I mention all of this not to be sentimental or fawning, but because it is a fact. When I stand here tonight and talk about what makes Reuters a trusted and independent news organisation, I am talking about something that Australia and Australians have helped to build.

Being associated with this kind of trusted news, built over nearly two centuries, should be valued by the AI companies.

There is abundant evidence that AI-generated content — which by some measures accounts for more than 50 per cent of overall online content — does not provide the accuracy users need. According to the Reuters News Institute, global trust in news is at 37 per cent. That, admittedly, is not great.

But look at what happens as you move further from the source of the news:

Trust in news reached via search drops to 32 per cent.

Trust in news via social media — to 22 per cent.

Trust in news via AI-generated answers: 20 per cent.

The further news travels from a human reporter, the less people believe it. The AI tech companies know it.

AI companies themselves have acknowledged that original, high-quality journalism is disproportionately valuable for training and grounding their models. OpenAI has said it would be impossible to train AI models without using copyrighted materials in general.

The costs of original reporting

I have spoken of how we think about our commercial relationships with clients. But as the editor of Reuters, my most important task is ensuring that we provide deep, original, fact-based reporting. This work is costly — in money and human terms — and most of it cannot be done by AI.

In my conversations with tech companies, I have often been struck by how little they understand about what original, first-hand, on the ground journalism is and looks like. And what it takes to produce this coverage.

A photographer in a hospital in Gaza, under fire, taking pictures of bodies piling up in a makeshift morgue.

A correspondent in a refugee camp on the Chad-Sudan border, speaking to the traumatised victims of a campaign of mass rape

A reporter with a well-informed but reluctant source, seeking evidence and explanation of a corporate misdeed.

For 175 years, Reuters — like The Associated Press, AFP, AAP and other wire services — has been in the business of being on the ground. In my news organisation, we have a global network of 2,600 journalists in 165 countries, with the training, judgement, and access to report what is actually happening.

Our journalists are a special mix of foreign correspondents and reporters in their own countries with their invaluable lived experience — of their heritage, their family, their community, their people, which informs their news judgement.

The dangers for journalists are not abating: Last year, 129 journalists and media workers were killed around the world, and 330 were imprisoned. (AFP)

Original reporting, on the ground, costs money. Take Russia's 4.5-year war against Ukraine. We have 70 colleagues — text journalists, photographers, video journalists, technical staff and safety advisers — working in both Ukraine and Russia.

Even as other news organisations left Moscow, we decided that it was important we stay to cover this conflict from both sides — as we have every war since the Crimean War in 1854-1856.

Here are some of our budget items:

rental of passenger planes to evacuate more than 100 of our staff and their families from Kabul: hundreds of thousands of dollars.

armoured vehicles in Ukraine and elsewhere: US$250K each

safety gear including anti-ballistic vests: US$1 million per year

electric generator for Kyiv and Baghdad — US$50K each

not to mention insurance for reporters in war zones

But this is nothing compared to the human cost. Over the past five years, four of my colleagues have been killed in conflict zones while covering the news for Reuters:

Danish Siddiqui, killed by the Taliban in Afghanistan

Issam Abdallah, killed by an Israel Defense Force strike, in southern Lebanon

Ryan Evans, killed by a Russian air strike in Kramatorsk, Ukraine

Hussam al-Masri, killed by an Israel Defense Force strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza.

The dangers for journalists are not abating: Last year, 129 journalists and media workers were killed around the world, and 330 were imprisoned.

In just the past few months, three of our own journalists have been detained for questioning — in various countries and at times in shocking circumstances — for doing nothing other than reporting the news.

NYT reporters issued subpoenas over Air Force One reporting The Trump administration has issued subpoenas to several New York Times journalists after its report this week on security concerns involving the new Air Force One, according to the paper.

There is little accountability from authorities for these acts against journalists: I have repeatedly asked for explanations and accountability for the deaths of our colleagues and have received none.

Press freedoms are being curtailed via legal means, every day around the world:

by leaders and governments who enact laws that criminalise reporting in the name of national security

by bogus investigations into journalists' private affairs or non-existent crimes

by measures that punish journalists' sources

The United States, where the flag of a free press used to fly high, has now become a minefield for reporters. As you will recall, early in the new Trump administration, the White House removed the Associated Press from official press briefings for refusing its demand to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

Since then, the Pentagon has restricted access to journalists. The administration has also changed rules governing how federal prosecutors can treat journalists when they are investigating leaks of sensitive or classified information from federal agencies, making it easier, for example, to subpoena documents or testimony from journalists.

Just last week, the US government subpoenaed NYT journalists over a story about Air Force One.

For news organisations like mine, this isn't about resistance or advocacy or political posturing — it's about bringing people the facts. Holding power to account. Hopefully making the world a little better.

AI can be a powerful tool

In 2025, we worked on a series of investigations that revealed how social-media giant Meta knowingly exposed users to harmful AI chatbots and profited from a torrent of fraudulent advertising on Facebook and Instagram.

Among the findings, the journalists exposed how Meta's internal guidelines explicitly allowed its AI chatbots to conduct "sensual" conversations with children. In response to the subsequent outcry after our story, Meta revised its AI guidelines to stop letting its bots engage in such conversations with kids.

Also last year, a group of our journalists investigated how President Donald Trump has used the formal levers of the US government and the informal rules of his mass following to exact vengeance on his foes and expand executive power. The reporters documented at least 470 targets, from federal employees and judges to universities and media, in a series we called The Revenge of Donald Trump.

Both series won us Pulitzer Prizes, and I raise them because they both held power to account — in this case, government and big corporate power with first-hand, primary-source, on the ground, painstaking original reporting.

AI can be a powerful tool — a force multiplier — in this crucial endeavour. But we have to use it responsibly.

AI is helping our reporters work faster, identify patterns, connect the dots in the reporting. In the revenge series, for example, the reporters used AI to build databases of thousands of media posts to document how the president and his allies targeted their retribution campaign against people.

AI was also used to mine transcripts of Trump's speeches and orders — and the writings and comments of his top appointees — for evidence of the political motivations behind the administration's threats and punitive acts.

Early in the new Trump administration, the White House removed the Associated Press from official press briefings for refusing its demand to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. (Reuters: Saul Loeb/Pool)

In a separate investigation last year on the fall of Syria's Bashar al-Assad, a team of our journalists in Damascus, Beirut, Cairo, London and Toronto employed AI tools to turn 20,000 pages of photographed documents into searchable texts — a trove of information that helped us reveal the existence of a mass grave — and the men behind it — that was at the heart of a campaign to conceal atrocities under Assad.

In this kind of multi-faceted reporting work, AI is now one of many tools in a journalist's toolbox.

Our newsroom uses AI in other ways too, helping us to distil information from press releases, speeches and other official documents and then provide it to financial clients and other audiences.

For example, we can produce headlines from a press release in seconds with a tool called Factgenie; we can draft the first, urgent paragraph of a breaking news story in under a minute, and we can have a multimedia package and a half-dozen translations just moments later.

We also use an AI tool to generate bullet point summaries at the top of stories — this is useful for many audiences, from the casual reader to the fast-moving trader.

While reliability is improving at warp speed, mistakes still happen. Hallucinations can be serious. Recently, a third-party AI tool we tested to apply key words to pictures mistook a SpaceX spaceship for a missile. We thankfully caught it. AI models in other newsrooms have falsely reported the deaths of living people and invented headlines.

This is why we do not publish without human checks. And the reason is not just accuracy. Our experience is that AI tools are great at finding news, but struggle with context, nuance, prioritisation — essentially, news judgement. So, in a central bank communication, for example, AI is likely not to capture the significance of a dove making hawkish comments.

Which, of course, is why experienced journalists doing original reporting remains so crucial!

We need guardrails and governance

And this brings me to the question of how we ensure that AI is used responsibly in the newsroom.

Let me give you a sense of how we apply AI guardrails and governance structures at Reuters. In broad terms, these are the principles:

Our journalists are responsible — and fully accountable — for everything we publish, just as they have always been.

When AI plays a foundational or defining role in what we publish, we disclose it. We leave no ambiguity about how, when and why we use AI.

Use of AI does not change our longstanding practice of correcting mistakes. When we publish an error, we must correct it quickly and openly.

We also have three levels of oversight, with checkpoints at each level:

Editors, reporters, and AI tool creators assume full accountability on a day-to-day basis for how tools are used and for their quality and accuracy.

A review committee monitors, tracks and evaluates experimental tools and workflows, ensuring they adhere to our Trust Principles.

An AI governance committee, presided over by me, makes final decisions on whether tools meet Reuters' standards for trust, safety and responsible use. If they don't, the tools may be paused, changed or scrapped.

I would like to end with a thought about what we all can do, collectively, to protect our journalism in the face of new challenges. We owe it to our audiences. We owe it to our clients. And we owe it to the AI companies that are now paying us for our content.

News organisations are, of course. competitors. That is healthy. Nine and Seven and the ABC and the Herald and The Australian compete every day, and the country is better for it. Reuters competes with Bloomberg, with the Associated Press, with Agence France-Presse, with virtually every major newspaper and broadcaster in the world at some level, including our clients. Competition is how journalism gets better and thrives.

But there are things we do not compete on. We do not compete over the safety of our journalists. When one of our reporters is in Kyiv or Khartoum or Gaza City, and a reporter of another news organisation is in the same street, our security teams talk to each other. We share what we know about the threat, about safe corridors, about medical evacuation.

We do this because the alternative — hoarding information about how to keep human beings alive as a form of competitive advantage — would be unconscionable, and because we have learned that shared knowledge about how to operate safely in dangerous places is worth more than any individual outlet's competitive edge.

A Volvo engineer invented the three-point seatbelt in 1959. It was one of the great consumer-safety advances of the 20th century. But instead of keeping the patent and the profits to itself, Volvo let the rest of the industry use the invention for free. It was a boon for public safety, and for the industry as a whole.

We're navigating uncharted waters

AI is still a very nascent technology. Our use of it is too, as are our partnerships with AI companies. We are navigating uncharted waters.

So what I propose to you all, as I come to a close, is that there could be a benefit from sharing openly what we all are learning every day about how to use AI responsibly in our newsrooms — and what are best practices.

How we caught an AI-generated fake before it aired. Or how we noticed a synthetic voice on a source's phone call. Or identified a coordinated campaign to seed a false story into a search index. What our governance committees are learning, quarter by quarter, about what the machines can and cannot yet be trusted with.

I would venture that it is our collective responsibility — to the public, to society — to enhance our and their understanding about the pitfalls and possibilities of AI.

Many of the challenges for news organisations in the era of AI are crystallising. There are legal, regulatory and technological challenges. But, for us, this is also a challenge of imagination.

What will a trusted, sustainable, global news organisation look like in an era of agentic AI? Hopefully, I have provided some insight into how we are imagining this future at Reuters. Over to you.

World.title: Indonesia sentences leader of baby-trafficking ring to seven years' jail
World.content:
A woman who led a baby-trafficking ring in Indonesia has been sentenced to seven years in prison.

Lie Siu Luan, 70, was the leader of a group of 19 people accused of trafficking babies in Indonesia and Singapore.

She was found guilty of committing crimes "for the purpose of exploitation", presiding judge Gatot Ardian Agustriono said on Tuesday.

The sentence was lower than prosecutors' demand of 10 years for Lie, who previously told the court that she had sent at least 12 babies to Singapore.

According to the indictment, Lie had trafficked a baby to Singapore for adoption in 2022, pocketing around $S17,000 ($18,800).

Another defendant, Astri Fitrinika, was found guilty of a similar charge and received six years and seven months in prison.

Babies sold online in Indonesia An infant was allegedly sold by his father to a married couple desperate to have children in one of the latest cases of baby trafficking in Indonesia.

The defendants were arrested last year after a parent reported a baby kidnapping to police in West Java province.

Police rescued several infants held by the syndicate before they could be sold.

Other children, rejected by would-be clients in Singapore, were sold domestically, including to adoptive parents in the capital, Jakarta.

Human trafficking is a problem in Indonesia, a sprawling nation of more than 17,000 islands.

In one of the worst cases in recent years, at least 57 people were found caged on a palm oil plantation in North Sumatra province in 2022.

AFP

World.title: Hobart prison sourcing meals from Victoria after floor fault shuts $19m kitchen
World.content:
Meals for hundreds of Tasmanian prisoners are being sourced from Victoria due to the forced closure of a brand-new kitchen, according to the union representing correctional staff.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) said the $19.8 million kitchen and bakery at the Risdon Prison Complex shut down on July 10, just three months after officially opening.

A spokesperson from the Department of Justice has said the cost of remediation work would fall to the building contractor as the issue was discovered during the defects liability period.

CPSU organiser Adam Gore said he understood the closure was related to issues with the kitchen's flooring being laid with the "incorrect mix of aggregate".

"The floor is not up to the required standard for wear and tear in a commercial kitchen that sees 850-odd people fed every day," Mr Gore said.

"One of the other issues they've had is the floor hasn't been draining correctly, which … doesn't allow the water to flow out to the drains."

Adam Gore said the imported meals could cost upwards of $90,000 a week. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Due to the old kitchens having also been decommissioned, staff have had to source an external contractor from Victoria to provide the daily meals for prisoners, which Mr Gore warned could cost upwards of $90,000 each week.

He said the situation had caused "a lot of stress" for workers, with details surrounding the length of the rectification works being unclear.

"One of the difficulties is not knowing what is happening, when it is happening and a lack of communication," Mr Gore said.

The union organiser said that, as of last week, equipment within the kitchen had not yet been removed to allow re-flooring works to begin.

The average number of inmates at the Risdon Prison Complex was 841, between July 2025 and March 2026.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said an issue "with the slip resistance of the flooring" in the kitchen had been identified and "alternative arrangements were in place to maintain essential food services for prisoners and detainees".

They said the kitchen was expected to be operational once the remedial works were completed.

In 2024, the government announced the construction contract had been awarded to Hansen Yuncken.

'Contemporary' kitchen promised

The state government committed funding to the construction of the new kitchen in October 2024, to replace the aging cooking facilities at the Ron Barwick Prison built in the 1970s.

It was suggested the new kitchen would be a "contemporary and modern" facility that would provide a safe environment for up to 70 inmates to undergo training and work experience.

Risdon prison's commercial kitchen caters for about 840 inmates. (Custodial Inspector Tasmania)

The construction reached practical completion in January 2026, with the project being handed over to the Tasmania Prison Service for operational commissioning.

Minister for Justice, Corrections and Rehabilitation Guy Barnett visited the site alongside his predecessor Madeleine Ogilvie, with both posting updates on social media.

Mr Barnett said the kitchen would allow inmates to prepare up to 1,000 meals each day, while Ms Ogilvie said she was "super proud" of the project.

The kitchen then entered full operations in early April, according to the CPSU, before it was shut down less than 100 days later.

Tasmanian Liberal politicians Madeleine Ogilvie and Guy Barnett (right) posted updates to social media about the new facility. (Facebook: Madeleine Ogilvie)

Staff warned of issues, union says

Mr Gore said multiple staff members had flagged concerns with the Tasmania Prison Service about the new kitchen during the planning and construction process.

He said those concerns included operational readiness, staffing levels, workplace safety, security arrangements and the practical operation of the facility.

"Staff want to see the best outcome at all times and often they can see a way forward," Mr Gore said.

" If they were just listened to, a lot of problems would be avoided. "

The new kitchen was commissioned to replace the aging cooking facilities at the prison, built in the 1970s. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden )

The union organiser said staff should be commended for ensuring prisoners continued to receive meals "without any disruption", avoiding what he described as a potentially "flammable situation".

Labor MP Jen Butler, the Shadow Minister for Corrections and Rehabilitation, said the situation raised serious questions and she sympathised with affected workers.

"The Liberals need to come clean about how much it is costing each week to ship meals for 1,000 prisoners to Tasmania, and how much will have been spent to fix the kitchen cock-up," Ms Butler said.

World.title: Will Latu Fainu’s heavy ban force Benji Marshall to gamble on rookie?
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 Will Latu Fainu’s heavy ban force Benji Marshall to gamble on rookie? Christian Nicolussi July 21, 2026 — 10:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wests Tigers rookie Javon Andrews is firming to make his NRL debut after Latu Fainu was hit with a three-match ban at the NRL judiciary on Tuesday night. Fainu pleaded not guilty to a controversial grade-three dangerous contact charge, which featured him going low and upending Canterbury prop Leo Thompson into a dangerous position during Saturday’s 32-0 loss. Latu Fainu arrives at NRL HQ on Tuesday night. Janie Barrett/SMH There was a lot of commentary about the tackle and whether Fainu was unlucky to go to the sin-bin let alone be charged. Stunned Immortal Andrew Johns said on Nine’s Sunday Footy Show: “He’s done nothing wrong, he’s tackled low. You can’t take accidents out of the game ... it’s not even a penalty.”



“You can’t tackle high because you’ll chin them … and you can’t go low? Where are you supposed to hit them?” NRL counsel Lachlan Gyles argued that “this is a very important case because we don’t see the tackle often”, adding that “it was akin to being hit with a blunt instrument”. Not only did Thompson risk injury to his neck, Gyles said, but there was also a chance to do damage to Thompson’s knees. Latu Fainu’s tackle on Leo Thompson. NRL Fainu’s lawyer Nick Ghabar put the blame on Thompson, and said, “an accidental series of events” instigated by the prop caused him to flip over.



Panel members Tony Puletua and Paul Simpkins were satisfied it was dangerous and could have caused an injury to Thompson’s knee or neck. Ghabar quickly challenged the grading in the hope of having the ban reduced to two matches, but the panel was told Fainu had received two concerning act notices for similar tackles. While Tigers teammate Adam Doueihi is free to play after he had his own careless high tackle charge downgraded earlier in the night at the judiciary, the Fainu suspension means Andrews, 19, is a huge chance of playing his first NRL game against the Raiders on Saturday. Coach Benji Marshall did not muck around by naming Andrews, a Queensland junior, in the No. 7 jersey for the club’s must-win game in the nation’s capital.



Related Article NRL 2026 Galvin gets the better of Luai in horror week for the Tigers There was speculation Andrews would be given a taste of first grade if the Tigers lost their next couple of games, and looked set to miss the finals for a 15th straight year. But the Fainu setback is likely to force Marshall’s hand, with Andrews every chance to come off the bench and spend time with Doueihi and Parramatta-bound Jarome Luai. Doueihi, meanwhile, was relieved he was never banned for a high shot on Dogs’ forward Harry Hayes. Had he lost in seeking a downgrade, Doueihi risked being banned for two games, but left NRL HQ with a $1000 fine.



“I love being out there with the boys and trying to help turn our season around again – I’ve got the opportunity to go to Canberra, they’re coming off the back of a few wins, and we’ll go there with an ambush mentality,” Doueihi said. Gyles said the level of force in Doueihi’s tackle “was moderate, not low”, and the way he raced out of the line meant there was little room to amend his tackling target. Adam Doueihi arrives at the NRL judiciary. Janie Barrett/SMH Ghabar said Hayes did not require a head injury assessment, and the contact to the head was with Doueihi’s bicep – not his shoulder. The first contact, he said, was also with the leg and torso. The panel agreed the contact to the head was “secondary”, and Doueihi tried to steady himself before he tackled Hayes.



Fifita ban adds to Bunnies woes The news for South Sydney somehow got worse on Tuesday evening when David Fifita failed to have a dangerous contact charge downgraded at the judiciary. Already without skipper Cameron Murray (calf), Tallis Duncan (hamstring), and with no clear return date for Latrell Mitchell (calf), the last thing Souths needed was to lose another experienced player like Fifita for Friday’s all-important clash against Melbourne. David Fifita failed in his bid to have a dangerous contact charge downgraded on Tuesday night. Janie Barrett/SMH Fifita landed in hot water for lashing out with his boot into the side of Hudson Young’s head just after half-time last Saturday.



Gyles said the level of carelessness was high, and Canberra backrower Young had no way of protecting himself. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The real NRL ladder, finals race and brutal injury tolls – explained in eight graphics Ghabar argued the tackle was no worse than Tyrell Sloan’s effort on Sam Walker during a 2024 Anzac Day clash. On that occasion, St George Illawarra flyer Sloan was trying to free himself to play the ball, and was hit with a grade-one dangerous contact offence. Ghabar also claimed Fifita’s actions were not intentional, the level of force was “at the bottom end”, and the referee, sideline official and bunker all felt no need to take the matter any further during the actual game. The guilty verdict means Fifita will also be forced to miss the following weeks’ clash against Cronulla. Tom Fletcher was named on the extended bench, but is likely to start in the backrow against the Storm. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Cosmetologists take their cue
World.content:
“Just wondering if Col8-ers have any special travel habits for each new country they visit,” writes Geoff Carey of Pagewood. “Mine is finding a barber to investigate the local nuances of a balding No. 1 buzz cut. My best experience is a tie between the Istanbul barber who denuded every orifice on my head with great intensity and the Omani barber’s pyrotechnic sterilisation of his blades by igniting alcohol, causing a brilliant metre long flame in the air.”

“I’m at my mum’s in The Kitchen that Time Forgot,” says Jo Rainbow, currently of Speen, Midsomer, UK. “Please can your learned readers explain the purpose of a pressure cooker, other than being donated to make Spitfires?” Chocks away!

The punchline challenge (C8) from Suzanne Saunders might just have a winner, in the form of George Manojlovic of Mangerton: “A lost sock and an old fart walk into a bar. Lost sock: I’m looking for a match. Old Fart: For my sake I hope you don’t find one.”

John Elmgreen of Mosman reviews the World Cup: “When Argentina beat England in the semi-final, we had the Argentinians in effect claiming to have reversed the result of the Falklands War. Australia beat Turkey in their opening match – but did Australia claim to have reversed the result of the Gallipoli campaign? Just as well England defeated France in the play-off for third place – otherwise we would have had a claim to reverse Waterloo!”

“The anticlimax of a third-place play-off game has all the lack of excitement, intensity and interest from players, fans and commentators of an exhibition game of a pre-season touring all-star team playing locals,” thinks George Zivkovic of Northmead. “Just give both teams bronze medals and concentrate on the final.”

World.title: ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Craig McRae has opened up about premiership-winning small forward Bobby Hill.

Negotiations continue with Tyson Stengle’s management over his likely exit from Geelong.

Tony Modra has taken to social media to thank the doctors and paramedics who saved his life.

Laura Kane has defended the AFL’s call to host the Australia v Ireland women’s clash at North Sydney Oval.

Chris Scott has heaped praise on assistant coach Nathan Buckley, who lost out on the Tasmania Devils coaching role to Ken Hinkley. ‘A lot of love and care’: McRae’s heartfelt message to premiership star Jon Pierik An emotional Craig McRae says Bobby Hill will forever be a beloved Magpie, as Collingwood and the Norm Smith medallist prepare to split. McRae said on Tuesday he had not seen Hill for some time, the star small forward and father of three dealing with personal issues.



Happier days: Bobby Hill embraces teammate Nick Daicos during a Collingwood training session. Eddie Jim Hill has spent significant time away from the club over the past year, managing only three VFL games this season, and appears certain to part ways with the club. “[I] haven’t seen Bobby in the building for a while, which it’s always something, as a coach, you go, ‘[I] hope the young lad’s going OK ’,” McRae said, his eyes almost welling up.
