Hill and Craig McRae speak to the media after their side’s famous 2023 premiership win. AFL Photos “If you’re out there, Bobby, we’ve got a lot of love and care for you, and still do, and [we] never, never change, [and] never waver in our love and support for the young man.



“We’re always trying to remain connected, and sometimes [it’s] a bit harder than other times.” Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Buckley at a ‘fork in the road’ after Tassie’s AFL coach call on Hinkley Hill is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal worth about $750,000 per season, league sources say. McRae said he had attempted to contact Hill, who has played 108 games across eight seasons with GWS and the Magpies. “There is an emotion attached to it ... there’s the playing part, the high performance of what he’s capable of doing for our team and for our supporter base, and then there’s the other personal part of, as a father, [you] get emotional thinking about a young man with three kids,” McRae said.



“We want the best for all our players [who have] come into our environment, [to] be good humans, and be a good father and a good husband. Those things that we’re trying to instil , but yeah, environments change and shift, and so [we’ve got] lots of love and care for them [Hill and his family].” The eighth-placed Magpies head to Adelaide for Thursday night’s clash against the Crows on a roll, having won five straight in a stretch of games they had targeted. Now comes a refresh with a new theme, but the Magpies may be without Scott Pendlebury, who could be rested. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making “Howey’s [Jeremy Howe is] back and someone has to go out – [there are] lots of [players in] good form, and players deserve to keep their spot ... I anticipate that ‘Pendles’ plays. That’s probably where it’s going to land,” McRae said. Josh Daicos (ankle) did not train on Tuesday, McRae adding a final call on his fitness could be as late as game time. Howe, the premiership backman, trained strongly and will return. Fellow defender Isaac Quaynor, who had a minor wrist issue in the last quarter against Carlton, is also expected to play.



The Magpies will celebrate Jordan De Goey’s 200th game, McRae saying the robust midfielder was in the best form he had been in during his coaching tenure. De Goey, pushing for All-Australian selection, is contracted until the end of 2027, and is keen on a multi-year extension, league sources say. The Crows, without the suspended Izak Rankine, won by 14 points when the two clubs met at the MCG in round one. Negotiations continue on Tyson Stengle’s Geelong exit Peter Ryan Geelong are continuing negotiations with premiership forward Tyson Stengle’s management to potentially wind up the 27-year-old’s time at the Cats with three years still remaining on his contract.



Stengle has not played an AFL game this season after a tumultuous pre-season, and although he was able to make a strong return to the VFL mid-season, he has not played since kicking four goals against the Gold Coast in round 12. View post on X There have been discussions about Stengle’s future since Christmas, and he took leave during January. The Cats have been discussing Stengle’s contract position for several months, and where the parties stood in relation to the contract that extends until 2029. Cats skipper Patrick Dangerfield told Fox Footy he was not privy to the contract discussions but as the captain of the club, and Stengle’s premiership teammate, he was just concerned that he is being supported. Tyson Stengle celebrates kicking a goal last season. Cameron Spencer



“What the future holds there, I am certainly uncertain of, but as a friend of his, and as captain, I look at it more [as a question of] ‘have we got the right support in place?’, of which I have no doubt we do and for me, footy isn’t really the ultimate priority there,” Dangerfield said. Stengle made a remarkable return to football at the Cats in 2022, winning a flag and being named All-Australian as a small forward. He kicked 53 goals in the premiership year, including four in the grand final win over Sydney. He has kicked 175 goals in 109 games with the Cats, Adelaide and Richmond. Modra ‘humbled’ by support after near-fatal accident Andrew Wu Adelaide goal-kicking great Tony Modra has thanked the doctors and paramedics who saved his life, in a heartfelt social media post.



Modra took to Instagram on Tuesday to express his gratitude to those who wished him well in the immediate aftermath to his near-fatal accident last month. The former Crows superstar revealed he had several titanium plates inserted into his face to “put me back together” during extensive facial surgery after the truck he was driving crashed into a tree that had fallen across the road. Tony Modra has posted a photo of himself and family after recovering from a truck accident in June. Instagram Former teammate Mark Ricciuto had quipped Modra, a glamour forward in the 1990s, may not retain his model looks after the accident, but he showed few visible signs of his injuries in a picture he shared on social media of him with his wife Erica and their two children, Luke and Hayley.



“Still as handsome as ever,” former Crows captain Rory Sloane wrote. There were grave fears for Tony Modra after a truck accident in June. Instagram Modra paid tribute to the SA Ambulance Service, the South Coast District Hospital and the Flinders Medical Centre for saving his life. “I’m getting out and about a bit now, and slowly catching up on everything I missed over the last month,” Modra wrote. “I’m so humbled to learn how many people were cheering these incredible medical teams on … and our family too. I’ll never be able to thank everyone enough.” Loading



The football world was in shock when news broke of Modra’s accident during the telecast of the game between one of his former clubs, Fremantle, and Geelong about five weeks ago. Renowned for his high-flying marks, Modra was one of the biggest stars of the game in the 1990s when forwards ruled. He burst onto the scene in 1993 when he booted 129 goals in 23 games, including finals, but was beaten for the Coleman Medal by Geelong great Gary Ablett, who kicked 124 goals in the home-and-away season. Modra finished with 588 goals from 165 games with Adelaide and Fremantle, and sits second on the Crows’ all-time goals list with 440, behind Taylor Walker. AFLW players Georgie Prespakis, Taylah Gatt, Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw and Sophie McKay. AFL Photos



Why pubs and Irish expats are behind the call not to move sold-out clash Danny Russell AFLW boss Laura Kane has defended a decision not to shift the competition’s looming international match to a bigger stadium, despite the game’s boutique venue, North Sydney Oval, selling out. The league has come under fire from fans and past players for not opening up the first-ever Irish-Australia women’s clash on August 1 to a larger live audience by relocating it to the SCG. The intimate North Sydney Oval holds fewer than 10,000 people.



But Kane said the league had monitored ticket sales and waiting lists to inform their decision. Related Article AFLW ‘Something in the water’: The massive footy boom Ireland didn’t see coming “When we announced this game, we wanted to create an amazing atmosphere, and so a sellout is incredible,” Kane said on Tuesday. “Do I want to be, you know, in future talking about the MCG, the SCG or Marvel Stadium? Absolutely, I do, and we will get there. “But for now, our priority is making sure that we have a packed-out stadium, and we are going to get that with North Sydney Oval.



“It’s such a great place to play footy, and really, it comes down to the data. What does the data tell us around what our fans want to do? When it tells us that we can fill the SCG, we’ll play there.” Laura Kane at the AFLW season launch. AFL Photos Instead of seeking a bigger venue, the league opted to work with Sydney pubs to set up fan zones for the city’s large Irish ex-pat community to watch the game. There are no AFL matches fixtured in Sydney that weekend. Former Carlton and Brisbane Lions star Lauren Arnell called the decision “baffling”.



“You’re already telling people two weeks out, ‘You can’t come’,” the former Port Adelaide coach told the ABC. “I just feel like you are limiting the game.” But Kane, the AFL’s executive general manager of AFLW, health and football operations said the league had turned its attention towards attracting a larger TV audience once the stadium sold out. “We want people watching it in their lounge rooms. We want people watching it at restaurants, at pubs, at venues all over the country – not just in Sydney,” she said. The AFLW season starts on August 9 when St Kilda and Carlton clash as part of an AFL double-header at Marvel Stadium, which coincides with ‘Spud’s Game’, held in memory of Saints great Danny Frawley and to raise money for and awareness of mental health.



Kane said the AFL was continually looking to reduce the number of AFLW venues, having already cut ground numbers from 38 to 27, and had done away with computer chips for ball-tracking technology. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Ben Long ban slashed to one-match for heavy Maynard bump; New video review system for AFLW “We want to make sure that we have the best technology available for both of our competitions, AFL and AFLW … and we felt that the time was right to evolve to vision and video review,” she said. “Both Greg Swann and I are looking at, ‘What does optical tracking look like?’, in the context of all venues that we play at, notwithstanding that there’s a few extra W venues that we play footy at. “What is the long-term solution? At the moment, the best technology that we feel [is] available for score review is video and the video review system, but it’s always something that we’re looking at improving.”



‘He would have been a great Tasmanian coach’: Scott’s praise for Buckley Danny Russell Chris Scott says his decorated assistant Nathan Buckley will escape any negative perception that is usually associated with applicants missing out on senior coaching jobs. Buckley joined the Geelong coaching panel at the start of this season to enhance his chances of landing the Tasmania Devils role. Nathan Buckley missed out to Ken Hinkley on the Tasmania Devils coaching job. Getty Images



But the fledgling club announced this week it had overlooked the Collingwood great for Ken Hinkley. “I suspect if Tassie get the opportunity to talk publicly about him, they would say similar things to me, ‘He was an outstanding candidate and would have been a great Tasmanian coach, but the fit wasn’t quite as good as the other guy’, who just happens to be one who coached for 15 years in the AFL, or thereabouts” Scott said. “There’s no shame in running, I don’t know whether he ran second, but let’s assume he ran second to Ken Hinkley – there’s no shame in that.” Loading The Geelong coach said Buckley’s willingness to publicly announce his interest in the Tasmanian position spoke to “how secure he is in his ability, and his position in the game”.



“It seems to me that it is quite rare that a coach puts their hand up and says, ‘This is something that I want, and I’m prepared to go through the process’,” Scott said. “He didn’t only go through the process, he went back to work, which, obviously, has been a real positive for us. “I suspect it won’t happen that much, so if you like his way of going about it, make the most of it now because I don’t think you will see it too often.” Scott said it was less likely younger candidates would put themselves on the line in the same manner as Buckley. Loading



“The likelihood for all the candidates for these positions is that you are probably going to miss, irrespective of how good a job you do,” he said. “Inevitably, the kind of perception could be, ‘Well, there must have been a good reason why someone didn’t get the job’. “I think the reality is more likely that you could actually be a fantastic candidate, you are just not the right fit for that point in time. “But again, the perception of that can hurt, in particular young coaches. In that context, I am certain that the negative perception won’t apply to ‘Bucks’.” Buckley, who coached Collingwood to the 2018 grand final, said missing out on the Tasmanian gig had left him at a “fork in the road”.



He has all but ruled out applying for the vacant Carlton and Essendon roles. “I haven’t really reflected on where those roles sit and I don’t think I would enter those processes,” Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night. “I’m absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out. I was committed to that [Tasmania job], and that ended a day ago. “The future there [at the Cats] for me will inform my next step in footy. I probably wouldn’t have come back [to AFL coaching] in unless I’d looked at Tassie, so it’s a fork in the road. “I’m really grateful for where I’m at, rather than maybe just being on the couch, [having spent] five years in media, without really knowing what I was doing with footy.



“But now that I’m back in a club, I don’t know what’s next.” Buckley said Devils CEO Brendon Gale informed him of their decision to appoint Hinkley on Sunday afternoon. “I think it’s taken me a little bit of time to reflect because I was really keen on it. I was in on it,” he said. “I texted back [to Gale] that, ‘I’m disappointed, but thanks for letting me know’. “I’ll come back around and touch base in time [with Tasmania, for some feedback] because it’s obviously a busy time for the Devils.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’ Holly Thompson July 21, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth property developer has taken the stand on the second day of a defamation trial more than seven years in the making, telling the WA Supreme Court the state government called on him to help with the removal of soil from a major infrastructure project. Strzelecki Group chairman Greg Poland and his daughter Jennifer Poland, who is also the managing director of the company, both gave evidence about allegations published by this masthead in 2019 regarding his role in trying to secure a deal with the state government to dump millions of tonnes of “toxic soil” from the Forrestfield Airport site in the Peel region. Greg Poland arriving at David Malcolm Justice Centre for his court case against WAtoday/Nine Publishing. Colin Murty A second article published a day later and also included in the proceedings alleged Mr Poland had claimed an attempt to increase WA’s lobster catch was his plan, but the government had “botched it”. The articles were based on covert recordings taken without Mr Poland’s consent at a meeting at the Subiaco Hotel, which he attended as part of his role as deputy chairman of the Peel Development Commission, but which he claims was a private meeting.



One of Mr Poland’s key contentions was that the soil was not toxic and should not have been labelled as such, with his lawyer Martin Bennett telling the court on Monday that a publicly available document and a background note from then-fisheries minister Dave Kelly’s office both supported the claim it was not toxic. On the stand on Tuesday, Mr Poland said he was told the cost of moving the soil from the Forrestfield Airport site was up to $300 million, and was a headache the state government had asked him to help resolve. “There were two million tonnes on the airport land, and they wanted it gone,” he said. In the recording of the meeting, Mr Poland can allegedly be heard telling a local business owner they could acquire a parcel of land in Myalup without going to tender, if they facilitated the dumping of “between two and eight tonnes” of soil from the Forrestfield Airport to his land in Waroona. Mr Poland told the court on Tuesday all he was trying to do was to get something down in writing that the government could work with.



Bennett asked if Mr Poland knew the meeting was being recorded, and if he would consent to it being recorded if he had been asked, to which he responded: “No.” Related Article Courts Andrew Hastie in court as businessman sues over ‘toxic soil’ claims “Why would I? It was a private meeting,” he said. Mr Poland said he had to work with government ministers, and he did not want them reading or seeing comments from an official meeting “saying they are useless shits”. Earlier on Tuesday, Mr Poland’s daughter Jennifer Poland was questioned over why her father had asked for note-taking to stop during the meeting.



She said he had invoked Chatham House Rules, because he was going to give his opinion on what minister would do a good job, and what departments would do a good job. “He didn’t want those comments going back to ministers because he had to work with them,” Ms Poland said. After receiving questions from a journalist at this masthead based on the recordings of the meeting, Mr Poland told the court he spoke with then-regional development minister Alannah MacTiernan about the allegations. “If its politics they [journalists] keep coming after you,” Mr Poland said MacTiernan had told him. “She told me, ‘I’ve accepted your resignation already [from the Peel Development Commission], that stops it’.”



Discussing the second story published, Mr Poland told the court he had mentioned the idea of licensing boats to catch lobsters for the domestic market at a Labor roundtable with then-premier Mark McGowan, and other ministers, who told him they loved the idea. Mr Poland claimed then-fisheries minister Kelly was also supportive of the proposal. The state government then released the report WA’s Western Rock Lobster Plan - Industry growth plan to create jobs. “I don’t like the way they took the idea and changed it, so the government owned the licences,” Mr Poland told the court. But he said the government had reached out to him asking for a public statement of support, which he supplied.



Mr Poland was then cross-examined by Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis, who asked whether he would agree the Peel region was cherished for its ecological significance. “They wouldn’t allow that level of mining and destruction there if it was all cherished,” Mr Poland replied. Questioned on the number of times he had met with the landowner he was discussing the deal with, Mr Poland said the Peel Development Commission chairman had largely been dealing with him and the plans regarding the transfer of the sand. Developer ‘angry’ over journalists’ questions Ms Poland said her father had been “very angry” when he first received questions from journalists, allegedly saying: “All I’ve tried to do is help.”



After the initial article was published, she said her father could not believe it was happening, or why ministers quoted in the article had “said what they had”. “He said, ‘They know me, they know my deal’,” Ms Poland recalled. “He was destroyed by it.” Ms Poland reached out to Bennett after her father received questions from this masthead, and the lawyer sent a letter to journalists before the publication of both stories. It was over these letters, and her recount of events, that Ms Poland was questioned by Nine’s lawyer Martin Goldblatt.



A letter sent to the journalists from Bennett on behalf of the Polands categorised the soil as “toxic” or “contaminated” several times. However, Ms Poland argued there were different levels of “contaminated” when asked why, if she believed that to be incorrect, she had approved the letter being sent. She also argued many of the direct quotes, taken from the recording at the Subiaco Hotel, were out of context and that her father often spoke a certain way due to his dyslexia. The trial continues, with Mr Poland expected to return to the stand tomorrow. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Sunshine Coast ‘freebirth’ baby could have survived, coroner finds
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPregnancy Sunshine Coast ‘freebirth’ baby could have survived, coroner finds Courtney Kruk July 21, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A baby that died from complications during a free birth on the Sunshine Coast would have likely survived with timely medical care, a coroner’s court has heard, with an expert calling for women’s birth trauma to be taken seriously to prevent disengagement with conventional systems. The baby girl – referred to as “Baby M” in the investigation – was “free birthed” on October 20, 2024. Freebirths take place outside the hospital or medical system, usually at home, with no medical professional present. Baby M, as she was referred to in the Queensland Coroners Court, died from asphyxia during a freebirth. Michele Mossop The coroner was told that Baby M’s mother was traumatised by the birth of her first child, which was delivered by emergency caesarean section in 2021 following an abnormal heart rate reading.



She subsequently suffered two miscarriages – at four and 10 weeks – and wanted to try for a vaginal birth at home for her second child, initially with a midwife present. Related Article Pregnancy The reason why some Queensland women are opting for unassisted births The court was told that a private midwife was engaged, but Baby M’s mother declined recommended ultrasound scans and glucose tolerance tests. At about 30 weeks, she dismissed the midwife for financial reasons and instead made plans to carry out a free birth at home with her partner. Baby M’s mother went into labour on the afternoon of October 20, 2024. A friend was contacted a few hours later “to come over to support and help”. Baby M was born at approximately 11.40pm. She was noted to be “hypotonic, pale with nil spontaneous limb movements nor attempts at crying”, Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher said.



A friend of the family – an off-duty paramedic – was called for help, arriving a short time later with a neonatal valve bag mask and an oxygen cylinder. Baby M apparently regained a heartbeat while being resuscitated. An ambulance arrived at 12.13am and took Baby M to Sunshine Coast University Hospital. Despite the efforts of paramedics and hospital staff, Baby M’s condition did not improve, and a decision was made to cease resuscitation efforts. Baby M was declared dead at 2.42am on October 21.



An autopsy determined her death was caused by meconium aspiration syndrome – when a newborn inhales a mixture of their first stool and amniotic fluid, usually after becoming distressed. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Inside freebirthing: Empowerment, distrust and a growing dogma Gallagher said if Baby M had been “delivered with the support of skilled personnel, an earlier identification of fetal distress and timely delivery with appropriate neonatal care and support would likely have prevented severe asphyxia resulting in neonatal death”. Associate Professor Renuka Sekar, an expert in obstetric and maternal fetal medicine who reviewed the case, said appropriate care and advice was offered by the private midwife and the hospital team. She said the case highlighted the real consequences of birth trauma.





That inquest has been paused to consider new evidence. Gallagher decided against holding an inquest into Baby M’s death and offered condolences to the family for their loss. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ben King set to leave the Suns for Hawks in a stunning about-face
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 Ben King set to leave the Suns for Hawks in a stunning about-face Sam McClure July 21, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ben King is poised to complete one of the most dramatic contract backflips in recent AFL history, with the Gold Coast spearhead set to reject the Suns’ lucrative long-term offer and instead nominate Hawthorn as his preferred destination for 2027. The stunning change of heart comes barely two months after King told The Age he intended to remain on the Gold Coast, insisting he loved the club and saw his future in Queensland. Ben King wants to play for Hawthorn next season. AFL Photos But three industry sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity because discussions remain confidential, have confirmed King’s position has shifted significantly in recent weeks, with Hawthorn now firmly in the box seat to secure one of the competition’s premier key forwards. King’s contract at Hawthorn is expected to be a six-year deal, taking him until the end of 2032.



Gold Coast have not yet officially been told of his intention to leave. King will be in Melbourne this week ahead of the Suns’ game against Carlton at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star The decision is a bitter blow for the Suns, who had been confident they would retain the 26-year-old despite intense Victorian interest and had tabled a massive long-term contract in a bid to keep him at the club. Several factors have contributed to King’s dramatic reversal. His partner is keen to return home to Victoria, while Gold Coast’s alarming on-field slide has also weighed heavily. The Suns have now lost eight consecutive matches after appearing well-placed to challenge for a second-consecutive finals campaign earlier this season.



King’s own form has only enhanced his value. The powerful key forward sits second in the Coleman Medal race and has established himself as one of the AFL’s most reliable goalkickers, kicking at least 40 goals in every completed season since 2021. Last year he produced a career-best campaign with 71 goals, underlining why Hawthorn have been prepared to aggressively pursue his signature. How the trade period plays out is yet to be determined. As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast have the power to match the bid and force a trade. But given the Suns’ disastrous form slump has now landed them 14th on the ladder, the Queensland club could opt to accept first-round compensation, which, if the season finished now, would be pick No.6.



The Hawks would much prefer to land King without a trade, given they are also in the box seat to land Essendon’s Zach Merrett, who will once again request a move to Hawthorn despite a failed move last year. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Hawthorn want Ben King and Zach Merrett. This is how Gold Coast losses help their cause For Hawthorn, landing King would represent another significant statement of intent as the club continues to build a list capable of challenging for premierships over the coming years. However, his arrival would also create a fascinating list-management dilemma. Mitch Lewis, who reminded the competition of his quality with a five-goal performance on the weekend, is also out of contract and now faces an uncertain future. Lewis has battled injury over the past two seasons but remains one of the league’s most talented key-position forwards when fit.



Whether Hawthorn believe they can accommodate both King and Lewis in the same forward line, or whether King’s impending arrival accelerates Lewis’ departure, looms as one of the major questions heading into the trade and free-agency period. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 How the Pies can avoid wildcard round, as we rate every team’s run home The Hawks have invested heavily in assembling one of the AFL’s youngest and most exciting lists under Sam Mitchell, and adding a proven goal kicking machine entering the prime of his career would significantly strengthen their premiership aspirations. For Gold Coast, meanwhile, losing a home-grown marquee player after years of investment would be another devastating retention blow. The Suns have long viewed King as a cornerstone of their future, but after months of confidence they would secure his signature, they are now confronting the prospect of watching one of the competition’s elite key forwards walk out the door.



If it results in a move, King’s decision would rank among the most extraordinary contract reversals in recent AFL memory – a player who only weeks ago expected to stay, now preparing to head home to Victoria and reshape the landscape of the upcoming trade period. King’s management has been contacted for comment. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Political heavyweights join campaign against 16-storey Hawthorn tower
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life Political heavyweights join campaign against 16-storey Hawthorn tower Rachael Ward July 21, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vacant except for a trio of empty shopfronts and the odd patch of grass, this land in the heart of one of Hawthorn’s busiest shopping strips must be developed, everyone agrees. But a new proposal to build a 16-storey tower at 846-858 Glenferrie Road – twice the height that has already been approved and four storeys above state government-imposed activity centre height limits – has sparked backlash from residents and political heavyweights in the inner east. Boroondara Community Group President Jane Oldham said the site at 850 Glenferrie Road must be developed but is among locals concerned about a new 16-storey proposal. Justin McManus Last year, Boroondara Council granted permission to build an eight-storey building comprising 41 apartments and retail space on the site. Now the developer wants to increase the number of apartments to 78 and has sought permission directly from Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny for the $65 million development through a government pathway that bypasses councils for planning approvals.



Related Article Property development Beloved Kew supermarket site headed to Supreme Court over controversial development Some 17.5 per cent of apartments would be affordable housing or the developer would make a cash contribution equivalent to 5.25 per cent of costs, which is above minimum requirements, plans show. No decision has been made, and Boroondara Council is urging the state government to stick to its own height limits and cap the building at 12 storeys, while federal MP for Kooyong Monique Ryan and former opposition leader John Pesutto are among residents supportive of the building topping out at eight levels. Boroondara Community Group president Jane Oldham, a local who advocates for better liveability in the inner east, also believes the site is perfect for an eight-storey development with housing. Oldham wants to spread out development in locations close to transport or activity and is concerned the new proposal will overshadow Glenferrie Road, which could undermine efforts to develop that end of the strip by attracting bars, restaurants and cafes.



“The concern with 16 storeys is about overdevelopment of a site that will impact on the amenity of future residents and of the public on Glenferrie Road,” she said. Boroondara Council has no decision-making power but is pushing for the development to be limited to 12 storeys. Mayor Wes Gault has urged the planning minister to pay attention to concerns about overshadowing, the amount of affordable housing, landscaping and public amenity. “If the minister allows this proposal to be built as designed, ignoring the [height] rules she put in place just months ago, it will be clear community views are irrelevant to this government, and the community should have no confidence in the state’s planning scheme,” he said. “We’re not arguing for the status quo or trying to stop developments – we agree this is a great site for a new development.”



Glenferrie Road Traders Association president Rajna Jollie said she was concerned a 16-storey development would change the look of the street and affect the shopping precinct’s vibrant atmosphere. An artist’s impression of a proposed 16-storey tower in Hawthorn. Outline Projects “We want to protect small businesses in these small local areas that have boutique-type style shopping experiences for our customers and our community,” she said. Hawthorn MP and former opposition leader John Pesutto described the proposal as “totally inappropriate” for the area, and hit out at the Labor government’s development facilitation pathway, which bypasses councils. “This is becoming a bit of a parody, it’s pretending to be a process where it’s really just an opportunity for a government, in my frank opinion, to slam onto communities projects like this,” Pesutto told a council meeting this week.



Federal MP for Kooyong Monique Ryan said she supported mixed-use, medium-density housing at the site. “I’m very much in favour of increased housing in Hawthorn and surrounding suburbs that’s done in a sensitive and inclusive way,” Ryan told the meeting. A $65 million 16-storey development is proposed for Glenferrie Road, Hawthorn. Justin McManus “But I’m deeply opposed to the lack of clarity and assurance regarding the affordable housing component of this site and to the state government’s failure to consult communities like us adequately.” Several neighbouring residents expressed concerns about the proposal at the council meeting, while others were broadly supportive of efforts to create more housing.



Peter Forsyth, managing director of the site’s developer, Outline Projects, said he was aware of community feedback and would work through the issues with the Department of Transport and Planning. Related Article City life Separation Street: The development dividing Melbourne’s inner north He said he was excited to deliver the “exemplar project” with leading architecture firm Wardle, and emphasised the application included generous affordable housing above government requirements. “We have engaged in the planning approval process via the state government’s planning pathway and have worked through a detailed design process in the context of the state government’s recent planning reforms for activity centres,” he said. YIMBY Melbourne lead organiser Jonathan O’Brien said taller buildings were more cost-effective for developers.



“People have this idea that quite tall buildings will ruin character. It’s not necessarily clear to me that people really notice how tall a building is once it’s built,” he said. “What tends to be more important is what’s at that ground level, and it seems like this is going to have an active frontage with retail people can engage with.” A Victorian government spokesperson claimed the council was blocking new homes in suburbs like Hawthorn and Kew which had the effect of “locking out” workers, families and young Victorians from well-connected areas. Editor's pick Opinion

Trade wars Trump wants to make his trade wall bigger and better than ever before Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “We’ve been focused on overhauling our planning system to get more homes built so more families and young Victorians can live close to what matters to them,” they said.



“Any proposal will be considered on its merits, and as this application is currently under assessment, it would be inappropriate to comment further.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: Will Latu Fainu’s heavy ban force Benji Marshall to gamble on rookie?
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 Will Latu Fainu’s heavy ban force Benji Marshall to gamble on rookie? Christian Nicolussi July 21, 2026 — 10:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wests Tigers rookie Javon Andrews is firming to make his NRL debut after Latu Fainu was hit with a three-match ban at the NRL judiciary on Tuesday night. Fainu pleaded not guilty to a controversial grade-three dangerous contact charge, which featured him going low and upending Canterbury prop Leo Thompson into a dangerous position during Saturday’s 32-0 loss. Latu Fainu arrives at NRL HQ on Tuesday night. Janie Barrett/SMH There was a lot of commentary about the tackle and whether Fainu was unlucky to go to the sin-bin let alone be charged. Stunned Immortal Andrew Johns said on Nine’s Sunday Footy Show: “He’s done nothing wrong, he’s tackled low. You can’t take accidents out of the game ... it’s not even a penalty.”



“You can’t tackle high because you’ll chin them … and you can’t go low? Where are you supposed to hit them?” NRL counsel Lachlan Gyles argued that “this is a very important case because we don’t see the tackle often”, adding that “it was akin to being hit with a blunt instrument”. Not only did Thompson risk injury to his neck, Gyles said, but there was also a chance to do damage to Thompson’s knees. Latu Fainu’s tackle on Leo Thompson. NRL Fainu’s lawyer Nick Ghabar put the blame on Thompson, and said, “an accidental series of events” instigated by the prop caused him to flip over.



Panel members Tony Puletua and Paul Simpkins were satisfied it was dangerous and could have caused an injury to Thompson’s knee or neck. Ghabar quickly challenged the grading in the hope of having the ban reduced to two matches, but the panel was told Fainu had received two concerning act notices for similar tackles. While Tigers teammate Adam Doueihi is free to play after he had his own careless high tackle charge downgraded earlier in the night at the judiciary, the Fainu suspension means Andrews, 19, is a huge chance of playing his first NRL game against the Raiders on Saturday. Coach Benji Marshall did not muck around by naming Andrews, a Queensland junior, in the No. 7 jersey for the club’s must-win game in the nation’s capital.



Related Article NRL 2026 Galvin gets the better of Luai in horror week for the Tigers There was speculation Andrews would be given a taste of first grade if the Tigers lost their next couple of games, and looked set to miss the finals for a 15th straight year. But the Fainu setback is likely to force Marshall’s hand, with Andrews every chance to come off the bench and spend time with Doueihi and Parramatta-bound Jarome Luai. Doueihi, meanwhile, was relieved he was never banned for a high shot on Dogs’ forward Harry Hayes. Had he lost in seeking a downgrade, Doueihi risked being banned for two games, but left NRL HQ with a $1000 fine.



“I love being out there with the boys and trying to help turn our season around again – I’ve got the opportunity to go to Canberra, they’re coming off the back of a few wins, and we’ll go there with an ambush mentality,” Doueihi said. Gyles said the level of force in Doueihi’s tackle “was moderate, not low”, and the way he raced out of the line meant there was little room to amend his tackling target. Adam Doueihi arrives at the NRL judiciary. Janie Barrett/SMH Ghabar said Hayes did not require a head injury assessment, and the contact to the head was with Doueihi’s bicep – not his shoulder. The first contact, he said, was also with the leg and torso. The panel agreed the contact to the head was “secondary”, and Doueihi tried to steady himself before he tackled Hayes.



Fifita ban adds to Bunnies woes The news for South Sydney somehow got worse on Tuesday evening when David Fifita failed to have a dangerous contact charge downgraded at the judiciary. Already without skipper Cameron Murray (calf), Tallis Duncan (hamstring), and with no clear return date for Latrell Mitchell (calf), the last thing Souths needed was to lose another experienced player like Fifita for Friday’s all-important clash against Melbourne. David Fifita failed in his bid to have a dangerous contact charge downgraded on Tuesday night. Janie Barrett/SMH Fifita landed in hot water for lashing out with his boot into the side of Hudson Young’s head just after half-time last Saturday.



Gyles said the level of carelessness was high, and Canberra backrower Young had no way of protecting himself. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The real NRL ladder, finals race and brutal injury tolls – explained in eight graphics Ghabar argued the tackle was no worse than Tyrell Sloan’s effort on Sam Walker during a 2024 Anzac Day clash. On that occasion, St George Illawarra flyer Sloan was trying to free himself to play the ball, and was hit with a grade-one dangerous contact offence. Ghabar also claimed Fifita’s actions were not intentional, the level of force was “at the bottom end”, and the referee, sideline official and bunker all felt no need to take the matter any further during the actual game. The guilty verdict means Fifita will also be forced to miss the following weeks’ clash against Cronulla. Tom Fletcher was named on the extended bench, but is likely to start in the backrow against the Storm. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Cosmetologists take their cue
World.content:
“Just wondering if Col8-ers have any special travel habits for each new country they visit,” writes Geoff Carey of Pagewood. “Mine is finding a barber to investigate the local nuances of a balding No. 1 buzz cut. My best experience is a tie between the Istanbul barber who denuded every orifice on my head with great intensity and the Omani barber’s pyrotechnic sterilisation of his blades by igniting alcohol, causing a brilliant metre long flame in the air.”

“I’m at my mum’s in The Kitchen that Time Forgot,” says Jo Rainbow, currently of Speen, Midsomer, UK. “Please can your learned readers explain the purpose of a pressure cooker, other than being donated to make Spitfires?” Chocks away!

The punchline challenge (C8) from Suzanne Saunders might just have a winner, in the form of George Manojlovic of Mangerton: “A lost sock and an old fart walk into a bar. Lost sock: I’m looking for a match. Old Fart: For my sake I hope you don’t find one.”

John Elmgreen of Mosman reviews the World Cup: “When Argentina beat England in the semi-final, we had the Argentinians in effect claiming to have reversed the result of the Falklands War. Australia beat Turkey in their opening match – but did Australia claim to have reversed the result of the Gallipoli campaign? Just as well England defeated France in the play-off for third place – otherwise we would have had a claim to reverse Waterloo!”

“The anticlimax of a third-place play-off game has all the lack of excitement, intensity and interest from players, fans and commentators of an exhibition game of a pre-season touring all-star team playing locals,” thinks George Zivkovic of Northmead. “Just give both teams bronze medals and concentrate on the final.”

World.title: ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Craig McRae has opened up about premiership-winning small forward Bobby Hill.

Negotiations continue with Tyson Stengle’s management over his likely exit from Geelong.

Tony Modra has taken to social media to thank the doctors and paramedics who saved his life.

Laura Kane has defended the AFL’s call to host the Australia v Ireland women’s clash at North Sydney Oval.

Chris Scott has heaped praise on assistant coach Nathan Buckley, who lost out on the Tasmania Devils coaching role to Ken Hinkley. ‘A lot of love and care’: McRae’s heartfelt message to premiership star Jon Pierik An emotional Craig McRae says Bobby Hill will forever be a beloved Magpie, as Collingwood and the Norm Smith medallist prepare to split. McRae said on Tuesday he had not seen Hill for some time, the star small forward and father of three dealing with personal issues.



Happier days: Bobby Hill embraces teammate Nick Daicos during a Collingwood training session. Eddie Jim Hill has spent significant time away from the club over the past year, managing only three VFL games this season, and appears certain to part ways with the club. “[I] haven’t seen Bobby in the building for a while, which it’s always something, as a coach, you go, ‘[I] hope the young lad’s going OK ’,” McRae said, his eyes almost welling up. Hill and Craig McRae speak to the media after their side’s famous 2023 premiership win. AFL Photos “If you’re out there, Bobby, we’ve got a lot of love and care for you, and still do, and [we] never, never change, [and] never waver in our love and support for the young man.



“We’re always trying to remain connected, and sometimes [it’s] a bit harder than other times.” Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Buckley at a ‘fork in the road’ after Tassie’s AFL coach call on Hinkley Hill is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal worth about $750,000 per season, league sources say. McRae said he had attempted to contact Hill, who has played 108 games across eight seasons with GWS and the Magpies. “There is an emotion attached to it ... there’s the playing part, the high performance of what he’s capable of doing for our team and for our supporter base, and then there’s the other personal part of, as a father, [you] get emotional thinking about a young man with three kids,” McRae said.



“We want the best for all our players [who have] come into our environment, [to] be good humans, and be a good father and a good husband. Those things that we’re trying to instil , but yeah, environments change and shift, and so [we’ve got] lots of love and care for them [Hill and his family].” The eighth-placed Magpies head to Adelaide for Thursday night’s clash against the Crows on a roll, having won five straight in a stretch of games they had targeted. Now comes a refresh with a new theme, but the Magpies may be without Scott Pendlebury, who could be rested. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making “Howey’s [Jeremy Howe is] back and someone has to go out – [there are] lots of [players in] good form, and players deserve to keep their spot ... I anticipate that ‘Pendles’ plays. That’s probably where it’s going to land,” McRae said. Josh Daicos (ankle) did not train on Tuesday, McRae adding a final call on his fitness could be as late as game time. Howe, the premiership backman, trained strongly and will return. Fellow defender Isaac Quaynor, who had a minor wrist issue in the last quarter against Carlton, is also expected to play.



The Magpies will celebrate Jordan De Goey’s 200th game, McRae saying the robust midfielder was in the best form he had been in during his coaching tenure. De Goey, pushing for All-Australian selection, is contracted until the end of 2027, and is keen on a multi-year extension, league sources say. The Crows, without the suspended Izak Rankine, won by 14 points when the two clubs met at the MCG in round one. Negotiations continue on Tyson Stengle’s Geelong exit Peter Ryan Geelong are continuing negotiations with premiership forward Tyson Stengle’s management to potentially wind up the 27-year-old’s time at the Cats with three years still remaining on his contract.



Stengle has not played an AFL game this season after a tumultuous pre-season, and although he was able to make a strong return to the VFL mid-season, he has not played since kicking four goals against the Gold Coast in round 12. View post on X There have been discussions about Stengle’s future since Christmas, and he took leave during January. The Cats have been discussing Stengle’s contract position for several months, and where the parties stood in relation to the contract that extends until 2029. Cats skipper Patrick Dangerfield told Fox Footy he was not privy to the contract discussions but as the captain of the club, and Stengle’s premiership teammate, he was just concerned that he is being supported. Tyson Stengle celebrates kicking a goal last season. Cameron Spencer



“What the future holds there, I am certainly uncertain of, but as a friend of his, and as captain, I look at it more [as a question of] ‘have we got the right support in place?’, of which I have no doubt we do and for me, footy isn’t really the ultimate priority there,” Dangerfield said. Stengle made a remarkable return to football at the Cats in 2022, winning a flag and being named All-Australian as a small forward. He kicked 53 goals in the premiership year, including four in the grand final win over Sydney. He has kicked 175 goals in 109 games with the Cats, Adelaide and Richmond. Modra ‘humbled’ by support after near-fatal accident Andrew Wu Adelaide goal-kicking great Tony Modra has thanked the doctors and paramedics who saved his life, in a heartfelt social media post.



Modra took to Instagram on Tuesday to express his gratitude to those who wished him well in the immediate aftermath to his near-fatal accident last month. The former Crows superstar revealed he had several titanium plates inserted into his face to “put me back together” during extensive facial surgery after the truck he was driving crashed into a tree that had fallen across the road. Tony Modra has posted a photo of himself and family after recovering from a truck accident in June. Instagram Former teammate Mark Ricciuto had quipped Modra, a glamour forward in the 1990s, may not retain his model looks after the accident, but he showed few visible signs of his injuries in a picture he shared on social media of him with his wife Erica and their two children, Luke and Hayley.



“Still as handsome as ever,” former Crows captain Rory Sloane wrote. There were grave fears for Tony Modra after a truck accident in June. Instagram Modra paid tribute to the SA Ambulance Service, the South Coast District Hospital and the Flinders Medical Centre for saving his life. “I’m getting out and about a bit now, and slowly catching up on everything I missed over the last month,” Modra wrote. “I’m so humbled to learn how many people were cheering these incredible medical teams on … and our family too. I’ll never be able to thank everyone enough.” Loading



The football world was in shock when news broke of Modra’s accident during the telecast of the game between one of his former clubs, Fremantle, and Geelong about five weeks ago. Renowned for his high-flying marks, Modra was one of the biggest stars of the game in the 1990s when forwards ruled. He burst onto the scene in 1993 when he booted 129 goals in 23 games, including finals, but was beaten for the Coleman Medal by Geelong great Gary Ablett, who kicked 124 goals in the home-and-away season. Modra finished with 588 goals from 165 games with Adelaide and Fremantle, and sits second on the Crows’ all-time goals list with 440, behind Taylor Walker. AFLW players Georgie Prespakis, Taylah Gatt, Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw and Sophie McKay. AFL Photos



Why pubs and Irish expats are behind the call not to move sold-out clash Danny Russell AFLW boss Laura Kane has defended a decision not to shift the competition’s looming international match to a bigger stadium, despite the game’s boutique venue, North Sydney Oval, selling out. The league has come under fire from fans and past players for not opening up the first-ever Irish-Australia women’s clash on August 1 to a larger live audience by relocating it to the SCG. The intimate North Sydney Oval holds fewer than 10,000 people.



But Kane said the league had monitored ticket sales and waiting lists to inform their decision. Related Article AFLW ‘Something in the water’: The massive footy boom Ireland didn’t see coming “When we announced this game, we wanted to create an amazing atmosphere, and so a sellout is incredible,” Kane said on Tuesday. “Do I want to be, you know, in future talking about the MCG, the SCG or Marvel Stadium? Absolutely, I do, and we will get there. “But for now, our priority is making sure that we have a packed-out stadium, and we are going to get that with North Sydney Oval.



“It’s such a great place to play footy, and really, it comes down to the data. What does the data tell us around what our fans want to do? When it tells us that we can fill the SCG, we’ll play there.” Laura Kane at the AFLW season launch. AFL Photos Instead of seeking a bigger venue, the league opted to work with Sydney pubs to set up fan zones for the city’s large Irish ex-pat community to watch the game. There are no AFL matches fixtured in Sydney that weekend. Former Carlton and Brisbane Lions star Lauren Arnell called the decision “baffling”.



“You’re already telling people two weeks out, ‘You can’t come’,” the former Port Adelaide coach told the ABC. “I just feel like you are limiting the game.” But Kane, the AFL’s executive general manager of AFLW, health and football operations said the league had turned its attention towards attracting a larger TV audience once the stadium sold out. “We want people watching it in their lounge rooms. We want people watching it at restaurants, at pubs, at venues all over the country – not just in Sydney,” she said. The AFLW season starts on August 9 when St Kilda and Carlton clash as part of an AFL double-header at Marvel Stadium, which coincides with ‘Spud’s Game’, held in memory of Saints great Danny Frawley and to raise money for and awareness of mental health.



Kane said the AFL was continually looking to reduce the number of AFLW venues, having already cut ground numbers from 38 to 27, and had done away with computer chips for ball-tracking technology. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Ben Long ban slashed to one-match for heavy Maynard bump; New video review system for AFLW “We want to make sure that we have the best technology available for both of our competitions, AFL and AFLW … and we felt that the time was right to evolve to vision and video review,” she said. “Both Greg Swann and I are looking at, ‘What does optical tracking look like?’, in the context of all venues that we play at, notwithstanding that there’s a few extra W venues that we play footy at. “What is the long-term solution? At the moment, the best technology that we feel [is] available for score review is video and the video review system, but it’s always something that we’re looking at improving.”



‘He would have been a great Tasmanian coach’: Scott’s praise for Buckley Danny Russell Chris Scott says his decorated assistant Nathan Buckley will escape any negative perception that is usually associated with applicants missing out on senior coaching jobs. Buckley joined the Geelong coaching panel at the start of this season to enhance his chances of landing the Tasmania Devils role. Nathan Buckley missed out to Ken Hinkley on the Tasmania Devils coaching job. Getty Images



But the fledgling club announced this week it had overlooked the Collingwood great for Ken Hinkley. “I suspect if Tassie get the opportunity to talk publicly about him, they would say similar things to me, ‘He was an outstanding candidate and would have been a great Tasmanian coach, but the fit wasn’t quite as good as the other guy’, who just happens to be one who coached for 15 years in the AFL, or thereabouts” Scott said. “There’s no shame in running, I don’t know whether he ran second, but let’s assume he ran second to Ken Hinkley – there’s no shame in that.” Loading The Geelong coach said Buckley’s willingness to publicly announce his interest in the Tasmanian position spoke to “how secure he is in his ability, and his position in the game”.



“It seems to me that it is quite rare that a coach puts their hand up and says, ‘This is something that I want, and I’m prepared to go through the process’,” Scott said. “He didn’t only go through the process, he went back to work, which, obviously, has been a real positive for us. “I suspect it won’t happen that much, so if you like his way of going about it, make the most of it now because I don’t think you will see it too often.” Scott said it was less likely younger candidates would put themselves on the line in the same manner as Buckley. Loading



“The likelihood for all the candidates for these positions is that you are probably going to miss, irrespective of how good a job you do,” he said. “Inevitably, the kind of perception could be, ‘Well, there must have been a good reason why someone didn’t get the job’. “I think the reality is more likely that you could actually be a fantastic candidate, you are just not the right fit for that point in time. “But again, the perception of that can hurt, in particular young coaches. In that context, I am certain that the negative perception won’t apply to ‘Bucks’.” Buckley, who coached Collingwood to the 2018 grand final, said missing out on the Tasmanian gig had left him at a “fork in the road”.



He has all but ruled out applying for the vacant Carlton and Essendon roles. “I haven’t really reflected on where those roles sit and I don’t think I would enter those processes,” Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night. “I’m absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out. I was committed to that [Tasmania job], and that ended a day ago. “The future there [at the Cats] for me will inform my next step in footy. I probably wouldn’t have come back [to AFL coaching] in unless I’d looked at Tassie, so it’s a fork in the road. “I’m really grateful for where I’m at, rather than maybe just being on the couch, [having spent] five years in media, without really knowing what I was doing with footy.



“But now that I’m back in a club, I don’t know what’s next.” Buckley said Devils CEO Brendon Gale informed him of their decision to appoint Hinkley on Sunday afternoon. “I think it’s taken me a little bit of time to reflect because I was really keen on it. I was in on it,” he said. “I texted back [to Gale] that, ‘I’m disappointed, but thanks for letting me know’. “I’ll come back around and touch base in time [with Tasmania, for some feedback] because it’s obviously a busy time for the Devils.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth developer tells defamation trial WA government called on him to solve ‘headache’ Holly Thompson July 21, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth property developer has taken the stand on the second day of a defamation trial more than seven years in the making, telling the WA Supreme Court the state government called on him to help with the removal of soil from a major infrastructure project. Strzelecki Group chairman Greg Poland and his daughter Jennifer Poland, who is also the managing director of the company, both gave evidence about allegations published by this masthead in 2019 regarding his role in trying to secure a deal with the state government to dump millions of tonnes of “toxic soil” from the Forrestfield Airport site in the Peel region. Greg Poland arriving at David Malcolm Justice Centre for his court case against WAtoday/Nine Publishing. Colin Murty A second article published a day later and also included in the proceedings alleged Mr Poland had claimed an attempt to increase WA’s lobster catch was his plan, but the government had “botched it”. The articles were based on covert recordings taken without Mr Poland’s consent at a meeting at the Subiaco Hotel, which he attended as part of his role as deputy chairman of the Peel Development Commission, but which he claims was a private meeting.



One of Mr Poland’s key contentions was that the soil was not toxic and should not have been labelled as such, with his lawyer Martin Bennett telling the court on Monday that a publicly available document and a background note from then-fisheries minister Dave Kelly’s office both supported the claim it was not toxic. On the stand on Tuesday, Mr Poland said he was told the cost of moving the soil from the Forrestfield Airport site was up to $300 million, and was a headache the state government had asked him to help resolve. “There were two million tonnes on the airport land, and they wanted it gone,” he said. In the recording of the meeting, Mr Poland can allegedly be heard telling a local business owner they could acquire a parcel of land in Myalup without going to tender, if they facilitated the dumping of “between two and eight tonnes” of soil from the Forrestfield Airport to his land in Waroona. Mr Poland told the court on Tuesday all he was trying to do was to get something down in writing that the government could work with.



Bennett asked if Mr Poland knew the meeting was being recorded, and if he would consent to it being recorded if he had been asked, to which he responded: “No.” Related Article Courts Andrew Hastie in court as businessman sues over ‘toxic soil’ claims “Why would I? It was a private meeting,” he said. Mr Poland said he had to work with government ministers, and he did not want them reading or seeing comments from an official meeting “saying they are useless shits”. Earlier on Tuesday, Mr Poland’s daughter Jennifer Poland was questioned over why her father had asked for note-taking to stop during the meeting.



She said he had invoked Chatham House Rules, because he was going to give his opinion on what minister would do a good job, and what departments would do a good job. “He didn’t want those comments going back to ministers because he had to work with them,” Ms Poland said. After receiving questions from a journalist at this masthead based on the recordings of the meeting, Mr Poland told the court he spoke with then-regional development minister Alannah MacTiernan about the allegations. “If its politics they [journalists] keep coming after you,” Mr Poland said MacTiernan had told him. “She told me, ‘I’ve accepted your resignation already [from the Peel Development Commission], that stops it’.”



Discussing the second story published, Mr Poland told the court he had mentioned the idea of licensing boats to catch lobsters for the domestic market at a Labor roundtable with then-premier Mark McGowan, and other ministers, who told him they loved the idea. Mr Poland claimed then-fisheries minister Kelly was also supportive of the proposal. The state government then released the report WA’s Western Rock Lobster Plan - Industry growth plan to create jobs. “I don’t like the way they took the idea and changed it, so the government owned the licences,” Mr Poland told the court. But he said the government had reached out to him asking for a public statement of support, which he supplied.



Mr Poland was then cross-examined by Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis, who asked whether he would agree the Peel region was cherished for its ecological significance. “They wouldn’t allow that level of mining and destruction there if it was all cherished,” Mr Poland replied. Questioned on the number of times he had met with the landowner he was discussing the deal with, Mr Poland said the Peel Development Commission chairman had largely been dealing with him and the plans regarding the transfer of the sand. Developer ‘angry’ over journalists’ questions Ms Poland said her father had been “very angry” when he first received questions from journalists, allegedly saying: “All I’ve tried to do is help.”



After the initial article was published, she said her father could not believe it was happening, or why ministers quoted in the article had “said what they had”. “He said, ‘They know me, they know my deal’,” Ms Poland recalled. “He was destroyed by it.” Ms Poland reached out to Bennett after her father received questions from this masthead, and the lawyer sent a letter to journalists before the publication of both stories. It was over these letters, and her recount of events, that Ms Poland was questioned by Nine’s lawyer Martin Goldblatt.



A letter sent to the journalists from Bennett on behalf of the Polands categorised the soil as “toxic” or “contaminated” several times. However, Ms Poland argued there were different levels of “contaminated” when asked why, if she believed that to be incorrect, she had approved the letter being sent. She also argued many of the direct quotes, taken from the recording at the Subiaco Hotel, were out of context and that her father often spoke a certain way due to his dyslexia. The trial continues, with Mr Poland expected to return to the stand tomorrow. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Sunshine Coast ‘freebirth’ baby could have survived, coroner finds
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPregnancy Sunshine Coast ‘freebirth’ baby could have survived, coroner finds Courtney Kruk July 21, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A baby that died from complications during a free birth on the Sunshine Coast would have likely survived with timely medical care, a coroner’s court has heard, with an expert calling for women’s birth trauma to be taken seriously to prevent disengagement with conventional systems. The baby girl – referred to as “Baby M” in the investigation – was “free birthed” on October 20, 2024. Freebirths take place outside the hospital or medical system, usually at home, with no medical professional present. Baby M, as she was referred to in the Queensland Coroners Court, died from asphyxia during a freebirth. Michele Mossop The coroner was told that Baby M’s mother was traumatised by the birth of her first child, which was delivered by emergency caesarean section in 2021 following an abnormal heart rate reading.



She subsequently suffered two miscarriages – at four and 10 weeks – and wanted to try for a vaginal birth at home for her second child, initially with a midwife present. Related Article Pregnancy The reason why some Queensland women are opting for unassisted births The court was told that a private midwife was engaged, but Baby M’s mother declined recommended ultrasound scans and glucose tolerance tests. At about 30 weeks, she dismissed the midwife for financial reasons and instead made plans to carry out a free birth at home with her partner. Baby M’s mother went into labour on the afternoon of October 20, 2024. A friend was contacted a few hours later “to come over to support and help”. Baby M was born at approximately 11.40pm. She was noted to be “hypotonic, pale with nil spontaneous limb movements nor attempts at crying”, Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher said.



A friend of the family – an off-duty paramedic – was called for help, arriving a short time later with a neonatal valve bag mask and an oxygen cylinder. Baby M apparently regained a heartbeat while being resuscitated. An ambulance arrived at 12.13am and took Baby M to Sunshine Coast University Hospital. Despite the efforts of paramedics and hospital staff, Baby M’s condition did not improve, and a decision was made to cease resuscitation efforts. Baby M was declared dead at 2.42am on October 21.



An autopsy determined her death was caused by meconium aspiration syndrome – when a newborn inhales a mixture of their first stool and amniotic fluid, usually after becoming distressed. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Inside freebirthing: Empowerment, distrust and a growing dogma Gallagher said if Baby M had been “delivered with the support of skilled personnel, an earlier identification of fetal distress and timely delivery with appropriate neonatal care and support would likely have prevented severe asphyxia resulting in neonatal death”. Associate Professor Renuka Sekar, an expert in obstetric and maternal fetal medicine who reviewed the case, said appropriate care and advice was offered by the private midwife and the hospital team. She said the case highlighted the real consequences of birth trauma.





That inquest has been paused to consider new evidence. Gallagher decided against holding an inquest into Baby M’s death and offered condolences to the family for their loss. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ben King set to leave the Suns for Hawks in a stunning about-face
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 Ben King set to leave the Suns for Hawks in a stunning about-face Sam McClure July 21, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ben King is poised to complete one of the most dramatic contract backflips in recent AFL history, with the Gold Coast spearhead set to reject the Suns’ lucrative long-term offer and instead nominate Hawthorn as his preferred destination for 2027. The stunning change of heart comes barely two months after King told The Age he intended to remain on the Gold Coast, insisting he loved the club and saw his future in Queensland. Ben King wants to play for Hawthorn next season. AFL Photos But three industry sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity because discussions remain confidential, have confirmed King’s position has shifted significantly in recent weeks, with Hawthorn now firmly in the box seat to secure one of the competition’s premier key forwards. King’s contract at Hawthorn is expected to be a six-year deal, taking him until the end of 2032.



Gold Coast have not yet officially been told of his intention to leave. King will be in Melbourne this week ahead of the Suns’ game against Carlton at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star The decision is a bitter blow for the Suns, who had been confident they would retain the 26-year-old despite intense Victorian interest and had tabled a massive long-term contract in a bid to keep him at the club. Several factors have contributed to King’s dramatic reversal. His partner is keen to return home to Victoria, while Gold Coast’s alarming on-field slide has also weighed heavily. The Suns have now lost eight consecutive matches after appearing well-placed to challenge for a second-consecutive finals campaign earlier this season.



King’s own form has only enhanced his value. The powerful key forward sits second in the Coleman Medal race and has established himself as one of the AFL’s most reliable goalkickers, kicking at least 40 goals in every completed season since 2021. Last year he produced a career-best campaign with 71 goals, underlining why Hawthorn have been prepared to aggressively pursue his signature. How the trade period plays out is yet to be determined. As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast have the power to match the bid and force a trade. But given the Suns’ disastrous form slump has now landed them 14th on the ladder, the Queensland club could opt to accept first-round compensation, which, if the season finished now, would be pick No.6.



The Hawks would much prefer to land King without a trade, given they are also in the box seat to land Essendon’s Zach Merrett, who will once again request a move to Hawthorn despite a failed move last year. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Hawthorn want Ben King and Zach Merrett. This is how Gold Coast losses help their cause For Hawthorn, landing King would represent another significant statement of intent as the club continues to build a list capable of challenging for premierships over the coming years. However, his arrival would also create a fascinating list-management dilemma. Mitch Lewis, who reminded the competition of his quality with a five-goal performance on the weekend, is also out of contract and now faces an uncertain future. Lewis has battled injury over the past two seasons but remains one of the league’s most talented key-position forwards when fit.



Whether Hawthorn believe they can accommodate both King and Lewis in the same forward line, or whether King’s impending arrival accelerates Lewis’ departure, looms as one of the major questions heading into the trade and free-agency period. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 How the Pies can avoid wildcard round, as we rate every team’s run home The Hawks have invested heavily in assembling one of the AFL’s youngest and most exciting lists under Sam Mitchell, and adding a proven goal kicking machine entering the prime of his career would significantly strengthen their premiership aspirations. For Gold Coast, meanwhile, losing a home-grown marquee player after years of investment would be another devastating retention blow. The Suns have long viewed King as a cornerstone of their future, but after months of confidence they would secure his signature, they are now confronting the prospect of watching one of the competition’s elite key forwards walk out the door.



If it results in a move, King’s decision would rank among the most extraordinary contract reversals in recent AFL memory – a player who only weeks ago expected to stay, now preparing to head home to Victoria and reshape the landscape of the upcoming trade period. King’s management has been contacted for comment. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: As a 40-year ALP member, I now question party’s integrity
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters As a 40-year ALP member, I now question party’s integrity July 21, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. VICTORIA As a Labor member for nearly 40 years, I never imagined I would struggle to support the party at an election. Yet, today I find myself deeply unsettled by what appears to be a pattern of avoidance, poor judgment, and troubling optics from the current leadership.

The refusal to call a royal commission into the Big Build — despite persistent concerns about governance and culture — is indefensible. To claim royal commissions “don’t change culture” is a furphy; most since the Costigan commission in the 1970s have done exactly that.

The (federal) Heydon royal commission into union corruption cited by the premier is an outlier.

No existing agency appears equipped to fully investigate these matters, making the government’s position even harder to justify.

For the first time in decades, I am questioning whether Labor still reflects the standards of integrity and leadership I have long supported.

To restore confidence, a royal commission into the Victorian Big Build should be initiated without delay.

Gary March, Elwood Premier needs to resign to save her best work

Premier Jacinta Allan has much to answer for. Consequently, her best work in partnership with First Nations people to deliver Victoria’s statewide Treaty in 2025, now recognised as “one of the most defining moments in Australia’s history since invasion” (″⁣Treaty negotiators win human rights award despite uncertainty over landmark document″⁣, 21/7 ) is under real and present threat.

The alternative coalition government, led by Jess Wilson, has committed to axe Treaty within 100 days of being elected. There is zero chance that a rising One Nation from the comfort of its new parliamentary seats would do anything but support this backward-looking wave of neo-colonialism.

Victorians have clearly had enough of Premier Allan. But to toss out Treaty and the promise that the First Peoples’ Assembly offers us and future generations should not be the price we all have to pay to see her gone.

Jean Ker Walsh, Richmond



Government seemingly incurious of cost spikes

The Victorian premier has recently stated of the big build investigations on “these new patterns of criminal behaviour being driven by too much organised crime” within the industry (‴⁣⁣Extraordinary, unforeseeable’ and extremely costly: CFMEU pricetag of each Metro station revealed”, 21/7).

Once again, Allan has failed to acknowledge any suggestion that such behaviour was driven by opportunities arising from an apathetic government, unwilling or unable to deal with suspected and sometimes obvious criminality, while seemingly barely even curious as to how costs blew out to such an unacceptable level.

It is also disconcerting that, as the former Big Build boss, she gets to set the agenda for how this alleged criminality is investigated.

Stephen Farrelly, Donvale Clear out the bad apples

The corruption re the Big Build and the money wasted is appalling. One hopes that the new CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby can clean out the union and remove all the bad apples (‴⁣⁣Idiots in Victoria’ holding back CFMEU: Administrator blasts former union bosses, demands reform″⁣, 20/7).

Christine Hammett, Richmond ALP national conference an orchestrated event

It’s a sad story for ALP voters and members that the Labor Party’s national conference will turn out to be an orchestrated exercise in which the ALP government and its weigh-in with full control.

This is unlike in western and northern Europe, where full membership of a political party has participating democratic voting rights to determine their party’s manifesto. Australia must change.

Henk van Leeuwen, Elsternwick THE FORUM



Joyce under pressure

Is Barnaby Joyce on another sinking ship?

After abandoning the Liberal/National coalition for the One Nation party, he now finds himself having to defend the indefensible. Anyone who watched him being interviewed on the ABC’s 7.30 on Monday night must ask if Joyce is uncomfortable having to defend his leader’s antics in England and justify her holidaying in Italy.

Yelling at the dog is usually a sign that you are under pressure. Joyce needs to decide what are his political convictions. What do you really stand for, Barnaby?

Marisa Di Giacomo, Beaumaris British didn’t assimilate

How ironic that Pauline Hanson of so-called One Nation is accusing migrants of the very thing that her ancestors and ours perpetrated on First Nations people. She accuses migrants of not assimilating. Neither did the British colonialists. The new “Australians″⁣ refused to speak the native dialect(s), refused to hunt with spears and gather and engage in practices like fish traps.

They did not socialise with the Indigenous people. They spoke English at home. They vowed allegiance to England.

How First Nations people would have liked to deport the new settlers. (“Joyce backs Hanson’s call for deportations of immigrants”, 21/7),

Jan Marshall, Brighton Migration, not so simple

Migration is a far more complex subject than your correspondent (Letters, 21/7) portrays. Consider the Afghan cameleers who dug the dams, put up the telephone poles and helped build the inland roads. Without that legendary contribution, Australia’s 20th century economy wouldn’t have soared “on the sheep’s back”, enabling post-World War II migrants from conflict-shattered Europe to find the prolific opportunity here.

The Afghans were Muslim, not “Judeo-Christian”, and were respected for their values. Today, we have The Ghan in their honour.

Also, generalisations about recent “migrant incompatibility with our culture, leading to criminal activity and antisemitism” conflict with the University of Sydney’s findings that, regrettably, antisemitism has been traced across the political spectrum to the late 1800s.
